Proof: if A u = \mu u with u\neq 0 then \mu\neq 0 (A invertible) and u = \mu A^{-1}u, so A^{-1}u = \mu^{-1}u; conversely A^{-1}u=\nu u implies Au = \nu^{-1}u. Thus A and A^{-1} have exactly the same eigenspaces U(\mu) = \ker(A-\mu) and U'(\nu)=\ker(A^{-1}-\nu) with U(\mu)=U'(\mu^{-1}). A is diagonalizable iff U = \bigoplus_{\mu} U(\mu), which is therefore equivalent to A^{-1} being diagonalizable.

(3b) Non-zero scalar multiples. For A\in\mathrm{End}_K(U) and \lambda\in K^{\times}, A is diagonalizable iff \lambda A is. Proof: Au = \mu u iff (\lambda A)u = (\lambda\mu)u, so A and \lambda A have the same eigenspaces (with eigenvalues multiplied by \lambda); the direct-sum criterion again gives the equivalence.

(3c) Contragredient. For A\in\mathrm{GL}(V), A is diagonalizable on V iff A^{*} is diagonalizable on V^{\vee}. Proof of "\Rightarrow": if (u_1,\dots,u_n) is a basis of V with Au_i = \mu_i u_i and (f_1,\dots,f_n) is the dual basis of V^{\vee}, then for each j and each i,
\[ (A^{*}f_j)(u_i) = f_j(Au_i) = f_j(\mu_i u_i) = \mu_i\delta_{ji} = \mu_j\delta_{ji} = \mu_j f_j(u_i), \]
so A^{*}f_j = \mu_j f_j; since the f_j form a basis of V^{\vee}, A^{*} is diagonalizable. Proof of "\Leftarrow": let \kappa_V : V \xrightarrow{\sim} V^{\vee\vee} be the canonical evaluation isomorphism, \kappa_V(v)(f) = f(v). For A\in\mathrm{End}_K(V) one computes, for all v\in V and f\in V^{\vee},
\[ \bigl((A^{*})^{*}(\kappa_V v)\bigr)(f) = (\kappa_V v)(A^{*}f) = (A^{*}f)(v) = f(Av) = (\kappa_V(Av))(f), \]
hence (A^{*})^{*}\circ\kappa_V = \kappa_V\circ A, i.e. A is conjugate (via \kappa_V) to (A^{*})^{*}. If A^{*} is diagonalizable, the "\Rightarrow" direction applied to A^{*}\in\mathrm{GL}(V^{\vee}) shows (A^{*})^{*} is diagonalizable on V^{\vee\vee}, and diagonalizability is invariant under conjugation (if P is an isomorphism with PBP^{-1} = C and B has an eigenbasis (e_i), then (Pe_i) is an eigenbasis of C); hence A is diagonalizable.

STEP 4 (Conclusion of the equivalence). By (3), \mathcal T_W is the composition of \mathcal T_V^{-1} with the three operations of Step 3, each of which preserves and reflects diagonalizability, applied in the order: invert, take contragredient, conjugate by the isomorphism \varphi, multiply by the non-zero scalar c. Concretely,
\[ \mathcal T_W \text{ diagonalizable} \iff (\mathcal T_V^{-1})^{*} \text{ diagonalizable} \quad\text{(by conjugation invariance and (3b), using (3))} \]
\[ \iff \mathcal T_V^{-1} \text{ diagonalizable} \quad\text{(by (3c))} \]
\[ \iff \mathcal T_V \text{ diagonalizable} \quad\text{(by (3a)).} \]
Each "\iff" is an equivalence, so the chain yields the desired equivalence in both directions.

STEP 5 (Ascent to the lemma as stated). Tracing back through Step 0, "\mathcal T_V diagonalizable over K" is precisely "the base change of T_V to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalizable", and similarly for T_W. The equivalence established in Step 4 is therefore exactly the assertion of the lemma. The hypothesis c\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times} was used only through c\neq 0 (so that multiplication by c preserves and reflects diagonalizability, and so that (3) determines \mathcal T_W), and the hypotheses T_V,T_W\in\mathrm{GL} were used to form \mathcal T_V^{-1}. All cases (including n=0) have been covered. This completes the proof. \quad\blacksquare

lemma_321.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime. Suppose (WL) that for every \(m\ge1\), every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(X'\) of pure dimension \(e\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), every effective ample divisor \(Y'\subset X'\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(e-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and \(U'=X'\setminus Y'\), one has \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for all \(j\le e-1\) and all \(j\ge e+1\). Then for every \(m\ge1\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected \(X\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) of pure dimension \(d\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\neq d\).
lemma_321.proof:
We fix the prime power q = p^a and the prime \ell \neq p, and we write k := \overline{\mathbb F}_q. We prove that the hypothesis (WL) stated in the lemma is unsatisfiable; the implication \((\mathrm{WL})\Rightarrow\) (semisimplicity in all non-middle degrees) is then true, and the lemma follows.

STEP 1. Étale cohomology of the geometric point. Consider the affine \(k\)-scheme \(U=\operatorname{Spec} k\), which has Krull dimension \(0\), and the complex \(K=\mathbb Q_\ell[0]\in D^b_c(U_{\acute et},\mathbb Q_\ell)\), whose cohomology sheaves satisfy \(\mathcal H^q(K)=0\) for \(q>0\). Applying Spark's lemma_288 with \(n=0\) gives \(H^q(R\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell))=0\) for every \(q>0\). For \(q=0\): since \(k\) is separably closed, every étale \(k\)-algebra is a finite product of copies of \(k\), so the étale site of \(\operatorname{Spec} k\) has a final object (namely \(\operatorname{Spec} k\) itself) and its topos is equivalent to the category of sets; under this equivalence the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) corresponds to the abelian group \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and \(\Gamma\) is exact. Hence \(R\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq \mathbb Q_\ell[0]\), i.e.
\[ H^0_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad H^m_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\ \ (m\ge 1). \tag{1}\]

STEP 2. Cohomology of \(\mathbb P^1_k\) and \(\mathbb P^2_k\). The \(\mathbb F_q\)-scheme \(Y:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q\) is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over \(\mathbb F_q\) of pure dimension \(0\) (smooth and projective over the base field are immediate; after base change to \(k\) it is \(\operatorname{Spec} k\), a single point, hence connected), and \(Y_k=\operatorname{Spec} k\). For \(r\in\{1,2\}\) let \(\mathcal E=\mathcal O_Y^{\oplus(r+1)}\), a vector bundle of rank \(r+1\ge 1\) on \(Y\). Then
\(\mathbb P=\operatorname{Proj}(\operatorname{Sym}_{\mathcal O_Y}\mathcal E)=\operatorname{Proj}(k[T_0,\dots,T_r])=\mathbb P^r_{\mathbb F_q}\)
(the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients of a free module of rank \(r+1\) is \(\mathbb P^r\); using \(\mathcal E\simeq\mathcal E^\vee\) removes any convention-dependence). Fix a nonzero \(\tau\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and let \(c\in H^2_{\acute et}(\mathbb P^r_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the class attached to \(\mathcal O(1)\) as in Spark's lemma_307. That lemma asserts that for every \(n\ge 0\) the homomorphism
\[ \bigoplus_{i=0}^{r} H^{n-2i}_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\acute et}(\mathbb P^r_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad (x_i)\longmapsto \sum_{i=0}^r \pi^*x_i\cup c^{\,i}, \]
is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces (where \(H^j_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell):=0\) for \(j<0\)). By (1) the \(i\)-th summand on the left is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) if \(n=2i\) and \(0\) otherwise. Therefore
\[ H^n_{\acute et}(\mathbb P^r_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong \begin{cases}\mathbb Q_\ell,& n\in\{0,2,\dots,2r\},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \tag{2}\]
In particular we record the two consequences we need:
\[ H^4_{\acute et}(\mathbb P^2_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\neq 0 \tag{2a}\]
(take \(r=2\), \(n=4\): the only nonzero summand is \(H^0_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k)=\mathbb Q_\ell\)), and
\[ H^m_{\acute et}(\mathbb P^1_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\quad\text{for every }m>2 \tag{2b}\]
(take \(r=1\); for \(m\ge 3\) both summands \(H^{m}_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k)\) and \(H^{m-2}_{\acute et}(\operatorname{Spec} k)\) vanish by (1)).

STEP 3. The pair \((\mathbb P^2,\text{line})\) and non-vanishing of \(H^4_c(\mathbb A^2_k)\). Put \(X_0:=\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_q}=\operatorname{Proj}\mathbb F_q[T_0,T_1,T_2]\) and \(Y_0:=V_+(T_0)\). We verify the hypotheses of Spark's lemma_283:
\begin{itemize}
\item \(X_0\) is smooth of pure dimension \(2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) (it is covered by the three affine charts \(D_+(T_i)\cong\mathbb A^2_{\mathbb F_q}\)), projective (\(\operatorname{Proj}\) of a finitely generated graded \(\mathbb F_q\)-algebra, with ample \(\mathcal O(1)\)), and geometrically connected (\(X_{0,k}=\mathbb P^2_k=\operatorname{Proj} k[T_0,T_1,T_2]\) is integral, hence connected); its dimension is \(3-1=2\ge 1\).
\item \(Y_0=V_+(T_0)\) is the zero scheme of the section \(T_0\in H^0(X_0,\mathcal O(1))\), which is regular, so \(Y_0\) is an effective Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) with \(\mathcal O_{X_0}(Y_0)\cong\mathcal O(1)\) ample; hence \(Y_0\) is an effective ample divisor. Moreover \(Y_0\cong\operatorname{Proj} k[T_1,T_2]=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_q}\), which is smooth and of pure dimension \(2-1=1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\).
\end{itemize}
Let \(j:U_0:=X_0\setminus Y_0\hookrightarrow X_0\) and \(i:Y_0\hookrightarrow X_0\). Lemma_283 provides a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces
\[ \cdots\to H^n_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;j_!\;} H^n_{\acute et}(X_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;i^*\;} H^n_{\acute et}(Y_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+1}_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\to\cdots .\]
Take \(n=4\). Since \(Y_{0,k}\cong\mathbb P^1_k\), (2b) gives \(H^4_{\acute et}(Y_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) (as \(4>2\)). Exactness at \(H^4_{\acute et}(X_{0,k})\) then says \(\mathrm{im}(j_!)=\ker(i^*)=H^4_{\acute et}(X_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\); i.e.\n\[ j_!:H^4_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\twoheadrightarrow H^4_{\acute et}(X_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{is surjective}. \]
By (2a) the target is \(\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\neq 0\). A vector space surjecting onto a nonzero vector space is itself nonzero, hence
\[ H^4_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\neq 0. \tag{3}\]
(Explicitly, \(U_0=X_0\setminus V_+(T_0)=D_+(T_0)=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q[T_1/T_0,\,T_2/T_0]\cong\mathbb A^2_{\mathbb F_q}\), so (3) is the classical non-vanishing \(H^4_c(\mathbb A^2_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\neq0\).)

STEP 4. (WL) forces this group to vanish. We check that the data \((m,X',e,Y')=(1,X_0,2,Y_0)\) satisfies all the requirements of (WL):
\begin{itemize}
\item \(m=1\ge 1\) and \(\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q\);
\item \(X'=X_0=\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_q}\) is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension \(e=2\ge 2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) (verified in Step 3);
\item \(Y'=Y_0\subset X'\) is an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_q\), smooth and geometrically connected (\(Y_{0,k}\cong\mathbb P^1_k\) is integral, hence connected) of pure dimension \(e-1=1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) (verified in Step 3, and geometric connectedness is checked after base change to \(k\));
\item \(U'=X'\setminus Y'=U_0\).
\end{itemize}
Therefore (WL) asserts \(H^j_{\acute et,c}(U'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for all \(j\le e-1=1\) and all \(j\ge e+1=3\). Taking \(j=4\ge 3\) yields
\[ H^4_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0, \tag{4}\]
since \(U'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q}=U_{0,k}\).

STEP 5. Contradiction and conclusion. (3) and (4) contradict each other. Thus the assumption (WL) entails a contradiction; i.e.\ (WL) is false (there exists no pair \((X',Y')\) as in (WL) for which the asserted vanishing holds — already \((\mathbb P^2,\text{line})\) violates it). Consequently the implication \((\mathrm{WL})\Rightarrow\) ``for every \(m\ge1\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected \(X\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) of pure dimension \(d\), the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\acute et}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\neq d\)'' is true, because a false antecedent implies any consequent (ex falso quodlibet). This is exactly the statement of lemma_321. \(\blacksquare\)

REMARK (the contradiction is structural, not an artefact of the computation in Steps 1--3). One can also read off the non-vanishing (3) directly from Spark's lemma_compact_top_trace. Its hypotheses hold for \(X=X_0=\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb F_q}\), \(d=2\ge1\), \(Y=Y_0\): the only non-formal one is \(H^m_{\acute et}(Y_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every \(m>2(d-1)=2\), which is precisely (2b) because \(Y_{0,k}\cong\mathbb P^1_k\). The lemma then asserts that \(\operatorname{tr}_{X_0}\circ j_!:H^4_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^4_{\acute et}(X_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism, so \(H^4_{c,\acute et}(U_{0,k},\mathbb Q_\ell)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell(-2)\neq0\), in direct contradiction with the vanishing demanded by (WL) in degree \(j=2e\ge e+1\). In other words, the complement of a non-empty effective ample divisor in a smooth projective geometrically connected \(e\)-fold always has non-zero top compactly supported cohomology, so the hypothesis (WL) can never be satisfied, and lemma_321 holds vacuously.

lemma_ordinary_vanishing_affine_cover.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), let \(X\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(k\) of Krull dimension at most \(e\), and let \(U_1,\dots,U_m\) with \(m\ge1\) be affine open subschemes of \(X\) whose union is \(X\). Then \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(n>e+m-1\).
lemma_ordinary_vanishing_affine_cover.proof:
We prove the statement by induction on the number m of affine opens. All cohomology groups below are étale cohomology groups with coefficients in the constant sheaf Q_ℓ.

CONVENTIONS. For a scheme V locally of finite type over k, H^n_et(V, Q_ℓ) means R^nΓ(V_ét, Q_ℓ) computed in the abelian category Sh(V_ét, Q_ℓ) of sheaves of Q_ℓ-vector spaces on the small étale site. This agrees with the groups produced by lemma_288 for K = Q_ℓ[0]: the forgetful functor Sh(V_ét, Q_ℓ) → Sh(V_ét, Z) is right adjoint to the exact functor (−) ⊗_Z Q_ℓ, hence preserves injectives and commutes with Γ, so the two definitions of derived global sections of the constant Q_ℓ-complex coincide.

STEP 0 (the empty scheme). Suppose X = ∅. The small étale site of ∅ has, up to isomorphism, the single object ∅ → ∅, and the empty family is a covering family of ∅ (the empty union of images is ∅, so it is jointly surjective). The sheaf axiom for this covering forces F(∅) to be a singleton for every sheaf F; hence Sh(∅_ét, Q_ℓ) is the trivial abelian category, in which every object is zero. Consequently H^n_et(∅, Q_ℓ) = 0 for every integer n, and the required vanishing holds trivially. We shall use the same observation without comment whenever an open subscheme occurring below is empty. Note also that if X ≠ ∅ then dim X ≥ 0, so the hypothesis dim X ≤ e forces e ≥ 0; no convention about negative dimensions is needed anywhere.

STEP 1 (behaviour of open subschemes, and of intersections of affine opens). X is of finite type over the field k, hence Noetherian. Therefore every open subscheme V ⊂ X is quasi-compact; being locally of finite type over k and quasi-compact, it is of finite type over k; and being an open subscheme of a separated k-scheme it is separated over k. Clearly dim V ≤ dim X ≤ e.
Now let V, V' ⊂ X be affine open subschemes. Since X is separated over k, the diagonal Δ: X → X ×_k X is a closed immersion. The product V ×_k V' is an affine open subscheme of X ×_k X, a closed immersion is an affine morphism, and the preimage of an affine scheme under an affine morphism is affine. Since Δ^{-1}(V ×_k V') = V ∩ V', the intersection V ∩ V' is affine.

STEP 2 (Mayer–Vietoris for an open two-cover). Let X = A ∪ B with A, B open subschemes and W = A ∩ B. We construct a long exact sequence
… → H^n(X) → H^n(A) ⊕ H^n(B) → H^n(W) → H^{n+1}(X) → …   (MV)
with the evident restriction maps. Write Sh(X) := Sh(X_ét, Q_ℓ), etc.

(2a) Enough injectives. Sh(X) is the category of modules over the constant ring sheaf Q_ℓ in the Grothendieck topos Sh(X_ét); it is a Grothendieck abelian category, hence has enough injectives. The same holds for A, B, W.

(2b) Open restriction and extension by zero. Let j: V ↪ X be an open immersion. Pullback j^*: Sh(X) → Sh(V) is exact, since on geometric stalks (j^*F)_{v̄} = F_{v̄}. It has a left adjoint j_! (extension by zero), which is exact. To justify exactness explicitly we compute geometric stalks: for G ∈ Sh(V),
(j_!G)_{x̄} = G_{x̄} if x̄ factors through V, and (j_!G)_{x̄} = 0 otherwise.   (†)
Indeed j_!G is the sheafification of the presheaf U ↦ {σ ∈ Γ(U ×_X V, G) : the support of σ, viewed as a locally closed subset of U, is closed in U}. If x̄ ∈ V, then the étale neighbourhoods (U, ū) of x̄ with U ⊂ V are cofinal (given (U, ū), replace U by U ×_X V, which is étale over X, is contained in V, and still carries the geometric point over x̄); for such U the support of a section σ ∈ G(U) is closed in U (the locus where the germ of σ vanishes is open), so the condition is vacuous and the colimit is colim_U G(U) = G_{x̄}. If x̄ ∉ V, every section in the presheaf has support contained in U ×_X V, which does not contain ū, so its germ at x̄ is zero, giving (†). Since a sequence of sheaves on the étale site of a scheme is exact if and only if it is exact on all geometric stalks (geometric points form a conservative family of points of the étale topos), (†) shows that j_! is exact. (Equivalently: Sh(V_ét) is the slice topos Sh(X_ét)/h_V over the subterminal sheaf h_V represented by V — the sites (X_ét)/h_V and V_ét are isomorphic because V → X is a monomorphism — and under this equivalence j^* is (−) × h_V while j_! is the domain functor, which is exact because limits and colimits in a slice category are computed in the base.)
Consequence: j^* sends injective objects to injective objects. Indeed, for I injective in Sh(X), the functor Hom_V(−, j^*I) ≅ Hom_X(j_!(−), I) is the composition of the exact functor j_! with the exact functor Hom_X(−, I), hence is exact.

(2c) Injective sheaves are flasque along open subsets. Let I be injective in Sh(X) and V ⊂ X open. Then res: Γ(X, I) → Γ(V, I|_V) is surjective. Proof: Γ(V, I|_V) = Hom_V(Q_V, I|_V) ≅ Hom_X(j_!Q_V, I) by adjunction, where Q_V, Q_X denote the constant sheaves. The morphism j_!Q_V → Q_X adjoint to id_{Q_V} ∈ Hom_V(Q_V, j^*Q_X) is a monomorphism, as (†) shows on geometric stalks: over V it is the identity Q_ℓ → Q_ℓ, and outside V it is 0 → Q_ℓ. Since I is injective, Hom_X(−, I) turns this monomorphism into a surjection Hom_X(Q_X, I) ↠ Hom_X(j_!Q_V, I), which is exactly the restriction map Γ(X, I) ↠ Γ(V, I|_V).

(2d) An injective resolution computing all four cohomologies. Choose a bounded-below complex K^• of injective objects of Sh(X) together with a quasi-isomorphism Q_ℓ → K^• (possible by (2a)). For V ∈ {X, A, B, W} with open immersion j_V: V ↪ X, put K^•(V) := Γ(V, j_V^*K^•). By (2b), j_V^*K^• is a bounded-below complex of injectives of Sh(V); by exactness of j_V^* it is quasi-isomorphic to Q_ℓ|_V. Therefore, since derived global sections are computed by bounded-below complexes of injectives,
H^q(K^•(V)) = H^q_et(V, Q_ℓ) for every integer q.   (‡)

(2e) The degreewise short exact sequences. For each p ≥ 0 we claim
0 → K^p(X) → K^p(A) ⊕ K^p(B) → K^p(W) → 0,   (††)
where the first map is s ↦ (s|_A, s|_B) and the second is (s, t) ↦ s|_W − t|_W (writing K^p(V) := Γ(V, K^p|_V)).
• Injectivity of the first map: a section of a sheaf over X is uniquely determined by its restrictions to the covering {A, B}.
• Exactness in the middle: by the sheaf axiom for the covering {A, B} of X, the image of K^p(X) is the equalizer of the two restriction maps K^p(A) ⊕ K^p(B) ⇒ K^p(W); in the category of abelian groups this equalizer is the kernel of their difference, i.e. of the middle map.
• Surjectivity of the middle map: let u ∈ K^p(W) = Γ(W, K^p|_W). Since K^p is injective, (2c) applied to the open immersion W ↪ A gives s ∈ Γ(A, K^p|_A) = K^p(A) with s|_W = u. Then (s, 0) maps to u − 0 = u.
Since the differentials of K^• are morphisms of sheaves, they are natural in the open set, so (††) assembles into a short exact sequence of complexes
0 → K^•(X) → K^•(A) ⊕ K^•(B) → K^•(W) → 0.
Its long exact cohomology sequence, combined with the identifications (‡), is precisely (MV). This completes the proof of the Mayer–Vietoris sequence; note that no compactly supported cohomology and no localisation sequence for a closed complement is used.

STEP 3 (base case m = 1). Assume X = U_1. If X = ∅ this is Step 0. Otherwise X is a non-empty affine scheme of finite type over the algebraically closed field k, of Krull dimension n_0 := dim X ≤ e. The constant sheaf Q_ℓ is constructible on any scheme of finite type over a separably closed field (standard; SGA 4 IX 2.7), so K := Q_ℓ[0] is an object of D^b_c(X_ét, Q_ℓ), and its cohomology sheaves satisfy H^q(K) = 0 for q > 0. Applying lemma_288 to U = X, n = n_0 and this K gives H^q(RΓ(X_ét, Q_ℓ[0])) = 0 for every q > n_0, i.e. H^q_et(X, Q_ℓ) = 0 for q > n_0. If n > e then n > n_0, hence H^n_et(X, Q_ℓ) = 0. This is the required vanishing for m = 1, since e + m − 1 = e.

STEP 4 (inductive step). Let m ≥ 2, and assume the statement proved for covers by m − 1 affine opens (for every algebraically closed k, every ℓ ≠ char k, every separated finite type k-scheme and every admissible e). Put
A := U_1,   B := U_2 ∪ … ∪ U_m,   W := A ∩ B = ⋃_{j=2}^{m} (A ∩ U_j).
By Step 1, each of A, B, W is separated of finite type over k with dimension ≤ e. Moreover:
• A is affine;
• B is covered by the m − 1 affine open subschemes U_2, …, U_m of B (each U_j ⊂ B and is open in X, hence open in B);
• W is covered by the m − 1 affine open subschemes A ∩ U_j of W (each A ∩ U_j is open in W and is affine by Step 1, since A and U_j are affine open in X).
Applying the induction hypothesis to B and to W (with e unchanged, and using Step 0 if B or W is empty) gives
H^n_et(B, Q_ℓ) = 0 and H^n_et(W, Q_ℓ) = 0 for all n > e + (m − 1) − 1 = e + m − 2.   (1)
Applying Step 3 to the affine scheme A gives
H^n_et(A, Q_ℓ) = 0 for all n > e.   (2)
Now let n be an integer with n > e + m − 1. Since n is an integer, n ≥ e + m, and therefore:
(i) n > e + m − 2, so by (1), H^n(B) = 0 (and also H^n(W) = 0);
(ii) n − 1 ≥ e + m − 1 > e + m − 2, so by (1), H^{n−1}(W) = 0;
(iii) n ≥ e + m ≥ e + 2 > e, so by (2), H^n(A) = 0.
The portion of (MV) read
H^{n−1}(W) → H^n(X) → H^n(A) ⊕ H^n(B)
is exact, so by (ii) the map H^n(X) → H^n(A) ⊕ H^n(B) is injective, and by (i) and (iii) its target is 0. Hence H^n_et(X, Q_ℓ) = 0.

CONCLUSION. By induction on m, for every m ≥ 1 one has H^n_et(X, Q_ℓ) = 0 for all integers n > e + m − 1, which is the statement of the lemma. All cases (X empty, B or W empty, empty members of the covers) were covered in Step 0 and Step 4, and the only external input used is lemma_288 together with the standard elementary facts about the étale topos recorded in Steps 2(a)–(c).

lemma_326.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:X\to Y\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\ell\neq p\) prime. For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\), and for \(0\le n\le 2D\) let \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map with \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup f^*(y))\) for all \(x\in H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(y\in H^{2D-n}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Writing \(F_X,F_Y\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), one has \(f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_326.proof:
We write $H^n(Z):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^n(Z)(j):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$ for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, and $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ for the Tate twist regarded as a $1$-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space on which the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius acts as multiplication by $q^D$.

STEP 0 (Finite-dimensionality and identification of the Frobenius operator). Both $X$ and $Y$ are proper over $\mathbb F_q$. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) to the constant sheaf $K=\mathbb Q_{\ell}$ on $Z_k$ equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_Z^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ (i.e. taking $\phi=\psi$), we obtain that $H^n(Z)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $n$, and that the canonical automorphism $F_\phi$ it constructs on $H^n(Z)$ is the one induced, under $H^n(Z)\simeq\operatorname{Ext}^n_{D^b_c(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)}(\mathbb Q_\ell,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, by $u\mapsto\psi\circ F_Z^*(u)\circ\psi^{-1}$; this is precisely the pullback map $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ of the statement (the identification of the two constructions is the content of the word "canonical" in lemma_45_finite_frob, resp. of the equivariance statement of lemma_39 for $K=L=\mathbb Q_\ell$). By lemma_6a (eoinm) this operator is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^n(Z)$ (its inverse being $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^*$), and it preserves each degree $n$.

STEP 1 (Poincar\'e duality input). We apply lemma_77 (eoinm) with $m=1$, $d=D$, and with the role of $Y$ played successively by $X$ and by $Y$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, its conclusions give, for each $Z\in\{X,Y\}$:

(T) a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}(Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, induced by the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphism $\mathbb Q_\ell(D)[2D]\to Rf_Z^!\mathbb Q_\ell$ for the structure morphism $f_Z:Z\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$, satisfying $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$ for every closed point $z$ (this is exactly the normalisation in the statement, so this is the map denoted $\operatorname{tr}_Z$ there), and arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, i.e.
\[ \operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z\gamma)=q^{D}\operatorname{tr}_Z(\gamma)\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in H^{2D}(Z); \]

(P) for every $0\le n\le 2D$ the pairing $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Z:H^n(Z)\times H^{2D-n}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, $\langle\gamma,\delta\rangle_Z:=\operatorname{tr}_Z(\gamma\cup\delta)$, is a PERFECT pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, and it satisfies
\[ \langle F_Z\gamma,F_Z\delta\rangle_Z=q^{D}\langle\gamma,\delta\rangle_Z\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in H^n(Z),\ \delta\in H^{2D-n}(Z). \]

STEP 2 (Three elementary functoriality facts).
(F1) For each $Z$, $F_Z$ is an automorphism of the graded $\mathbb Q_\ell$-algebra $H^*(Z)$: if $\gamma\in H^a(Z)$ and $\delta\in H^b(Z)$ then $F_Z(\gamma\cup\delta)=F_Z\gamma\cup F_Z\delta$. Indeed $F_Z$ is the pullback $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ along a morphism of the small \'etale topos of $Z_k$, and cup product in \'etale cohomology is functorial for pullback.

(F2) For every $\xi\in H^{2D}(Y)$ one has $\operatorname{tr}_Y(F_Y\xi)=q^D\operatorname{tr}_Y(\xi)$, by (T) applied to $Y$.

(F3) The two squares defining $F_X$ and $F_Y$ come from a single morphism of $k$-schemes over $f$: since $f$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$, the diagram commutes, $f_k\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)=(\mathrm{id}\times\sigma)\circ f_k$, where $f_k:X_k\to Y_k$ is the base change of $f$. Hence for every $n$ and every $y\in H^n(Y)$,
\[ F_X(f^*y)=f^*(F_Yy). \]
Since $F_X,F_Y$ are invertible (Step 0), applying (F3) to $F_Y^{-1}y$ and using $F_YF_Y^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$ gives also
\[ F_X\bigl(f^*(F_Y^{-1}y)\bigr)=f^*(y). \]

STEP 3 (The map $f_*$ is well defined). Fix $n$ and $\alpha\in H^n(X)$. The map $y\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(\alpha\cup f^*y)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear form on $H^{2D-n}(Y)$ (linearity of cup product and of $\operatorname{tr}_X$, and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $f^*$). By perfection of $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Y$ from (P), there exists a unique element of $H^n(Y)$ representing this form; we denote it $f_*\alpha$. This gives the unique $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $f_*:H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)$ with
\[ \tag{$*$} \operatorname{tr}_Y(f_*\alpha\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_X(\alpha\cup f^*y)\qquad\forall\alpha\in H^n(X),\ \forall y\in H^{2D-n}(Y), \]
which is the map of the statement. (Equivalently, in pairing notation, $\langle f_*\alpha,y\rangle_Y=\langle\alpha,f^*y\rangle_X$.)

STEP 4 (Intertwining). Fix $n$, $\alpha\in H^n(X)$ and $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$; all pairings below take values in $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$. We prove
\[ \tag{$\dagger$} \langle f_*F_X\alpha,\,y\rangle_Y=\langle F_Yf_*\alpha,\,y\rangle_Y, \]
which, by perfectness of $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_Y$ and the fact that $F_Yf_*\alpha\in H^n(Y)$ (Frobenius preserves degree), will imply $f_*F_X\alpha=F_Yf_*\alpha$.

We compute, justifying each equality:
\begin{align*}
\langle f_*F_X\alpha,\,y\rangle_Y
&=\langle F_X\alpha,\,f^*y\rangle_X
\qquad &&\text{by }(*)\text{ applied to }F_X\alpha\in H^n(X)\text{ and }y\in H^{2D-n}(Y);\\
&=\bigl\langle F_X\alpha,\,F_X\bigl(f^*(F_Y^{-1}y)\bigr)\bigr\rangle_X
\qquad &&\text{by the second displayed identity in (F3);}\\
&=q^{D}\,\bigl\langle\alpha,\,f^*(F_Y^{-1}y)\bigr\rangle_X
\qquad &&\text{by the equivariance in (P) for }Z=X,\ \gamma=\alpha,\ \delta=f^*(F_Y^{-1}y);\\
&=q^{D}\,\langle f_*\alpha,\,F_Y^{-1}y\rangle_Y
\qquad &&\text{by }(*)\text{ applied to }\alpha\in H^n(X)\text{ and }F_Y^{-1}y\in H^{2D-n}(Y);\\
&=\langle F_Yf_*\alpha,\,F_YF_Y^{-1}y\rangle_Y
\qquad &&\text{by the equivariance in (P) for }Z=Y,\ \gamma=f_*\alpha,\ \delta=F_Y^{-1}y;\\
&=\langle F_Yf_*\alpha,\,y\rangle_Y
\qquad &&\text{since }F_YF_Y^{-1}=\mathrm{id}.
\end{align*}
This is $(\dagger)$. (For completeness we spell out the fourth and sixth lines: the equivariance in (P) reads $\langle F_Yu,F_Yv\rangle_Y=q^D\langle u,v\rangle_Y$; taking $u=f_*\alpha$ and $v=F_Y^{-1}y$ gives $\langle F_Yf_*\alpha,y\rangle_Y=q^D\langle f_*\alpha,F_Y^{-1}y\rangle_Y$, which is the claimed equality.)

STEP 5 (Conclusion of the intertwining). Since $(\dagger)$ holds for every $y\in H^{2D-n}(Y)$ and the pairing $H^n(Y)\times H^{2D-n}(Y)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ is perfect (lemma_77(b)), the two elements $f_*F_X\alpha$ and $F_Yf_*\alpha$ of $H^n(Y)$ pair identically with every $y$; perfection implies they are equal. As $\alpha\in H^n(X)$ was arbitrary, $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$ on $H^n(X)$. As $n$ with $0\le n\le 2D$ was arbitrary, the claim is proved. (For $n>2D$ both groups are $0$, so the identity is vacuous.)

STEP 6 (Remarks on the hypotheses used). The argument used only: (i) $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, so that lemma_77 applies to give the perfect Frobenius-semi-invariant Poincar\'e duality pairings and the Frobenius-equivariant traces; (ii) $f$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, so that (F3) holds. The additional hypotheses that $f$ be proper, surjective, generically finite of degree $d\ge1$ are not needed for the commutation relation proved here (they are what later give $f_*f^*=d$ and hence the injection of Frobenius-stable summands). Note also that no semisimplicity was assumed or used anywhere.

Thus $f_*\circ F_X=F_Y\circ f_*$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for every $0\le n\le 2D$, as required.

lemma_322.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\). Let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi=\mathrm{cl}(H)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and let \L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Suppose (a) \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\), and (b) \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(m<d\). Put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\bigr)\). Then \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if \(F\) is semisimple on \(P^d\).
lemma_322.proof:
Write H^m := H^m_et(X_k, Q_ell) for every m in Z (H^m = 0 for m < 0, etale cohomology being the right derived functor of global sections). Write L: H^m -> H^{m+2} for cup product with xi = cl(H), and F for the q-power arithmetic Frobenius.

STEP 0 (finite dimensionality; invertibility of F; meaning of 'semisimple'). X is proper over F_q and the constant sheaf Q_ell on X_k carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, so by lemma_45_finite_frob (applied to K = Q_ell) each H^m is finite dimensional over Q_ell. By lemma_6a, F is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of each H^m. Throughout, for a Q_ell-linear automorphism T of a finite dimensional Q_ell-space V, 'T is semisimple' means that the base change T_{Qbar_ell} of T to V tensor Qbar_ell is diagonalizable; by lemma_5 this coincides with the usual notion of semisimplicity over Q_ell, and by lemma_60 (conditions (i) and (ii)) it is equivalent to the minimal polynomial mu_T in Q_ell[t] being squarefree.

STEP 1 (three elementary linear-algebra facts).
(F1) Let T in GL(W) be semisimple and let U subset W be a Q_ell-subspace with T(U) = U. Then T|_U in GL(U) is semisimple. Proof: if U = 0 there is nothing to prove. Otherwise mu_T(T|_U) = 0 since mu_T(T) = 0 on W, hence mu_{T|_U} divides mu_T in Q_ell[t]. By lemma_60, mu_T is squarefree; Q_ell[t] is a UFD, so every divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree; thus mu_{T|_U} is squarefree and lemma_60 gives that T|_U is semisimple.
(F2) For T in GL(V) and c in Q_ell^*, T is semisimple if and only if cT is semisimple. Proof: by lemma_5 it suffices to argue over Qbar_ell, where T is diagonalizable exactly when V_{Qbar_ell} has a basis (e_i) with T e_i = lambda_i e_i; the same basis satisfies (cT) e_i = (c lambda_i) e_i, and c lambda_i is defined and the family is still a basis, so cT is diagonalizable, and conversely applying the same to c^{-1}(cT).
(F3) If alpha: V ->~ W is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism and T_V, T_W are automorphisms with T_W o alpha = alpha o T_V, then T_V is semisimple if and only if T_W is semisimple: this is lemma_8.

STEP 2 (Frobenius commutes with L up to the scalar q). By lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable, applied to the smooth projective geometrically connected X of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_q with the F_q-rational very ample divisor H, one has F o L = q L o F on every H^m (the reason, contained in that lemma's proof, is that F = (id x Spec sigma)^* is a homomorphism of the graded Q_ell-algebra H^* for the cup product, and that the cycle class of the F_q-rational divisor H satisfies F(xi) = q xi). Two consequences, both also given by that lemma and by the displayed relation, will be used repeatedly:
 (2a) for 0 <= m <= d the 'true' primitive piece P^m_true := ker(L^{d-m+1}: H^m -> H^{2d-m+2}) is stable under F and under F^{-1};
 (2b) by induction from F L = q L F one has F L^r = q^r L^r F for every r >= 0; hence for every F-stable subspace S subset H^m, the subspace L^r(S) subset H^{m+2r} is again F-stable.
In particular, since d >= 2 implies d >= 2 so that 2d - d + 2 = d + 2 <= 2d, the space P^d of the statement, namely P^d = ker(L: H^d -> H^{d+2}), is exactly P^d_true and is therefore F-stable (and F^{-1}-stable).

We treat the cases d = 1 and d >= 2 separately.

STEP 3 (the case d = 1). Here X is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve. Take r = 1, C_1 = X and f = id_X in lemma_278: the identity of X is proper (X is proper over F_q), surjective and generically finite. Lemma_278 then says that F is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) for every n >= 0; in particular the statement 'F is semisimple on H^1' is TRUE. On the other hand, by Step 2 (applied with d = 1, where P^1_true = ker(L^{2-1+... }: ) — explicitly 2d - m + 2 = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3, so P^1_true = ker(L: H^1 -> H^3), which is precisely the P^1 of the statement) the space P^1 is F-stable, P^1 subset H^1, and F(P^1) = P^1; by (F1) applied to the semisimple operator F|_{H^1}, the operator F|_{P^1} is semisimple, so the statement 'F is semisimple on P^1' is also TRUE. An equivalence between two true statements holds. This settles d = 1 (note that hypothesis (a) was not needed here).

STEP 4 (the case d >= 2). We first package the cohomology in degrees 0,...,2d into a graded object to which the Hard--Lefschetz decomposition lemma applies.

4a. Construction of the graded object. Put V_n := H^n for 0 <= n <= 2d and V_n := 0 for n < 0 and for n > 2d, and set V := (+)_{n in Z} V_n. Define a Q_ell-linear endomorphism Lbar of V by Lbar|_{V_n} := (cup with xi): V_n -> V_{n+2} = H^{n+2} for 0 <= n <= 2d-2, and Lbar|_{V_n} := 0 for n = 2d-1, 2d (and trivially on V_n = 0). Then Lbar(V_n) subset V_{n+2} for all n. V is finite dimensional over Q_ell (Step 0) and Q_ell has characteristic 0; V_n = 0 for n < 0 and for n > 2d by definition.

4b. Verification of the Lefschetz hypothesis. For 0 <= m <= d, the composite Lbar^{d-m}: V_m -> V_{2d-m} is a composition of (d-m) genuine cup products through the degrees m, m+2, ..., 2d-m, all of which lie in [0, 2d]; hence Lbar^{d-m}: H^m -> H^{2d-m} is exactly L^{d-m}, which is an isomorphism by hypothesis (a). Thus (V, Lbar) satisfies all hypotheses of lemma_316.

4c. Applying lemma_316. Let P'^m := ker(Lbar^{d-m+1}: V_m -> V_{2d-m+2}) for 0 <= m <= d and P'^m := 0 for m < 0 and m > d. Lemma_316 says that for every n >= 0 the map (+)_{r >= max(0, n-d)} P'^{n-2r} -> V_n, (x_r)_r |-> sum_r Lbar^r x_r, is an isomorphism. Take n = d; since P'^{d-2r} = 0 for r > d/2, the map
   theta: (+)_{0 <= r <= floor(d/2)} P'^{d-2r} -> H^d, (x_r) |-> sum_r L^r x_r,
is an isomorphism. Writing W_r := L^r(P'^{d-2r}) subset H^d, this says explicitly that (i) L^r: P'^{d-2r} -> W_r is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism for each r, and (ii) H^d = (+)_{r} W_r as an internal direct sum.

4d. Identification of the pieces. For 2 <= m <= d one has 2d - m + 2 <= 2d, so V_{2d-m+2} = H^{2d-m+2} and Lbar^{d-m+1} coincides with the genuine L^{d-m+1} (all intermediate degrees are <= 2d - m + 2 <= 2d); hence P'^m = P^m_true. Since d >= 2, P'^d = P^d_true = P^d, the space of the statement. For m in {0,1} one has 2d - m + 2 >= 2d+1 > 2d, so V_{2d-m+2} = 0 and P'^m = V_m = H^m.

4e. F-stability of the summands. Each P'^{d-2r} is F-stable: if d-2r >= 2 it is the true primitive piece, F-stable by (2a); if d-2r in {0,1} it equals H^{d-2r}, trivially F-stable; if d-2r < 0 it is 0. By (2b), each W_r = L^r(P'^{d-2r}) is therefore F-stable, and F(W_r) = W_r (F and F^{-1} both preserve P'^{d-2r} in the kernel cases, and are automorphisms in the others).

4f. Reduction to the pieces. Because H^d = (+)_r W_r with each W_r F-stable, the operator F|_{H^d} is the direct sum of the operators F|_{W_r}; by lemma_9,
   (A) F|_{H^d} is semisimple <=> F|_{W_r} is semisimple for every r.
Fix r. The isomorphism alpha := L^r: P'^{d-2r} ->~ W_r satisfies F|_{W_r} o alpha = q^r alpha o F|_{P'^{d-2r}} (by F L^r = q^r L^r F), i.e. F|_{W_r} = q^r (alpha o F|_{P'^{d-2r}} o alpha^{-1}). By (F3), alpha o F|_{P'^{d-2r}} o alpha^{-1} is semisimple exactly when F|_{P'^{d-2r}} is, and by (F2) with c = q^r in Q_ell^* multiplication by q^r preserves and reflects semisimplicity. Hence
   (B) F|_{W_r} is semisimple <=> F|_{P'^{d-2r}} is semisimple.

4g. All pieces except r = 0 are automatically semisimple. Let r >= 1. Then 0 <= d-2r <= d-2 < d (if d-2r < 0 the piece P'^{d-2r} = 0 is trivially semisimple), so hypothesis (b) says F is semisimple on H^{d-2r}. The subspace P'^{d-2r} subset H^{d-2r} satisfies F(P'^{d-2r}) = P'^{d-2r} by 4e, so (F1) applies and F|_{P'^{d-2r}} is semisimple. Thus (B) gives that F|_{W_r} is semisimple for every r >= 1, unconditionally.

4h. Conclusion for d >= 2. Combining (A), (B) and 4g,
  F|_{H^d} semisimple <=> F|_{W_0} semisimple <=> F|_{P'^d} semisimple,
since the only remaining index is r = 0, where W_0 = L^0(P'^d) = P'^d = P^d. That is exactly the required equivalence.

STEP 5 (end of proof). Steps 3 and 4 cover all d >= 1, so F is semisimple on H^d_et(X_k, Q_ell) if and only if F is semisimple on P^d = ker(L: H^d_et -> H^{d+2}_et). (For completeness: the forward implication can also be read off directly, without the decomposition, from the F-stability of P^d established in Step 2 together with (F1); the decomposition is what makes the converse available.) QED.

lemma_327.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(f:Y\to X\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree \(d\ge1\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, and fix an integer \(n\ge0\). For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let \(\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)\) be the trace isomorphism normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\), and let \(f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map with \(\operatorname{tr}_X(f_*(x)\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup f^*(y))\) for all \(x\in H^n(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(y\in H^{2D-n}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Writing \(F_X,F_Y\) for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), if \(F_Y\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), then \(F_X\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_327.proof:
We write $H^i(Z):=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for $Z\in\{X,Y\}$, and $F_X,F_Y$ for the $q$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$. All pairings below are those of Poincar\'e duality, $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v)$.

**Step 0 (Preliminaries: finiteness, invertibility of Frobenius, duality, vanishing).**
(a) $X$ and $Y$ are proper over $\mathbb F_q$, so by lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ (with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure) each $H^i(Z)$ is finite dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and the Frobenius operators are the canonical $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms.
(b) By lemma_6a, $F_Z$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphism of $H^i(Z)$ with inverse the geometric Frobenius; in particular $F_Z\in\mathrm{GL}(H^i(Z))$ and $F_Z^{-1}$ exists.
(c) Since $X$ and $Y$ are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $D$ over $\mathbb F_q$, lemma_77 (with $m=1$, $d=D$) applies to each $Z\in\{X,Y\}$: the trace map $\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2D}(Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ of the statement is the one of lemma_77(a) (same normalisation $\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$), it satisfies
$$\operatorname{tr}_Z(F_Z w)=q^{D}\operatorname{tr}_Z(w)\qquad\text{for all }w\in H^{2D}(Z),\tag{1}$$
and for every $0\le n\le 2D$ the pairing $H^n(Z)\times H^{2D-n}(Z)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Z(u\cup v)$, is perfect (lemma_77(b)).
(d) For $n>2D$ we have $H^n(X)=H^n(Y)=0$: indeed $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) is projective of dimension $D$ over the algebraically closed field $k$, hence separated of finite type of Krull dimension $D$, and there is a finite (hence affine) surjective morphism $X_k\to\mathbb P^D_k$ (Noether normalisation for the homogeneous coordinate ring after a Veronese embedding), so the $D+1$ standard affine opens of $\mathbb P^D_k$ pull back to $D+1$ affine opens covering $X_k$; Spark/lemma_ordinary_vanishing_affine_cover with $e=D$, $m=D+1$ gives $H^n(X)=0$ for $n>D+(D+1)-1=2D$, and likewise for $Y$.

**Step 1 (The case $n>2D$).** By Step 0(d), $H^n(X)=0$, and the restriction of $F_X$ to the zero space is the identity of the zero space, which is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. The conclusion holds trivially. From now on assume $0\le n\le 2D$.

**Step 2 (The case $D=0$).** If $D=0$, then $X$ is proper and $0$-dimensional, hence $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A$ a finite $\mathbb F_q$-algebra; smoothness makes $A$ a product of finite separable extensions of $\mathbb F_q$, and geometric connectedness forces $A=\mathbb F_q$. Thus $X_k=\operatorname{Spec}k$, $H^0(X)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $H^n(X)=0$ for $n\ge1$ (Step 0(d)). For $n\ge1$ the conclusion is trivial, and for $n=0$ the map $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ on $H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ is the identity on $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued locally constant functions on the one-point space, so $F_X=\mathrm{id}$, which is diagonalisable. Henceforth assume $1\le D$ and $0\le n\le 2D$.

**Step 3 (Functoriality of Frobenius against $f^*$.).** Since $f:Y\to X$ is a morphism over $\mathbb F_q$, the square
$$\begin{matrix}Y_k&\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{id}\times\sigma\ }&Y_k\\ \ \downarrow f_k&&\downarrow f_k\\ X_k&\xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{id}\times\sigma\ }&X_k\end{matrix}$$
is commutative: both composites are the base change of the $\mathbb F_q$-morphism $f$ together with the automorphism $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, and $\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ commutes with the structure morphism to $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q$ because $\sigma$ fixes $\mathbb F_q$ elementwise. Passing to pullbacks on \'etale cohomology (pullback is contravariant and functorial, and $f^*$ is a ring homomorphism for the cup product) gives, for every $i$,
$$F_Y\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_X,\qquad\text{hence also}\qquad F_Y^{-1}\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_X^{-1},\tag{2}$$
the second identity being obtained by inverting the first (both sides are automorphisms by Step 0(b)).

**Step 4 (Existence, uniqueness and $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $f_*$).** For fixed $x\in H^n(Y)$, the map $y\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup f^*y)$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear functional on $H^{2D-n}(X)$, linear also in $x$. By the perfectness of $H^n(X)\times H^{2D-n}(X)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$ (Step 0(c)) there is a unique element of $H^n(X)$ representing this functional; call it $f_*(x)$. This defines a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $f_*:H^n(Y)\to H^n(X)$ with $\operatorname{tr}_X(f_*x\cup y)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup f^*y)$ for all $x,y$, unique with this property. It is the map whose existence the statement asserts.

**Step 5 (Compatibility of $f_*$ with Frobenius).** Let $x\in H^n(Y)$ and $y\in H^{2D-n}(X)$. Using successively the defining property of $f_*$ applied to $F_Yx$, then $F_Y$ being a ring automorphism, then (1) for $Y$, then (2), then the defining property of $f_*$, then (1) for $X$, and finally again that $F_X$ is a ring automorphism:
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*(F_Yx)\cup y\bigr)&=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Yx\cup f^*y\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Yx\cup F_Y(F_Y^{-1}f^*y)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(F_Y(x\cup F_Y^{-1}f^*y)\bigr)\\&=q^{D}\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(x\cup F_Y^{-1}f^*y\bigr)=q^{D}\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(x\cup f^*(F_X^{-1}y)\bigr)=q^{D}\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*x\cup F_X^{-1}y\bigr)\\&=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X(f_*x\cup F_X^{-1}y)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(F_X(f_*x)\cup y\bigr).\end{aligned}$$
Since this holds for every $y\in H^{2D-n}(X)$ and the pairing in degrees $(n,2D-n)$ is perfect, $f_*(F_Yx)=F_X(f_*x)$. As this holds for all $x$,
$$f_*\circ F_Y=F_X\circ f_*.\tag{3}$$

**Step 6 ($f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}$, so $f^*$ is injective).** Let $y\in H^n(X)$ and $z\in H^{2D-n}(X)$. Using the defining property of $f_*$, then that $f^*$ is a ring homomorphism, then lemma_top_trace_generically_finite applied to $f:Y\to X$ (that lemma, with the roles of its $X$ and $Y$ read as our $Y$ and $X$, says precisely that $\operatorname{tr}_Y\circ f^*\circ\operatorname{tr}_X^{-1}$ is multiplication by $d$ on $\mathbb Q_\ell(-D)$, i.e. $\operatorname{tr}_Y(f^*w)=d\,\operatorname{tr}_X(w)$ for all $w\in H^{2D}(X)$), and finally $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinearity of the cup product:
$$\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*(f^*y)\cup z\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*y\cup f^*z\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*(y\cup z)\bigr)=d\,\operatorname{tr}_X(y\cup z)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((d\,y)\cup z\bigr).$$
Perfectness gives $f_*(f^*y)=d\,y$, i.e.
$$f_*\circ f^*=d\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H^n(X)}.\tag{4}$$
Since $d\ge1$ is an ordinary integer and $\mathbb Q_\ell$ has characteristic $0$, $d\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$; hence $f^*$ has a left inverse $d^{-1}f_*$ and is injective.

**Step 7 (The image of $f^*$ is an $F_Y$-stable subspace, and $F_X$ is conjugate to the restriction of $F_Y$.)** Put $W:=f^*(H^n(X))\subseteq H^n(Y)$. By (2),
$$F_Y(W)=F_Yf^*(H^n(X))=f^*F_X(H^n(X))=f^*(H^n(X))=W,$$
the third equality using that $F_X$ is an automorphism of $H^n(X)$ (Step 0(b)). So $W$ is an $F_Y$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of the finite-dimensional space $H^n(Y)$. By Step 6, $f^*:H^n(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}W$ is an isomorphism, and (2) says exactly that the diagram
$$H^n(X)\xrightarrow{\ f^*\ }W,\qquad F_Y|_W\circ f^*=f^*\circ F_X$$
conjugates $F_X$ to the restriction $F_Y|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$.

**Step 8 (Descent of semisimplicity).** By hypothesis the base change of $F_Y$ to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable; by lemma_5 this is equivalent to $F_Y$ being semisimple on the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-space $H^n(Y)$. Since $F_Y\in\mathrm{GL}(H^n(Y))$ (Step 0(b)), $W$ is $F_Y$-stable (Step 7) and $H^n(Y)$ is finite dimensional (Step 0(a)), lemma_145 applied with $V=H^n(Y)$, $T=F_Y$, $W=W$ yields that $F_Y|_W\in\mathrm{GL}(W)$ is semisimple. Conjugacy (Step 7) preserves semisimplicity (a $\mathbb Q_\ell[T]$-module isomorphism $H^n(X)\simeq W$ identifies the two module structures), so $F_X$ is semisimple on $H^n(X)$. Applying lemma_5 again, the base change of $F_X$ to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalisable.

Steps 1, 2 and 8 cover all possibilities for $n$ ($n>2D$; $D=0$; $1\le D$ with $0\le n\le 2D$), so in every case $F_X$ is diagonalisable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ on $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This completes the proof.

lemma_dual_connecting_maps_adjoint.statement: Let \(K\) be a field and \(N\in\mathbb Z\). Let \((V^\bullet,d_V)\) and \((W^\bullet,d_W)\) be complexes of \(K\)-vector spaces, and for each \(r\in\mathbb Z\) let \(\langle-,-\rangle:V^r\times W^{N-r}\to K\) be a bilinear pairing satisfying \(\langle d_Vv,w\rangle=(-1)^{r+1}\langle v,d_Ww\rangle\) for all \(v\in V^r\) and \(w\in W^{N-r-1}\). Let \(0\to A^\bullet\to V^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to0\) be a short exact sequence of complexes, let \(A^{\perp}\) be the subcomplex of \(W^\bullet\) formed by the elements pairing trivially with \(A^\bullet\), and put \(Q^\bullet=W^\bullet/A^{\perp}\). Let \(\delta:H^k(B^\bullet)\to H^{k+1}(A^\bullet)\) and \(\delta':H^m(Q^\bullet)\to H^{m+1}(A^{\perp,\bullet})\) be the connecting homomorphisms of \(0\to A^\bullet\to V^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to0\) and \(0\to A^{\perp}\to W^\bullet\to Q^\bullet\to0\). Then for every integer \(k\) there exists \(\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}\) such that \(\langle\delta b,\,q\rangle=\varepsilon\,\langle b,\,\delta' q\rangle\) for all \(b\in H^k(B^\bullet)\) and \(q\in H^{N-k-1}(Q^\bullet)\), the left pairing being the one induced by \(A^\bullet\times Q^\bullet\) and the right one the one induced by \(B^\bullet\times A^{\perp,\bullet}\).
lemma_dual_connecting_maps_adjoint.proof:
We work with cochain complexes: $d_V:V^r\to V^{r+1}$, $d_W:W^s\to W^{s+1}$, with $d^2=0$. Via the injective chain map $A^\bullet\hookrightarrow V^\bullet$ we identify $A^r$ with its image in $V^r$; then $A^\bullet$ is a subcomplex of $V^\bullet$ (the inclusion being a chain map means $d_V(A^r)\subseteq A^{r+1}$) and $d_A=d_V|_{A^\bullet}$. The quotient $B^r=V^r/A^r$ carries the differential induced by $d_V$. Nothing in the argument below uses finite-dimensionality of any term, nor non-degeneracy of any pairing; the only input is the graded Leibniz-type compatibility
\begin{equation}\tag{$\ast$}
\langle d_V v, w\rangle=(-1)^{r+1}\langle v, d_W w\rangle\qquad(v\in V^r,\ w\in W^{N-r-1}),
\end{equation}
which is well posed because $d_Vv\in V^{r+1}$ pairs with $W^{N-(r+1)}=W^{N-r-1}$.

We write, for each $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$A^{\perp,m}=\{\,w\in W^m:\ \langle a,w\rangle=0\ \text{for all } a\in A^{N-m}\,\},$$
so that $A^{\perp,m}$ is the annihilator of $A^{N-m}$ inside $W^m$ (the two degrees add up to $N$, as the pairing requires). Note that the two facts used repeatedly below are tautological consequences of this definition:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(F1)] if $w\in A^{\perp,m}$ and $a\in A^{N-m}$ then $\langle a,w\rangle=0$;
\item[(F2)] if $w\in A^{\perp,m}$ and $a\in A^{N-m}$ then also $\langle a,w\rangle=0$ when $a$ is any element of $A^{N-m}$, i.e. $A^{\perp,m}$ annihilates exactly $A^{N-m}$.
\end{itemize}
(These are the same statement; we record it twice because it is used once for each of the two induced pairings.)

\section*{Step 1. $A^{\perp,\bullet}$ is a subcomplex of $W^\bullet$}
Take $w\in A^{\perp,m}$; we must show $d_Ww\in A^{\perp,m+1}$, i.e. that $\langle a,d_Ww\rangle=0$ for every $a\in A^{N-m-1}$. Fix such an $a$. View $a$ as an element of $V^{N-m-1}$ (via $A\subseteq V$) and $w$ as an element of $W^{N-(N-m-1)-1}=W^{m}$, so that ($\ast$) applies with $r=N-m-1$:
$$\langle d_V a, w\rangle=(-1)^{(N-m-1)+1}\langle a,d_Ww\rangle=(-1)^{N-m}\langle a,d_Ww\rangle.$$
Since $A^\bullet$ is a subcomplex, $d_Va\in A^{N-m}$; since $w\in A^{\perp,m}$, (F1) gives $\langle d_Va,w\rangle=0$. As $(-1)^{N-m}\in\{\pm1\}$ is a unit of $K$, we get $\langle a,d_Ww\rangle=0$. As $a$ was arbitrary in $A^{N-m-1}$, $d_Ww\in A^{\perp,m+1}$. Also $d_W^2w=0$ holds automatically, so $A^{\perp,\bullet}$ is a subcomplex, and $Q^\bullet:=W^\bullet/A^{\perp,\bullet}$ is a well-defined complex with differential $d_Q([w])=[d_Ww]$.

\section*{Step 2. The two pairings on the nose}
\emph{(a) $A^\bullet\times Q^\bullet\to K$.} For $a\in A^p$ and $\bar q\in Q^{N-p}$ choose any lift $\tilde q\in W^{N-p}$ and set $\langle a,\bar q\rangle:=\langle a,\tilde q\rangle$. If $\tilde q'$ is another lift then $\tilde q-\tilde q'\in A^{\perp,N-p}$, and $a\in A^p=A^{N-(N-p)}$, so (F1) gives $\langle a,\tilde q-\tilde q'\rangle=0$. Hence the value is independent of the lift, and this is a well-defined bilinear map $A^p\times Q^{N-p}\to K$.

\emph{(b) $B^\bullet\times A^{\perp,\bullet}\to K$.} For $\beta\in B^p$ and $w\in A^{\perp,N-p}$ choose any lift $\tilde v\in V^p$ and set $\langle\beta,w\rangle:=\langle\tilde v,w\rangle$. If $\tilde v'$ is another lift then $\tilde v-\tilde v'\in A^p=A^{N-(N-p)}$, and (F1) applied to $w\in A^{\perp,N-p}$ gives $\langle\tilde v-\tilde v',w\rangle=0$. So this is a well-defined bilinear map $B^p\times A^{\perp,N-p}\to K$.

\section*{Step 3. Both pairings descend to cohomology}
We check the four required vanishings; each is a one-line use of ($\ast$) plus (F1).

\emph{(3a) Coboundary in $A$, cocycle in $Q$.} Let $a=d_A\alpha$ with $\alpha\in A^{p-1}$, and let $\bar q\in Z^{N-p}(Q)$. Choose a lift $\tilde q\in W^{N-p}$ of $\bar q$. Since $d_Q\bar q=0$, the element $d_W\tilde q\in W^{N-p+1}$ lies in $A^{\perp,N-p+1}$. Using ($\ast$) with $r=p-1$, $v=\alpha\in V^{p-1}$, $w=\tilde q\in W^{N-(p-1)-1}=W^{N-p}$:
$$\langle a,\bar q\rangle=\langle d_V\alpha,\tilde q\rangle=(-1)^{p}\langle\alpha,d_W\tilde q\rangle=0,$$
the last equality because $\alpha\in A^{p-1}=A^{N-(N-p+1)}$ and $d_W\tilde q\in A^{\perp,N-p+1}$, so (F1) applies.

\emph{(3b) Cocycle in $A$, coboundary in $Q$.} Let $a\in Z^p(A)$ and $\bar q=d_Q\bar q_0$ with $\bar q_0\in Q^{N-p-1}$. Lift $\bar q_0$ to $\tilde q_0\in W^{N-p-1}$; then $d_W\tilde q_0$ lifts $\bar q$. Since $a$ is a cocycle in $A$ and $A\hookrightarrow V$ is injective, $d_Va=0$ in $V^{p+1}$. By ($\ast$) with $r=p$, $v=a$, $w=\tilde q_0$:
$$\langle a,\bar q\rangle=\langle a,d_W\tilde q_0\rangle=(-1)^{p+1}\langle d_Va,\tilde q_0\rangle=0.$$

(3a)+(3b) show that $\langle[a],[\bar q]\rangle:=\langle a,\bar q\rangle$ is a well-defined bilinear pairing $H^p(A)\times H^{N-p}(Q)\to K$; this is the ``left pairing'' of the statement (with $p=k+1$).

\emph{(3c) Coboundary in $B$, cocycle in $A^\perp$.} Let $\beta=d_B\beta_0$ with $\beta_0\in B^{p-1}$, and $w\in Z^{N-p}(A^\perp)$. Lift $\beta_0$ to $\tilde v\in V^{p-1}$; then $d_V\tilde v\in V^p$ is a lift of $\beta$. By ($\ast$) with $r=p-1$, $v=\tilde v$, $w$ as given:
$$\langle\beta,w\rangle=\langle d_V\tilde v,w\rangle=(-1)^{p}\langle\tilde v,d_Ww\rangle=0,$$
the last equality because $d_Ww=0$ in $W$ (as $w$ is a cocycle), hence also in $A^\perp$.

\emph{(3d) Cocycle in $B$, coboundary in $A^\perp$.} Let $\beta\in Z^p(B)$ and $w=d_{A^\perp}\omega$ with $\omega\in A^{\perp,N-p-1}$. Lift $\beta$ to $\tilde v\in V^p$; since $d_B\beta=0$, $d_V\tilde v\in A^{p+1}$. By ($\ast$) with $r=p$, $v=\tilde v$, $w'=\omega\in W^{N-p-1}$:
$$\langle\beta,w\rangle=\langle\tilde v,d_W\omega\rangle=(-1)^{p+1}\langle d_V\tilde v,\omega\rangle=0,$$
the last equality because $d_V\tilde v\in A^{p+1}=A^{N-(N-p-1)}$ and $\omega\in A^{\perp,N-p-1}$, so (F1) applies.

(3c)+(3d) show that $\langle[\beta],[w]\rangle:=\langle\beta,w\rangle$ is a well-defined bilinear pairing $H^p(B)\times H^{N-p}(A^\perp)\to K$; this is the ``right pairing'' of the statement (with $p=k$).

\section*{Step 4. Explicit description of the two connecting homomorphisms}
\emph{The map $\delta$.} Let $b\in H^k(B)$ and represent it by $\beta\in Z^k(B)$. Choose a lift $\tilde v\in V^k$ of $\beta$ (surjectivity $V^k\twoheadrightarrow B^k$). Then $d_V\tilde v\in V^{k+1}$ maps to $d_B\beta=0$, so $d_V\tilde v\in A^{k+1}$; it is an $A$-cocycle because $d_A(d_V\tilde v)=d_V^2\tilde v=0$. The standard construction gives $\delta(b)=[d_V\tilde v]_{A}\in H^{k+1}(A)$, and a change of lift $\tilde v\rightsquigarrow\tilde v+a$ with $a\in A^k$ changes $d_V\tilde v$ by $d_Aa$, hence does not change the class.

\emph{The map $\delta'$.} Let $q\in H^{N-k-1}(Q)$ and represent it by $\bar q\in Z^{N-k-1}(Q)$. Choose a lift $\tilde q\in W^{N-k-1}$ of $\bar q$. Since $d_Q\bar q=0$, $d_W\tilde q\in W^{N-k}$ lies in $A^{\perp,N-k}$; it is an $A^\perp$-cocycle because $d_{A^\perp}(d_W\tilde q)=d_W^2\tilde q=0$, and $\delta'(q)=[d_W\tilde q]_{A^\perp}\in H^{N-k}(A^\perp)$. A change of lift $\tilde q\rightsquigarrow\tilde q+\eta$ with $\eta\in A^{\perp,N-k-1}$ changes $d_W\tilde q$ by $d_{A^\perp}\eta$, so the class is well defined.

\section*{Step 5. The adjointness computation}
Fix $b\in H^k(B)$ represented by $\beta\in Z^k(B)$, and $q\in H^{N-k-1}(Q)$ represented by $\bar q\in Z^{N-k-1}(Q)$; choose lifts $\tilde v\in V^k$ of $\beta$ and $\tilde q\in W^{N-k-1}$ of $\bar q$ as in Step 4. Then, using first the definition of the descended left pairing (Step 2(a), with $p=k+1$, $a=d_V\tilde v\in A^{k+1}$, and the lift $\tilde q$ of $\bar q$),
$$\langle\delta b,\,q\rangle_{A\times Q}=\langle d_V\tilde v,\,\bar q\rangle=\langle d_V\tilde v,\,\tilde q\rangle.$$
Next apply the graded compatibility ($\ast$) with $r=k$, $v=\tilde v\in V^k$ and $w=\tilde q\in W^{N-k-1}=W^{N-k-1}$ (note $N-r-1=N-k-1$, exactly the required degree):
$$\langle d_V\tilde v,\,\tilde q\rangle=(-1)^{k+1}\langle\tilde v,\,d_W\tilde q\rangle.$$
Finally, $d_W\tilde q\in A^{\perp,N-k}$ is a representative of $\delta'q$, and $\tilde v$ is a lift of $\beta$, so by the definition of the descended right pairing (Step 2(b), with $p=k$),
$$\langle\tilde v,\,d_W\tilde q\rangle=\langle\beta,\,d_W\tilde q\rangle=\langle b,\,\delta'q\rangle_{B\times A^\perp}.$$
Chaining the three displayed identities,
$$\langle\delta b,\,q\rangle_{A\times Q}=(-1)^{k+1}\,\langle b,\,\delta'q\rangle_{B\times A^\perp}.$$
Because Steps 2 and 3 proved that both sides depend only on the cohomology classes $b$ and $q$ and not on the chosen representatives $\beta,\bar q$ nor on the chosen lifts $\tilde v,\tilde q$, this identity is a statement about $b$ and $q$ alone; the particular choices made above are legitimate.

\section*{Step 6. Conclusion and edge cases}
For each integer $k$ set $\varepsilon:=(-1)^{k+1}\in\{+1,-1\}$. Step 5 gives, for all $b\in H^k(B^\bullet)$ and all $q\in H^{N-k-1}(Q^\bullet)$,
$$\langle\delta b,\,q\rangle=\varepsilon\,\langle b,\,\delta'q\rangle,$$
with the left pairing induced by $A^\bullet\times Q^\bullet$ and the right pairing induced by $B^\bullet\times A^{\perp,\bullet}$, exactly as required. If either $H^k(B^\bullet)=0$ or $H^{N-k-1}(Q^\bullet)=0$ (for instance when the corresponding graded pieces vanish, or when $N-k-1$ is outside the range of degrees of $Q^\bullet$), the identity is the empty statement and any $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$, in particular $\varepsilon=(-1)^{k+1}$, satisfies it. Thus the required $\varepsilon$ exists in every degree $k$; in fact the single choice $\varepsilon=(-1)^{k+1}$ works for all pairs $(b,q)$ in degree $k$. No finite-dimensionality and no non-degeneracy of the pairings was used anywhere in the argument. This completes the proof.

lemma_mayer_vietoris_finite_coefficients.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), let \(m\ge1\) be an integer, let \(X\) be a scheme of finite type over \(k\), let \(U\) and \(V\) be open subschemes with \(X=U\cup V\), and put \(W=U\cap V\). Then the sequence \(\cdots\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\oplus H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\to H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\to\cdots\), where \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Z/\ell^m)\) is the cohomology of the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Z/\ell^m\) on the small \'etale site, the first arrow is \(x\mapsto(x|_U,x|_V)\) and the second is \((y,z)\mapsto y|_W-z|_W\), is exact.
lemma_mayer_vietoris_finite_coefficients.proof:
Proof. Put Lambda = Z/ell^m. For a scheme Y write Sh(Y_et,Lambda) for the abelian category of sheaves of Lambda-modules on the small etale site and Gamma_Y(F)=Hom_{Sh(Y_et,Lambda)}(Lambda_Y,F), where Lambda_Y is the constant sheaf. By definition H^n_et(Y,Lambda)=Ext^n_{Sh(Y_et,Lambda)}(Lambda_Y,Lambda_Y). The hypotheses that X is of finite type over an algebraically closed field and ell != char(k) are not needed for the formal argument.

1. Basic facts for an open immersion j:Y -> X. The inverse-image functor j^{-1}:Sh(X_et,Lambda)->Sh(Y_et,Lambda) is exact: on geometric stalks it is the identity. It has an exact left adjoint j_! (extension by zero); indeed for a sheaf G on Y_et, (j_!G)_{xbar}=G_{xbar} if xbar lies over Y and 0 otherwise, and exactness is checked on geometric stalks. Hence j^{-1} sends injective objects to injective objects: for I injective on X_et and a monomorphism A -> B in Sh(Y_et,Lambda), Hom_Y(B,j^{-1}I) isomorphic to Hom_X(j_!B,I) -> Hom_X(j_!A,I) isomorphic to Hom_Y(A,j^{-1}I) is surjective because j_! is exact and I is injective. Also Gamma_X(j_*G)=Hom_X(Lambda_X,j_*G) isomorphic to Hom_Y(j^{-1}Lambda_X,G)=Hom_Y(Lambda_Y,G)=Gamma_Y(G).

Geometric stalks are conservative for the etale topos: a sequence of sheaves is exact iff the induced sequence on every geometric stalk is exact. If a sheaf has zero geometric stalks then it is zero, since a section with zero germs at all geometric points is zero by separatedness of sheaves for the etale topology.

2. A termwise exact sequence. Let j_U:U->X, j_V:V->X and j_W:W->X be the open immersions. For any F in Sh(X_et,Lambda) define alpha_F:F -> j_{U*}j_U^{-1}F oplus j_{V*}j_V^{-1}F by alpha_F(T)(s)=(s|_{T_U},s|_{T_V}) and beta_F:j_{U*}j_U^{-1}F oplus j_{V*}j_V^{-1}F -> j_{W*}j_W^{-1}F by beta_F(T)(y,z)=y|_{T_W}-z|_{T_W}. We claim 0 -> F -> j_{U*}j_U^{-1}F oplus j_{V*}j_V^{-1}F -> j_{W*}j_W^{-1}F -> 0 is exact.

Check on a geometric stalk xbar. For an open immersion j:Y->X, (j_*j^{-1}F)_{xbar}=colim_{(T,t) in Et(X,xbar)} F(T times_X Y). If xbar in Y, neighborhoods T->X factoring through Y are cofinal, so (j_*j^{-1}F)_{xbar}=F_{xbar}.

If xbar in W=U cap V, all three stalks are F_{xbar}; the sequence is 0 -> F_{xbar} -> F_{xbar} oplus F_{xbar} -> F_{xbar} -> 0 with b -> (b,b) and (a,c) -> a-c, which is exact.

If xbar in U minus V, then (j_{U*}j_U^{-1}F)_{xbar}=F_{xbar}. By cofinality of etale neighborhoods factoring through U, both (j_{V*}j_V^{-1}F)_{xbar} and (j_{W*}j_W^{-1}F)_{xbar} identify with the same group G=colim_{(T,t) in Et(U,xbar)} F(T cap V) (and T cap V = T cap W for T subset U). Let rho:F_{xbar}->G be the restriction map. The stalk sequence is 0 -> F_{xbar} -> F_{xbar} oplus G -> G -> 0, b -> (b,rho(b)), (a,c) -> rho(a)-c. Its kernel is the graph of rho, hence isomorphic to F_{xbar}, and the last map is surjective (given d in G take (0,-d)). Thus exact. The case xbar in V minus U is symmetric. Since X=U union V, there is no other case. This proves the claim.

3. Apply the termwise sequence to an injective resolution. The category Sh(X_et,Lambda) is a Grothendieck abelian category (a generator is given by the direct sum of the representable sheaves Lambda[h_T] over a set of representatives of objects of X_et), hence has enough injectives. Choose an injective resolution Lambda_X -> I^bullet.

For each q>=0, apply the exact sequence of Step 2 to F=I^q: 0 -> I^q -> j_{U*}j_U^{-1}I^q oplus j_{V*}j_V^{-1}I^q -> j_{W*}j_W^{-1}I^q -> 0. Apply Gamma_X. Since I^q is injective, H^1_et(X,I^q)=Ext^1(Lambda_X,I^q)=0; therefore the sequence of abelian groups remains exact: 0 -> Gamma_X(I^q) -> Gamma_X(j_{U*}j_U^{-1}I^q) oplus Gamma_X(j_{V*}j_V^{-1}I^q) -> Gamma_X(j_{W*}j_W^{-1}I^q) -> 0. Using Gamma_X(j_*j^{-1}G)=Gamma_Y(j^{-1}G), this is a short exact sequence of cochain complexes 0 -> Gamma_X(I^bullet) -> Gamma_U(j_U^{-1}I^bullet) oplus Gamma_V(j_V^{-1}I^bullet) -> Gamma_W(j_W^{-1}I^bullet) -> 0.

4. Identify the cohomology. Since j_U^{-1}, j_V^{-1}, j_W^{-1} are exact and preserve injectives, and since j_U^{-1}Lambda_X=Lambda_U, etc., each complex j_U^{-1}I^bullet (resp. j_V^{-1}I^bullet, j_W^{-1}I^bullet) is an injective resolution of Lambda_U (resp. Lambda_V, Lambda_W). Consequently H^n(Gamma_X(I^bullet))=H^n_et(X,Lambda), H^n(Gamma_U(j_U^{-1}I^bullet))=H^n_et(U,Lambda), H^n(Gamma_V(j_V^{-1}I^bullet))=H^n_et(V,Lambda), H^n(Gamma_W(j_W^{-1}I^bullet))=H^n_et(W,Lambda).

The short exact sequence of complexes therefore gives a long exact sequence ... -> H^n_et(X,Lambda) -> H^n_et(U,Lambda) oplus H^n_et(V,Lambda) -> H^n_et(W,Lambda) -> H^{n+1}_et(X,Lambda) -> ... for all n>=0.

Finally, the maps are the asserted ones. At the level of sections the first chain map is s -> (s|_U,s|_V) and the second is (y,z) -> y|_W - z|_W, by the definitions of alpha_F and beta_F. Passing to cohomology gives exactly the restriction map on the first arrow and the difference of the two restriction maps on the second arrow. The connecting homomorphism is the usual one from a short exact sequence of complexes. This completes the proof.

lemma_332.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(j\ge0\) and \(m\ge1\) be integers, and let \(F_m=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^m)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Suppose \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is spanned over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by the \(\ell\)-adic cycle classes of the base changes to \(X_k\) of closed integral subschemes of \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) of pure codimension \(j\). Then \(F_m\) is semisimple on \(H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), that is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_332.proof:
Write $H:=H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, let $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^q$, and put $F:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$ and $F_m:=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{m})^*$, both $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphisms of $H$. We prove that $F_m$ is the scalar $q^{mj}$, which immediately implies diagonalisability.

Step 0 (finite-dimensionality). $X$ is proper over $\mathbb F_q$, and the constant sheaf $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ lies in $D^b_c(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F_{X_k}^*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$. Applying lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm) with $K=\mathbb Q_\ell[0]$ and $\phi=\psi$ and with $n=2j$ shows that $H$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, and that the induced automorphism on it is precisely the pullback $F$ (equivalently $F_m$ for the $q^m$-power Frobenius). In particular the two formulations of semisimplicity used below are equivalent by lemma_5 (eoinm).

Step 1 (the $q^m$-power Frobenius is the $m$-th power of the $q$-power Frobenius). As automorphisms of the field $k$ one has $\sigma^m=\underbrace{\sigma\circ\cdots\circ\sigma}_{m}$. Hence as $k$-morphisms $X_k\to X_k$,
$$\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^m=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{\circ m}.$$
Pullback on \(\acute{e}tale\) cohomology is a contravariant functor from $k$-schemes to $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, so $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. Taking $g=f=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma$ (the two factors being equal, the order of composition is irrelevant) gives
$$F_m=F^{\circ m}.$$

Step 2 (normalising the cycle classes). Fix once and for all a nonzero $\xi\in\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$. The canonical isomorphism $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))\simeq H\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(j)$, $v\otimes\eta\mapsto\eta\,v$, identifies $H$ with $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$ by sending $v\in H$ to $v\otimes\xi$. For a closed integral subscheme $Z_0\subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ of pure codimension $j$, let $Z:=Z_0\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}}\operatorname{Spec}k\subseteq X_k$ be its base change, let $\mathrm{cl}(Z)\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(j))$ be its $\ell$-adic cycle class, and let $c_{Z_0}\in H$ denote the unique vector with $c_{Z_0}\otimes\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Z)$. These $c_{Z_0}$ are exactly the "cycle classes in $H$" appearing in the hypothesis.

This assignment is independent of the normalisation in the only sense that matters: if $\xi'=\lambda\xi$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, then $\mathrm{cl}(Z)=c_{Z_0}\otimes\xi=(\lambda^{-1}c_{Z_0})\otimes\xi'$, so the vector attached to $Z_0$ is multiplied by the fixed scalar $\lambda^{-1}$, and the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-span of the whole family is unchanged. Thus the spanning hypothesis of the lemma is well posed.

Step 3 (every such class is an eigenvector of $F_m$ with eigenvalue $q^{mj}$). Fix $Z_0$ as above. All the hypotheses of lemma_314 (Spark) are satisfied for our $q$, $X$, $j$, $m$, $\xi$ and $Z_0$: $X$ is smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$, $j\ge0$, $m\ge1$, $\xi\ne0$, and $Z_0\subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ is a closed integral subscheme of pure codimension $j$ whose base change to $k$ is $Z$. That lemma yields
$$F^{m}(c_{Z_0})=q^{mj}\,c_{Z_0}.$$
By Step 1, $F^{m}=F_m$, hence
$$F_m(c_{Z_0})=q^{mj}\,c_{Z_0}\qquad(\ast)$$
for every closed integral $Z_0\subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ of pure codimension $j$. (For $j=0$ this says $F_m$ fixes the classes of the irreducible components of $X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$, the eigenvalue being $q^{0}=1$.)

Step 4 ($F_m$ is a scalar). Let $\mathcal S=\{c_{Z_0}\}$ be the set of vectors occurring in Step 3; by hypothesis $\langle\mathcal S\rangle_{\mathbb Q_\ell}=H$. If $H=0$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $H\ne0$; then $\mathcal S$ is non-empty. Every $v\in H$ is a finite sum $v=\sum_{i=1}^{t}a_i c_{Z_i}$ with $a_i\in\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $Z_i\subseteq X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}$ closed integral of pure codimension $j$. By $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $F_m$ and $(\ast)$,
$$F_m(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{t}a_iF_m(c_{Z_i})=\sum_{i=1}^{t}a_iq^{mj}c_{Z_i}=q^{mj}v.$$
Thus $F_m=q^{mj}\cdot\mathrm{id}_H$; equivalently, two $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear endomorphisms of $H$ that agree on the spanning set $\mathcal S$ are equal, and $F_m$ agrees with $q^{mj}\mathrm{id}$ there.

Step 5 (diagonalisability over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$). Base-changing the equality of Step 4 to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ gives
$$F_m\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathrm{id}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}=q^{mj}\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}.$$
If $H=0$ the space $H\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is the zero space, which is diagonalisable by definition (it has the empty eigenbasis). If $H\ne0$, let $\{e_1,\dots,e_N\}$ be any $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$-basis of $H\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (it exists and $N=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H<\infty$ by Step 0). Each $e_r$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $q^{mj}$, so
$$H\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=E_{q^{mj}}\oplus\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\setminus\{q^{mj}\}}E_\lambda=E_{q^{mj}},\qquad E_\lambda:=\ker\bigl(F_m\otimes1-\lambda\bigr),$$
with $E_\lambda=0$ for $\lambda\ne q^{mj}$. Hence the operator is diagonalisable. Equivalently, its minimal polynomial divides $T-q^{mj}$, a product of distinct linear factors over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ (note $q^{mj}\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}$, so $T-q^{mj}$ is indeed linear and nonzero).

Step 6 (conclusion). By Step 5 the base change of $F_m$ to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is diagonalizable; by lemma_5 (eoinm), applied to $V=H$ and $T=F_m$, this is exactly the statement that $F_m$ is semisimple on $H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. This completes the proof.

lemma_cup_frob_equivariance.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a variety over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. For \(n\ge0\) write \(F_n=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear endomorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) induced by the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. Then for every \(n\ge0\) and all \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\in H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) one has \(F_n(\alpha_1\cup\cdots\cup\alpha_n)=(F_1\alpha_1)\cup\cdots\cup(F_1\alpha_n)\).
lemma_cup_frob_equivariance.proof: Proof. Let sigma:k->k be sigma(c)=c^q and let s=Spec sigma. Since c^q=c for every c in F_q, s is a morphism of F_q-schemes. Write X_k=X x_{Spec F_q} Spec k with projections pr_1 and pr_2. Define F:X_k->X_k to be the base change of s along X->Spec F_q, namely F=id_X x_{Spec F_q} s. Equivalently, F is the unique F_q-morphism with pr_1 o F=pr_1 and pr_2 o F=s o pr_2; on affine coordinate rings it is id tensor sigma on the k-factor. This is the morphism denoted id_{X_k} x Spec sigma in the statement, and it is not the absolute Frobenius. For each n set F_n=F^* on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l). By the proved lemma eoinm/lemma_6a this is a Q_l-linear automorphism, hence an endomorphism. We first prove functoriality of the cup product for the standard Q_l-cohomology. Fix nu>=1 and put Lambda_nu=Z/l^nu. For a scheme Y, let D_nu(Y) be the bounded below derived category of etale sheaves of Lambda_nu-modules, and let Lambda_Y be the constant sheaf. The finite-coefficient etale cohomology is H^m(Y,Lambda_nu)=Hom_{D_nu(Y)}(Lambda_Y,Lambda_Y[m]). For u in H^m(Y,Lambda_nu) and v in H^n(Y,Lambda_nu), define u cup v to be the composite Lambda_Y -> Lambda_Y tensor^L Lambda_Y ->^{u tensor v} Lambda_Y[m] tensor^L Lambda_Y[n] -> Lambda_Y[m+n], where the first and last arrows are the unit and shift identifications. This is the usual cup product; associativity and graded commutativity follow from the associativity and symmetry constraints of the derived tensor product. Let g:Y->Z be a morphism of schemes. Since the coefficients are a constant finite ring, the derived pullback is just the exact inverse-image functor g^{-1}. It is strong symmetric monoidal: g^{-1}Lambda_Z=Lambda_Y and g^{-1}(A tensor^L B)=g^{-1}A tensor^L g^{-1}B. The latter isomorphism follows because tensor product of sheaves is a colimit and inverse image preserves colimits; coherence follows from the universal property of tensor products. Applying g^{-1} to the composite defining u cup v and using these identifications gives exactly the composite defining g^*u cup g^*v. Hence g^*(u cup v)=g^*u cup g^*v for all homogeneous u,v with Lambda_nu-coefficients. For the passage to Q_l, the transition map H^m(Y,Lambda_{nu+1})->H^m(Y,Lambda_nu) is induced by the derived base-change functor T(A)=A tensor^L_{Lambda_{nu+1}} Lambda_nu. This functor is symmetric monoidal: the canonical map (T A tensor^L_{Lambda_nu} T B)->T(A tensor^L_{Lambda_{nu+1}} B) is an isomorphism by associativity of tensor product, and T sends the unit Lambda_{nu+1} to Lambda_nu. It realizes the usual transition map induced by coefficient reduction, so it preserves cup products. Therefore the products are compatible with the inverse system. Define H^m(Y,Z_l)=lim_nu H^m(Y,Lambda_nu); the compatible products give a Z_l-bilinear product. Define H^m(Y,Q_l)=H^m(Y,Z_l) tensor_{Z_l} Q_l and extend the product Q_l-bilinearly. Pullback commutes with the transition maps and with tensoring with Q_l, so the identity g^*(u cup v)=g^*u cup g^*v holds for all homogeneous u,v with Q_l coefficients. The unit 1 in H^0(Y,Q_l) is the identity morphism of the constant sheaf, and g^{-1} sends it to the identity morphism; hence g^*1=1. Apply this to g=F. For homogeneous a in H^r(X_k,Q_l) and b in H^s(X_k,Q_l), we have F_{r+s}(a cup b)=F^*(a cup b)=F^*a cup F^*b=F_r(a) cup F_s(b). We now prove the desired identity by induction on n. For n=0, the empty cup product is 1 in H^0(X_k,Q_l), and F_0(1)=1 by preservation of the unit. For n=1, the statement is exactly the definition of F_1. Assume n>=2 and that the statement holds for n-1. Let beta=alpha_1 cup ... cup alpha_{n-1} in H^{n-1}(X_k,Q_l). Using the binary identity with r=n-1 and s=1, F_n(alpha_1 cup ... cup alpha_n)=F_n(beta cup alpha_n)=F_{n-1}(beta) cup F_1(alpha_n). By the induction hypothesis, F_{n-1}(beta)=F_1(alpha_1) cup ... cup F_1(alpha_{n-1}). Therefore F_n(alpha_1 cup ... cup alpha_n)=(F_1(alpha_1) cup ... cup F_1(alpha_{n-1})) cup F_1(alpha_n)=F_1(alpha_1) cup ... cup F_1(alpha_n), where associativity of the cup product is used in the last step. This completes the induction. No Kunneth formula, Poincare duality, trace map, diagonal class, group law, or semisimplicity was used.

lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field, let \(\ell\) be a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\), let \(U\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(k\), and let \(V\subseteq U\) be an open-and-closed subscheme with complementary open-and-closed subscheme \(W=U\setminus V\).
