Then for all integers \(a\) and \(b\) the restriction homomorphisms identify \(H^{a}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) with \(H^{a}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\oplus H^{a}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^{b}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) with \(H^{b}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\oplus H^{b}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and under these identifications the cup-product pairing \(H^{a}_{c}(U)\times H^{b}(U)\to H^{a+b}_{c}(U)\) is the direct sum of the cup-product pairings of \(V\) and of \(W\).
lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum.proof:
{
  "lemma_id": "lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum",
  "cited_lemmas": [
    {"user_id": "eoinm", "lemma_id": "lemma_hc_affine_space"}
  ],
  "cited_references": [],
  "proof": "PROOF. Throughout, \(\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) denotes the abelian category of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaves (sheaves of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces) on the small \'etale site of \(X\).

CONVENTIONS AND DEFINITIONS. For a separated scheme \(X\) of finite type over \(k\) with structure morphism \(f_X:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) we use the definition of compactly supported cohomology used in the library (the one made explicit in eoinm:lemma_hc_affine_space):
\[ H^n_{c}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^n(\operatorname{Spec}k,\,Rf_{X,!}\mathbb Q_{\ell,X}),\qquad H^n(X,\mathbb Q_\ell):=H^n(\operatorname{Spec}k,\,Rf_{X,*}\mathbb Q_{\ell,X}). \]
Because \(k\) is algebraically closed, the small \'etale topos of \(\operatorname{Spec}k\) is the trivial topos, so \(\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}k,-)\) is exact and there is no spectral sequence when passing from \(Rf_!\) to global sections. The standard identification of \(Rf_!\) with the derived functor of sections with proper support (SGA 4 XVII, 3.2.3) says that for every \(\mathcal F\in\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\),
\[ H^n(\operatorname{Spec}k,Rf_{X,!}\mathcal F)\;=\;R^n\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F),\qquad \Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F): \operatorname{supp}(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k \text{ is proper}\}, \]
where \(\operatorname{supp}(s)=\{x\in|X|: s_{\bar x}\neq 0\}\) is a closed subset of \(X\) (if \(s_{\bar x}=0\) then \(s\) vanishes on an \'etale neighbourhood of \(\bar x\), hence, by descent, on an open neighbourhood of \(x\)). Hence, for every complex \(\mathcal I^\bullet\) of injective objects of \(\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) with \(H^0(\mathcal I^\bullet)=\mathbb Q_{\ell,X}\) and \(H^{q}=0\) for \(q\neq0\),
\[ H^n(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^n(\Gamma(X,\mathcal I^\bullet)),\qquad H^n_c(X,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^n(\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal I^\bullet)). \tag{0.1}\]
(The category \(\mathrm{Sh}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is a Grothendieck category, so it has enough injectives.) Also, for every abelian sheaf \(\mathcal F\) on any site with an initial object, \(\mathcal F(\emptyset)=0\), since the empty family is a covering of \(\emptyset\) and the sheaf condition then forces \(\mathcal F(\emptyset)\) to be the terminal object, which is the zero group.

STEP 0 (trivial case). If \(V=\emptyset\) then \(W=U\), \(H^*_c(\emptyset,\mathbb Q_\ell)=H^*(\emptyset,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) (the terminal scheme \(\emptyset\) has \(\Gamma(\emptyset,\mathcal F)=\mathcal F(\emptyset)=0\)), and both claimed identifications and the compatibility statement reduce to the identity on \(U\). The same holds if \(W=\emptyset\). In the sequel we argue in a way that covers these cases automatically (the summand \((0,0)\) contributes the zero complex).

STEP 1 (\(V\) and \(W\) are separated of finite type over \(k\)). Since \(U\) is of finite type over the field \(k\), \(U\) is noetherian; every subspace of a noetherian space is noetherian, hence quasi-compact, so the open subschemes \(V\) and \(W\) are quasi-compact. An open immersion is locally of finite type, and a quasi-compact locally of finite type morphism is of finite type; thus \(V\to U\) and \(W\to U\) are of finite type, and so are \(V\to k\) and \(W\to k\) by composition. An open immersion is a monomorphism, hence separated, and a composition of separated morphisms is separated; since \(U\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is separated, so are \(V\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) and \(W\to\operatorname{Spec}k\). Thus all four cohomology groups occurring in the statement are defined (in particular \(R(-)_!\) applies).

STEP 2 (\(U\) is the coproduct \(V\amalg W\)). The canonical morphism \(V\amalg W\to U\) obtained by gluing the two open immersions is an open immersion; it is bijective on underlying sets because \(|V|\) and \(|W|=|U|\setminus|V|\) are disjoint and cover \(|U|\). An open immersion that is surjective on points is an isomorphism. Hence \(V\amalg W\xrightarrow{\sim}U\); in particular each of \(j_V:V\hookrightarrow U\) and \(j_W:W\hookrightarrow U\) is simultaneously an open immersion and a closed immersion.

STEP 3 (the \'etale topos of \(U\) is the product of those of \(V\) and \(W\)). Consider
\[ \iota: U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\longrightarrow V_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\times W_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\qquad T\longmapsto (T\times_UV,\;T\times_UW). \]
It is an equivalence of categories, with quasi-inverse \((T_1,T_2)\mapsto T_1\amalg T_2\): indeed \((T_1\amalg T_2)\times_UV=T_1\amalg(T_2\times_UV)=T_1\amalg\emptyset=T_1\), because \(|T_2|\subset |W|\) and \(V\cap W=\emptyset\), and similarly for \(W\); conversely \((T\times_UV)\amalg(T\times_UW)\xrightarrow{\sim}T\) since \(V\amalg W\xrightarrow{\sim}U\) and fibre products commute with coproducts. A family \(\{T_i\to T\}\) in \(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) is an \'etale covering iff each \(T_i\to T\) is \'etale and \(\coprod|T_i|\to|T|\) is surjective; since \(|T|=|T\times_UV|\amalg|T\times_UW|\) and \(|T_i|=|T_i\times_UV|\amalg|T_i\times_UW|\), surjectivity is equivalent to surjectivity of \(\coprod|T_i\times_UV|\to|T\times_UV|\) and of \(\coprod|T_i\times_UW|\to|T\times_UW|\). Thus \(\iota\) is an equivalence of sites (coverings correspond to pairs of coverings), and therefore restriction induces an equivalence of abelian categories
\[ \Phi:\mathrm{Sh}(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathrm{Sh}(V_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\times\mathrm{Sh}(W_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell), \qquad \Phi(\mathcal G)=\bigl(\mathcal G|_{V_{\mathrm{\acute et}}},\ \mathcal G|_{W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}}\bigr), \]
with quasi-inverse \(\Psi(A,B)(T_1,T_2)=A(T_1)\times B(T_2)\) (direct product \(=\) direct sum of abelian groups). Both functors are exact: limits, colimits and the sheaf condition are computed objectwise in a product category, so \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) are exact (equivalently, \(\Phi\) is exact because it is a product of the exact pullback functors \(j_V^*,j_W^*\), and \(\Psi\) is exact as an equivalence with exact quasi-inverse).

Under \(\Phi\) the direct and extension-by-zero images are the two canonical inclusions. Indeed, for \(A\in\mathrm{Sh}(V_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) the direct image along the open immersion is \(j_{V,*}A(T)=A(T\times_UV)\), so
\[ \Phi(j_{V,*}A)(T_1,T_2)=A\bigl((T_1\amalg T_2)\times_UV\bigr)=A(T_1\amalg\emptyset)=A(T_1)\times A(\emptyset)=A(T_1), \]
i.e. \(\Phi(j_{V,*}A)=(A,0)\); similarly \(\Phi(j_{W,*}B)=(0,B)\). For the extension by zero of an open immersion, \(j_{V,!}A(T)=\{s\in A(T\times_UV):\operatorname{supp}(s)\to T \text{ proper}\}\). Since \(j_V\) is also a closed immersion, the base change \(T_1=(T_1\amalg T_2)\times_UV\to T_1\amalg T_2=T\) is a closed immersion, hence proper; for any \(s\in A(T_1)\) the support \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\to T_1\) is a closed immersion, so \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\to T\) is a composition of closed immersions, hence proper. Thus the support condition is vacuous and \(\Phi(j_{V,!}A)=(A,0)=\Phi(j_{V,*}A)\), the canonical map \(j_{V,!}\to j_{V,*}\) being the identity under this description. So
\[ j_{V,!}=j_{V,*}\ \text{is the exact functor}\ A\mapsto(A,0),\qquad j_{W,!}=j_{W,*}\ \text{is the exact functor}\ B\mapsto(0,B). \tag{3.1}\]
Since \(\iota_1:A\mapsto(A,0)\) is both left and right adjoint to the first projection \(\mathrm{pr}_1\), uniqueness of adjoints identifies \(j_V^*\) with \(\Phi^{-1}\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\Phi\) (using that \(j_{V,*}\) is right adjoint to \(j_V^*\)); in particular \(j_V^*\) is exact and, because its right adjoint \(j_{V,*}\) is exact, it preserves injective objects; the same holds for \(j_W^*\).

Pullback of a constant sheaf is the constant sheaf (\(f^*\) is a left adjoint, hence preserves colimits, and the constant \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaf is the colimit of copies of the constant \(\mathbb Z_\ell\)-sheaf). Hence \(\Phi(\mathbb Q_{\ell,U})=(\mathbb Q_{\ell,V},\mathbb Q_{\ell,W})\), and by (3.1)
\[ \mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\ \cong\ j_{V,!}\mathbb Q_{\ell,V}\ \oplus\ j_{W,!}\mathbb Q_{\ell,W} \tag{3.2}\]
(the isomorphism is the sum of the counit maps \(j_{\sigma,!}j_\sigma^*\to\mathrm{id}\); on sections over \(T_1\amalg T_2\) it is the canonical identification of a locally constant \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-valued function on a disjoint union with a pair of such functions).
Finally, the ring \(\Gamma(U,\mathbb Q_{\ell,U})=\Gamma(V,\mathbb Q_{\ell,V})\oplus\Gamma(W,\mathbb Q_{\ell,W})\) contains the orthogonal idempotents \(e_V:=(1_{V},0)\), \(e_W:=(0,1_W)\) with \(e_V+e_W=1\) and \(e_We_V=0\); the decomposition (3.2) is precisely the eigenspace decomposition of the action of \(e_V\). No connectedness of \(V\) or \(W\) is used.

STEP 4 (a compatible system of injective resolutions). Choose injective resolutions \(\mathbb Q_{\ell,V}\to I_V^\bullet\) in \(\mathrm{Sh}(V_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(\mathbb Q_{\ell,W}\to I_W^\bullet\) in \(\mathrm{Sh}(W_{\mathrm{\acute et}},\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and put
\[ J^\bullet:=j_{V,!}I_V^\bullet\oplus j_{W,!}I_W^\bullet . \]
Then \(J^\bullet\) is an injective resolution of \(\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\): exactness of \(0\to\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\to J^\bullet\) is checked by applying the exact equivalence \(\Phi\), which sends it to \(0\to(\mathbb Q_{\ell,V},\mathbb Q_{\ell,W})\to(I_V^\bullet,I_W^\bullet)\), exact by construction; and each term is injective because \(\operatorname{Hom}_U(-,j_{V,!}A)=\operatorname{Hom}_V(j_V^*(-),A)\) is exact when \(A\) is injective (using exactness of \(j_V^*\)), and similarly for \(W\). Define complexes of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces
\[ D^\bullet:=\Gamma_c(U,J^\bullet),\quad D_V^\bullet:=\Gamma_c(V,I_V^\bullet),\quad D_W^\bullet:=\Gamma_c(W,I_W^\bullet), \]
\[ C^\bullet:=\Gamma(U,J^\bullet),\quad C_V^\bullet:=\Gamma(V,I_V^\bullet),\quad C_W^\bullet:=\Gamma(W,I_W^\bullet). \]
By (0.1), \(H^a(D^\bullet)=H^a_c(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^a(D_V^\bullet)=H^a_c(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^a(D_W^\bullet)=H^a_c(W,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(H^b(C^\bullet)=H^b(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), etc.

STEP 5 (the two complexes split literally as direct sums). For each \(q\), the object \(U\in U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) corresponds under \(\iota\) to \((V,W)\), since \(U\times_UV=V\) and \(U\times_UW=W\). Hence, using \(\Phi(J^q)=(I_V^q,I_W^q)\),
\[ \Gamma(U,J^q)=J^q(U)=I_V^q(V)\times I_W^q(W)=\Gamma(V,I_V^q)\oplus\Gamma(W,I_W^q), \]
and the differentials of \(C^\bullet\) are componentwise because they are induced by the morphisms of the pair \((I_V^\bullet,I_W^\bullet)\). Thus
\[ C^\bullet=C_V^\bullet\oplus C_W^\bullet \tag{5.1}\]
as complexes. For \(\Gamma_c\) we must compare properness of supports. Write a section of \(J^q\) over \(U\) as \(s=(s_V,s_W)\) with \(s_V\in I_V^q(V)\), \(s_W\in I_W^q(W)\). Since the stalk of \((A,B)\) at a geometric point of \(V\) (resp. of \(W\)) is the stalk of \(A\) (resp. of \(B\)),
\[ \operatorname{supp}(s)=\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\ \amalg\ \operatorname{supp}(s_W)\subset|U|=|V|\amalg|W|, \]
where \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\subset|V|\) is the support of \(s_V\) as a section over \(V\). We claim \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is proper if and only if both \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(s_W)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) are proper. (\(\Rightarrow\)) \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)=\operatorname{supp}(s)\cap V\) is closed in \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\) because \(V\) is closed in \(U\); a closed subscheme (with its reduced structure) of a proper \(k\)-scheme is proper over \(k\). (\(\Leftarrow\)) Both supports are closed in \(U\) and are open and closed in \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\), and they cover \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\); the morphism \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is of finite type (a closed subscheme of the noetherian \(k\)-scheme \(U\) is of finite type over \(k\)) and separated (\(U\) is separated over \(k\)), so the valuative criterion applies. Uniqueness: the image of \(\operatorname{Spec}R\) for a DVR \(R\) is connected, and \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\) is the disjoint union of the two open-and-closed subsets \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V),\operatorname{supp}(s_W)\), so any two extensions landing in the same one coincide by the uniqueness part for that summand. Existence: a \(K\)-point (\(K=\operatorname{Frac}R\)) has a single image point, lying in one of the two summands, say \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\); the map then factors through \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\), and properness of \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) gives an extension, which cannot land in the other summand because its generic point maps into \(\operatorname{supp}(s_V)\cap\operatorname{supp}(s_W)=\emptyset\). Hence the valuative criterion holds and \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is proper. Therefore, for every sheaf \(\mathcal G=(A,B)\) on \(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\),
\[ \Gamma_c(U,\mathcal G)=\Gamma_c(V,A)\oplus\Gamma_c(W,B), \tag{5.2}\]
functorially; applying this to \(\mathcal G=J^q\) gives, as complexes,
\[ D^\bullet=D_V^\bullet\oplus D_W^\bullet. \tag{5.3}\]

STEP 6 (the restriction homomorphisms are the projections). For the open immersion \(j_V\) (which is also closed) the restriction homomorphism on compact supports is the map induced by the natural transformation \(\Gamma_c(U,-)\to\Gamma_c(V,j_V^*(-))\), \(s\mapsto s|_V\); it is well defined because \(\operatorname{supp}(s|_V)=\operatorname{supp}(s)\cap V\) is closed in \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\) (here one uses that \(V\) is closed in \(U\)) and hence proper over \(k\). Since \(j_V^*\) is exact and preserves injectives and \(j_V^*J^\bullet=I_V^\bullet\) is an injective resolution of \(j_V^*\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}=\mathbb Q_{\ell,V}\), this natural transformation applied to \(J^\bullet\) computes the derived homomorphism \(H^a_c(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^a_c(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Under the identifications (5.3) the map \(D^q\to D_V^q\) is \((s_V,s_W)\mapsto s_V\), the projection onto the first factor; similarly for \(W\). Hence the homomorphism
\[ (i_V^*,i_W^*):H^a_c(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^a_c(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\oplus H^a_c(W,\mathbb Q_\ell) \]
is induced degreewise by the projection \(D_V^\bullet\oplus D_W^\bullet\to (D_V^\bullet\oplus D_W^\bullet)\), i.e. it is the identity, and is therefore an isomorphism. The identical argument with \(\Gamma\) in place of \(\Gamma_c\) (the restriction map \(\Gamma(U,J^q)\to\Gamma(V,I_V^q)\) is the projection, and it computes the usual pullback because \(j_V^*\) is exact) shows that
\[ (i_V^*,i_W^*):H^b(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^b(V,\mathbb Q_\ell)\oplus H^b(W,\mathbb Q_\ell) \]
is an isomorphism. (Equivalently: the inverse of \((i_V^*,i_W^*)\) is the map \((x_V,x_W)\mapsto i_{V,!}(x_V)+i_{W,!}(x_W)\) built from the extension-by-zero homomorphisms, which at the cochain level is literally the inclusion of the direct summands; the relations \(i_\sigma^*i_{\sigma',!}=\delta_{\sigma\sigma'}\mathrm{id}\) and \(i_{V,!}i_V^*+i_{W,!}i_W^*=\mathrm{id}\) hold on the nose, the last one being the action of \(e_V+e_W=1\).)

STEP 7 (the cup product is the direct sum of the component cup products). We use the standard chain-level model of the cup product. Since \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) is a field, every complex of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces is K-flat, so the underived tensor product computes \(\otimes^{\mathbb L}\). The pairing
\[ \mu_U:D^\bullet\otimes C^\bullet\longrightarrow D^\bullet \]
representing the cup product \(H^a_c(U)\times H^b(U)\to H^{a+b}_c(U)\) is the composite
\[ D^\bullet\otimes C^\bullet \xrightarrow{\ \nu\ } \Gamma_c(U,\,J^\bullet\otimes J^\bullet)\xrightarrow{\ \Gamma_c(U,\tilde m)\ } \Gamma_c(U,J^\bullet)=D^\bullet, \tag{7.1}\]
where \(\nu(s\otimes t)=s\otimes t\) and \(\tilde m:J^\bullet\otimes J^\bullet\to J^\bullet\) is a chain map lifting the multiplication \(m_U:\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\otimes\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\to\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\). The map \(\nu\) is well defined: \(\operatorname{supp}(s\otimes t)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(s)\cap\operatorname{supp}(t)\), which is closed in the proper \(k\)-scheme \(\operatorname{supp}(s)\), hence proper over \(k\). The chain map \(\tilde m\) exists and is unique up to homotopy by the comparison theorem for injective resolutions, since \(J^\bullet\otimes J^\bullet\) is a complex of flat sheaves (all \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-sheaves are flat over the field \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), and \(\otimes\) is exact) with cohomology \(\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\otimes^{\mathbb L}\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\simeq\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\), while \(J^\bullet\) is a K-injective resolution of \(\mathbb Q_{\ell,U}\); the composite (7.1) is independent of the choice of \(\tilde m\) up to chain homotopy and computes the usual cup product.

Now compute everything componentwise. The equivalence \(\Phi\) is compatible with the tensor product: bilinear maps of sheaves on \(U_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) are the same as pairs of bilinear maps on \(V_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\) and \(W_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\), so \(\Phi(\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal G)=\Phi(\mathcal F)\otimes\Phi(\mathcal G)\) componentwise, i.e. \((A,B)\otimes(A',B')=(A\otimes A',\,B\otimes B')\). Together with (3.1) this gives
\[ J^p\otimes J^q=\bigl(j_{V,!}(I_V^p\otimes I_V^q)\bigr)\oplus\bigl(j_{W,!}(I_W^p\otimes I_W^q)\bigr),\qquad j_{V,!}A\otimes j_{W,!}B=(A,0)\otimes(0,B)=(0,0)=0, \tag{7.2}\]
the vanishing of the mixed terms being the sheaf-theoretic shadow of \(e_Ve_W=0\) (equivalently, it is the restriction to \(V\cap W=\emptyset\)). Applying (5.2) to the sheaves \(I_V^\bullet\otimes I_V^\bullet\) and \(I_W^\bullet\otimes I_W^\bullet\) yields
\[ \Gamma_c(U,J^\bullet\otimes J^\bullet)=\Gamma_c(V,I_V^\bullet\otimes I_V^\bullet)\oplus\Gamma_c(W,I_W^\bullet\otimes I_W^\bullet). \tag{7.3}\]
Under (5.1), (5.3) and (7.3) the map \(\nu\) is block diagonal by construction:
\[ \nu(D_V^p\otimes C_V^q)\subseteq\Gamma_c(V,I_V^p\otimes I_V^q),\quad \nu(D_W^p\otimes C_W^q)\subseteq\Gamma_c(W,I_W^p\otimes I_W^q),\quad \nu(D_V^p\otimes C_W^q)=\nu(D_W^p\otimes C_V^

q)=0,
because the mixed tensor product in (7.2) is zero. More explicitly, under the identifications (5.1), (5.3) and (7.3), a section of D_V^p\otimes C_W^q is represented by (s_V,0)\otimes(0,t_W)=(0,0), and similarly for D_W^p\otimes C_V^q.

It remains to identify the diagonal blocks. The cross Hom groups vanish:
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_U(j_{V,!}A,j_{W,!}B)
=\operatorname{Hom}_V(A,j_V^*j_{W,!}B)
=\operatorname{Hom}_V(A,0)=0,
\]
and similarly \operatorname{Hom}_U(j_{W,!}A,j_{V,!}B)=0, because j_V^*j_{W,!}=0 (equivalently V\cap W=\emptyset). Hence any chain map J^ ullet\otimes J^ ullet	o J^ ullet is block diagonal with respect to the decomposition (7.2). In particular \tilde m has the form
\[
	ilde m=	ilde m_V\oplus	ilde m_W,
\quad
	ilde m_V:j_{V,!}(I_V^ ullet\otimes I_V^ ullet)	o j_{V,!}I_V^ ullet,
\quad
	ilde m_W:j_{W,!}(I_W^ ullet\otimes I_W^ ullet)	o j_{W,!}I_W^ ullet.
\]
Applying the exact monoidal pullback j_V^* gives a chain map
\[
j_V^*	ilde m_V:I_V^ ullet\otimes I_V^ ullet	o I_V^ ullet
\]
which lifts the multiplication map m_V:\mathbb Q_{\ell,V}\otimes\mathbb Q_{\ell,V}	o\mathbb Q_{\ell,V}, because j_V^*m_U=m_V. The standard cup product on V is, by the same construction as in (7.1), the map on cohomology induced by any chain map lifting m_V; uniqueness up to chain homotopy (comparison theorem for injective resolutions, using that all \mathbb Q_\ell-sheaves are flat) shows that this induced map is independent of the chosen lift. Therefore, for cocycles s_V\in D_V^a and t_V\in C_V^b,
\[
[	ilde m_V(s_V\otimes t_V)]=[s_V]\cup_V[t_V].
\]
The analogous statement holds for W.

Now take x\in H^a_c(U,\mathbb Q_\ell) and y\in H^b(U,\mathbb Q_\ell). Under the isomorphisms proved in Step 6 write
\[
x\leftrightarrow(x_V,x_W),\qquad y\leftrightarrow(y_V,y_W).
\]
Choose cocycle representatives (s_V,s_W)\in D^a and (t_V,t_W)\in C^b. Then the composite (7.1) sends s\otimes t to
\[
\Gamma_c(U,	ilde m)(s\otimes t)
=
(	ilde m_V(s_V\otimes t_V),	ilde m_W(s_W\otimes t_W)).
\]
Passing to cohomology and using the preceding paragraph gives
\[
x\cup_U y
=
(x_V\cup_V y_V,\;x_W\cup_W y_W).
\]
This is precisely the assertion that, under the restriction identifications of Step 6, the cup-product pairing on U is the direct sum of the cup-product pairings on V and on W. The same formula is valid when V or W is empty, since the corresponding summand is the zero complex and the zero cohomology group.

Thus the restriction homomorphisms identify both H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^b_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell) with the direct sums of the corresponding groups for V and W, and the cup-product pairing is compatible with these identifications as claimed. QED."
}

lemma_333.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell be a prime different from p, let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_q, let k be an algebraic closure of F_q, let H be a very ample divisor on X defined over F_q, let xi be the ell-adic cycle class of H in H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell) via a fixed choice of a nonzero element of Q_ell(1), and let L be cup product with xi. For every integer n with 0 <= n <= d, the Q_ell-linear map L^{d-n}: H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ell) is injective if and only if it is surjective.
lemma_333.proof:
Fix an integer n with 0 <= n <= d, and put
  V := H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell),   W := H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ell).
We prove that T := L^{d-n} : V -> W is injective if and only if it is surjective. The argument has four steps: the map is a well-defined linear map; both V and W are finite dimensional; Poincare duality forces dim V = dim W; and for linear maps between equal-dimensional finite-dimensional spaces injectivity and surjectivity coincide.

Step 0 (T is a well-defined Q_ell-linear map V -> W).
Since H is very ample on X, it is an effective Cartier divisor of pure codimension 1 defined over F_q, so its l-adic cycle class is an element of H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell(1)). By definition of the Tate twist, Q_ell(1) is a one-dimensional Q_ell-vector space; fixing a nonzero xi_0 in Q_ell(1) identifies H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell) with H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell) tensor Q_ell(1) = H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell(1)) via v |-> v tensor xi_0 (this is an isomorphism because tensoring by a one-dimensional vector space is an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces). Hence there is a unique vector, denoted xi, in H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell) with cl(H) = xi tensor xi_0, exactly as in the statement. Thus xi is a well-defined element of H^2_et(X_k, Q_ell).
For m >= 0 write xi^m for the m-fold cup product xi cup ... cup xi, an element of H^{2m}_et(X_k, Q_ell) (m = 0 gives the unit 1 in H^0). Cup product is Q_ell-bilinear H^a_et(X_k,Q_ell) x H^b_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{a+b}_et(X_k,Q_ell); therefore for y, y' in V and lambda in Q_ell,
  T(lambda y + y') = (lambda y + y') cup xi^{d-n} = lambda (y cup xi^{d-n}) + (y' cup xi^{d-n}) = lambda T(y) + T(y'),
by additivity in the first argument and Q_ell-homogeneity in the first argument. Also T(y) lies in H^{n + 2(d-n)} = H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) = W by the grading of the cup product. So T = L^{d-n} is a well-defined Q_ell-linear homomorphism V -> W. (Note that neither the very ampleness of H nor its being defined over F_q is used anywhere below; only that xi is some element of H^2.)

Step 1 (finite dimensionality).
X is projective over F_q, hence proper over F_q. Apply the proved lemma lemma_45_finite_frob (user eoinm) with X there equal to our X and with K equal to the constant sheaf Q_ell on X_k, equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism psi: F_X^* Q_ell -> Q_ell supplied by that lemma. Its first assertion gives, for every integer r, that H^r_et(X_k, Q_ell) is finite dimensional over Q_ell. In particular
  dim_{Q_ell} V < infinity   and   dim_{Q_ell} W < infinity.

Step 2 (Poincare duality: a perfect pairing V x W -> Q_ell(-d)).
Apply the proved lemma lemma_77 (user eoinm) with m := 1 and Y := X. Its hypotheses are satisfied: X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected and of pure dimension d over F_q = F_{q^1}, k is an algebraic closure of F_q and ell != p. Because 0 <= n <= d we have 0 <= n <= 2d and d <= 2d - n <= 2d, so part (b) of that lemma applies with r := n: the pairing
  <-,-> : V x W -> Q_ell(-d),   <x, y> := tr(x cup y),
where tr = tr_X : H^{2d}_et(X_k, Q_ell) ~-> Q_ell(-d) is the normalised Poincare-duality trace, is PERFECT. By definition, perfectness means that both induced maps
  phi_V : V -> Hom_{Q_ell}(W, Q_ell(-d)),  x |-> (y |-> <x,y>),
  phi_W : W -> Hom_{Q_ell}(V, Q_ell(-d)),  y |-> (x |-> <x,y>)
are isomorphisms of Q_ell-vector spaces.

Step 3 (dim V = dim W).
We compute dim Hom_{Q_ell}(W, Q_ell(-d)) explicitly. The Tate twist Q_ell(-d) is, by definition, a one-dimensional Q_ell-vector space; fix a nonzero eta in Q_ell(-d). Let w_1, ..., w_s be a Q_ell-basis of W (s = dim W, possibly s = 0, in which case W = 0 and the computation below is the empty one giving dimension 0). For 1 <= i <= s define f_i : W -> Q_ell(-d) on the basis by f_i(w_j) = delta_{ij} eta and extend Q_ell-linearly; this is legitimate because a function on a basis determines a unique linear map into any target space.
- Linear independence: if sum_i a_i f_i = 0 with a_i in Q_ell, evaluating at w_j gives 0 = (sum_i a_i f_i)(w_j) = a_j eta; since eta != 0 and Q_ell(-d) is a Q_ell-vector space with trivial annihilator, a_j = 0 for every j.
- Spanning: given g : W -> Q_ell(-d), write g(w_j) = b_j eta with b_j in Q_ell (possible since eta spans the one-dimensional target). Then g and sum_j b_j f_j agree on the basis w_1,...,w_s, hence agree everywhere by linearity.
Thus f_1,...,f_s is a basis, so dim Hom_{Q_ell}(W, Q_ell(-d)) = s = dim W. Composing with the isomorphism phi_V of Step 2 yields
  dim_{Q_ell} V = dim_{Q_ell} Hom_{Q_ell}(W, Q_ell(-d)) = dim_{Q_ell} W.
(One may equally use phi_W; both halves of perfectness give the same conclusion.)

Step 4 (rank-nullity: injective <=> surjective when dim V = dim W).
Both ker T and im T are Q_ell-subspaces. Choose a basis e_1,...,e_r of ker T and extend it to a basis e_1,...,e_r, v_1,...,v_t of V (possible by the standard basis-extension theorem for vector spaces, valid in every dimension, in particular in finite dimension). Then:
- the family T(v_1),...,T(v_t) spans im T, since any element of im T has the form T(x) with x = sum_i a_i e_i + sum_j b_j v_j and T(e_i) = 0, so T(x) = sum_j b_j T(v_j);
- it is linearly independent, since sum_j b_j T(v_j) = 0 means T(sum_j b_j v_j) = 0, so sum_j b_j v_j in ker T = span(e_1,...,e_r), forcing all b_j = 0 because e_1,...,e_r,v_1,...,v_t are linearly independent.
Hence dim V = r + t = dim ker T + dim im T (the rank-nullity relation).

(=>) Suppose T is injective. Then ker T = 0, so dim im T = dim V. By Step 3, dim im T = dim W. A subspace U of a finite-dimensional space W with dim U = dim W equals W: indeed, if U were a proper subspace, a basis of U would extend to a basis of W containing at least one vector outside U, giving dim U < dim W, a contradiction. Applying this to U = im T gives im T = W, i.e. T is surjective.

(<=) Suppose T is surjective. Then im T = W, so dim im T = dim W = dim V by Step 3, and rank-nullity gives dim ker T = dim V - dim im T = 0. A vector space of dimension 0 is the zero space, so ker T = 0 and T is injective.

Combining the two implications, L^{d-n} : H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> H^{2d-n}_et(X_k, Q_ell) is injective if and only if it is surjective.

Edge cases. For n = d the map is L^0 = id_{H^d}, which Steps 1-4 cover verbatim (dim V = dim W holds by Step 3, and the identity is both injective and surjective, consistent with the equivalence). For n = 0 the same argument applies with V = H^0_et(X_k,Q_ell) and W = H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_ell); since X is geometrically connected these are both one-dimensional, and the equivalence again follows from Steps 3-4. If some H^n happens to vanish, then Step 3 shows H^{2d-n} also vanishes and the unique map 0 -> 0 is both injective and surjective, so the equivalence holds trivially, as already contained in the rank-nullity argument above. This completes the proof of the lemma.

lemma_gysin_trace_compatibility.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let \ell \neq \operatorname{char}(k) be prime, and let d \ge 1. Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over k, let Y be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d-1 over k, and let i: Y \hookrightarrow X be a regular closed immersion of pure codimension 1. Let i_*: H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell(d-1)) \to H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(d)) be the Gysin homomorphism, and for Z \in \{X,Y\} let \operatorname{tr}_Z: H^{2\dim Z}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(\dim Z)) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell be the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}_Z(z)) = [\kappa(z):k] for closed points z of Z. Then \operatorname{tr}_X(i_*\alpha) = \operatorname{tr}_Y(\alpha) for every \alpha \in H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell(d-1)).
lemma_gysin_trace_compatibility.proof:
Proof. We use the standard étale-cohomological conventions for the symbols appearing in the statement. For a regular closed immersion j:Z\hookrightarrow W of pure codimension c between smooth k-varieties, the cycle class of Z in W is the Gysin image of the unit, cl_W(Z)=j_*(1). In particular, if z is a closed point of a smooth e-dimensional k-variety Z, then the closed immersion z_0:\operatorname{Spec}k\hookrightarrow Z is regular of pure codimension e, and cl_Z(z)=z_{0*}(1), where 1\in H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell). We also use the standard functoriality of Gysin maps for composites of regular closed immersions: if Z\xrightarrow{j}Y\xrightarrow{i}X are regular closed immersions, then (i\circ j)_*=i_*\circ j_*. No trace-adjunction identity for the Gysin map is used.

Since k is algebraically closed, every closed point of a finite type k-scheme has residue field k. Hence for every closed point z of a k-scheme of finite type, [\kappa(z):k]=1. The variety Y is non-empty of finite type over k, so it has a closed point y; because k is algebraically closed, y is k-rational. Put x=i(y). The case d=1 is included: then Y=\operatorname{Spec}k and y_0 is the identity.

First we record the dimension of the top twisted cohomology groups. Let Z be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension e over k. Poincaré duality gives a perfect \mathbb Q_\ell-linear pairing
H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(e))\longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell,
(a,b)\longmapsto \operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup b).
Because Z is geometrically connected, H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell. Perfectness says that the linear map
H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(e))\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell),\mathbb Q_\ell),
b\longmapsto (a\longmapsto \operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup b))
is an isomorphism. Taking a=1 and using that 1\cup b=b identifies this map with \operatorname{tr}_Z itself. Since H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell, its dual is also one-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell. Hence H^{2e}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(e)) is one-dimensional and \operatorname{tr}_Z is an isomorphism.

Apply this to Z=Y, where e=d-1, and to Z=X, where e=d. The normalisation in the statement gives
\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y))=[\kappa(y):k]=1,
\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}_X(x))=[\kappa(x):k]=1.
Therefore \mathrm{cl}_Y(y) is a basis of H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell(d-1)), and \mathrm{cl}_X(x) is a basis of H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(d)).

We claim that i_*(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y))=\mathrm{cl}_X(x). Let y_0:\operatorname{Spec}k\hookrightarrow Y be the closed immersion corresponding to y. Since Y is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k and y is a k-rational point, y_0 is a regular closed immersion of pure codimension d-1. By the definition of the cycle class of a closed point,
\mathrm{cl}_Y(y)=y_{0*}(1).
The composite x_0=i\circ y_0:\operatorname{Spec}k\hookrightarrow X is the closed immersion corresponding to the closed point x=i(y). It is regular of pure codimension d, and again by the definition of the cycle class of a closed point,
\mathrm{cl}_X(x)=x_{0*}(1)=(i\circ y_0)_*(1).
By functoriality of Gysin maps for composites of regular closed immersions,
(i\circ y_0)_*=i_*\circ y_{0*}.
Therefore
i_*(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y))=i_*(y_{0*}(1))=(i\circ y_0)_*(1)=x_{0*}(1)=\mathrm{cl}_X(x).

Now let \alpha\in H^{2d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Q_\ell(d-1)) be arbitrary. Since \mathrm{cl}_Y(y) is a basis, there is a unique \lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell such that
\alpha=\lambda\,\mathrm{cl}_Y(y).
Using the linearity of i_* and the claim above,
i_*(\alpha)=\lambda\,i_*(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y))=\lambda\,\mathrm{cl}_X(x).
Applying the traces and using their normalisation gives
\operatorname{tr}_Y(\alpha)=\lambda\,\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}_Y(y))=\lambda,
and
\operatorname{tr}_X(i_*(\alpha))=\lambda\,\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}_X(x))=\lambda.
Hence \operatorname{tr}_X(i_*\alpha)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(\alpha) for every \alpha. This proves the lemma.

lemma_gysin_frobenius_weight.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(c\ge1\) be an integer, and let \(Z\subset Y\) be a closed subscheme which is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-c\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), with closed immersion \(i:Z\hookrightarrow Y\). Let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and for \(T\in\{Y,Z\}\) put \(t_T:=\dim T\) and let \(\operatorname{tr}_T:H^{2t_T}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(T_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-t_T)\) be the trace isomorphism normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_T(\mathrm{cl}(t_0))=[\kappa(t_0):\mathbb F_q]\) for closed points \(t_0\in T\); for \(s\ge0\) set \(\operatorname{tr}_T^{(s)}:=\operatorname{tr}_T\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell(-s)}\). Let \(0\le m\le 2(d-c)\) and let \(i_{!}:H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(-c)\to H^{m+2c}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the unique \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map such that \(\operatorname{tr}_Y(i_{!}u\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Z^{(c)}(u\cup i^*b)\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), under the identification \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-(d-c))\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell(-c)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), for every \(b\in H^{2d-m-2c}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F_Y\circ i_{!}=i_{!}\circ(F_Z\otimes q^{c}\,\mathrm{id})\), where \(F_T=(\mathrm{id}_{T_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) and \(\sigma(x)=x^q\).
lemma_gysin_frobenius_weight.proof:
We prove the required Frobenius compatibility.

Notation. For T in {Y,Z}, let t_T=dim T and let f_T:T_k->T_k be the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism id_T x Spec sigma, so F_T=f_T^*. All tensor products are over Q_l. We use the standard identifications H^*(T_k,Q_l(-s))=H^*(T_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(-s) and Q_l(-(d-c)) tensor Q_l(-c)=Q_l(-d). For s>=0 write F_T^{(-s)} for the automorphism F_T tensor q^s id on H^*(T_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(-s).

1. Preliminary facts.
(i) Pullback by a morphism is a ring homomorphism. Hence F_T(alpha cup beta)=F_T alpha cup F_T beta. This follows from alpha cup beta=Delta_T^*(alpha boxtimes beta) and (f_T x f_T) Delta_T=Delta_T f_T.
(ii) Since i is defined over F_q, the base-changed square commutes: i_k f_Z=f_Y i_k. Therefore i^*F_Y=F_Z i^*.
(iii) Frobenius on negative Tate twists. Lemma_78 says that arithmetic Frobenius on Q_l(j), j>=0, is multiplication by q^{-j}; for j=0 this is the identity. Identify Q_l(-s)=Hom_{Q_l}(Q_l(s),Q_l). The induced action on the dual is phi -> (v -> phi(F_{Q_l(s)}^{-1}v)), because F on Q_l is identity. Since F_{Q_l(s)}=q^{-s} id, its inverse is q^s id, so F phi=q^s phi. Thus F acts on Q_l(-s) as multiplication by q^s. Consequently F_T^{(-s)}(x tensor eta)=F_T x tensor q^s eta.
(iv) Traces. The variety Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_q. The closed subscheme Z is projective over F_q because it is closed in the projective F_q-scheme Y, and by hypothesis it is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-c. Hence lemma_77(a), applied with extension exponent 1 to Y and to Z, gives canonical isomorphisms tr_T:H^{2t_T}_et(T_k,Q_l) -> Q_l(-t_T), normalised by tr_T(cl(t_0))=[kappa(t_0):F_q] for closed points t_0 in T, and satisfying tr_T(F_T w)=q^{t_T} tr_T(w). For s>=0 define tr_T^{(s)}=tr_T tensor id_{Q_l(-s)}. Then for w in H^{2t_T}_et(T_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(-s), tr_T^{(s)}(F_T^{(-s)}w)=q^{t_T+s} tr_T^{(s)}(w): on a pure tensor w=w_0 tensor eta this is tr_T(F_T w_0) tensor q^s eta=q^{t_T}tr_T(w_0) tensor q^s eta=q^{t_T+s}tr_T^{(s)}(w), and the general case follows by linearity.

2. Existence and uniqueness of i_!.
Fix u in H^m_et(Z_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(-c). The degrees match: deg(u)+deg(i^*b)=m+(2d-m-2c)=2(d-c), so u cup i^*b lies in H^{2(d-c)}_et(Z_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(-c). Define a Q_l-linear functional L_u on H^{2d-m-2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l) by L_u(b)=tr_Z^{(c)}(u cup i^*b). The condition 0<=m<=2(d-c) implies 0<=m+2c<=2d. By lemma_45_finite_frob, applied to the constant Q_l-sheaf with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure on the proper F_q-schemes Y and Z, these cohomology groups are finite-dimensional over Q_l. By lemma_77(b) applied to Y and to n=m+2c, the pairing P_Y(a,b)=tr_Y(a cup b) from H^{m+2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l) x H^{2d-m-2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l) to Q_l(-d) is perfect. Therefore there exists a unique element a_u in H^{m+2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l) such that P_Y(a_u,b)=L_u(b) for all b. Define i_!u=a_u. If u,u' are two elements and lambda,mu in Q_l, then L_{lambda u+mu u'}=lambda L_u+mu L_{u'} by bilinearity of cup product and linearity of traces; uniqueness gives i_!(lambda u+mu u')=lambda i_!u+mu i_!u'. Thus i_! is Q_l-linear.

3. Comparison of Frobenius.
Let u be in H^m_et(Z_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(-c) and b in H^{2d-m-2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l). We prove that F_Y i_!u and i_!F_Z^{(-c)}u have the same pairing with every element of H^{2d-m-2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l). Since F_Y preserves cohomological degree and is an automorphism of this group by lemma_6a, it suffices to compare their pairings with F_Y b.

First compute:
tr_Y(F_Y(i_!u) cup F_Y b)
=tr_Y(F_Y(i_!u cup b)) by (i)
=q^d tr_Y(i_!u cup b) by trace equivariance for Y in (iv)
=q^d tr_Z^{(c)}(u cup i^*b) by the defining property of i_!.

Second compute:
tr_Y(i_!(F_Z^{(-c)}u) cup F_Y b)
=tr_Z^{(c)}(F_Z^{(-c)}u cup i^*F_Y b) by the defining property of i_! applied to F_Z^{(-c)}u and F_Y b
=tr_Z^{(c)}(F_Z^{(-c)}u cup F_Z i^*b) by (ii)
=tr_Z^{(c)}(F_Z^{(-c)}(u cup i^*b)) by compatibility of the twisted cup product with Frobenius. Indeed, if u=x tensor eta with x in H^m_et(Z_k,Q_l) and eta in Q_l(-c), and gamma=i^*b, then (F_Z^{(-c)}u) cup (F_Z gamma)=(F_Z x tensor q^c eta) cup (F_Z gamma)=(F_Z x cup F_Z gamma) tensor q^c eta=F_Z(x cup gamma) tensor q^c eta=F_Z^{(-c)}((x tensor eta) cup gamma); the general case follows by linearity.
=q^{(d-c)+c} tr_Z^{(c)}(u cup i^*b) by twisted trace equivariance for Z in (iv), using t_Z=d-c
=q^d tr_Z^{(c)}(u cup i^*b).

Thus tr_Y(F_Y(i_!u) cup F_Y b)=tr_Y(i_!(F_Z^{(-c)}u) cup F_Y b) for all b. Put D=F_Y i_!u - i_!F_Z^{(-c)}u in H^{m+2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l). Then tr_Y(D cup F_Y b)=0 for all b. Since F_Y is surjective on H^{2d-m-2c}_et(Y_k,Q_l), every c in this group is F_Y b for some b; hence tr_Y(D cup c)=0 for all c. By perfectness of P_Y, D=0. Therefore F_Y i_!u=i_!F_Z^{(-c)}u for every u. Since F_Z^{(-c)}=F_Z tensor q^c id, this is exactly F_Y o i_!=i_! o (F_Z tensor q^c id).

All cases are covered by the hypothesis 0<=m<=2(d-c); no degenerate case m+2c>2d occurs. This proves the lemma.

lemma_338.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p>0\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(U\) be a separated scheme of finite type over \(k\) of pure dimension \(d\ge1\). Write \(H^a_c=H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^a=H^a_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), and suppose that for every integer \(a\) the cup-product pairing \(H^a_c\times H^{2d-a}\to H^{2d}_c\) induces an isomorphism \(H^a_c\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{2d-a},H^{2d}_c)\). If \(H^m=0\) for every integer \(m>d\), then \(H^m_c=0\) for every integer \(m<d\).
lemma_338.proof:
We prove the claim by a direct degree count against the hypothesised Poincar\'e--duality-type isomorphism; no finiteness, purity, or characteristic hypothesis is actually needed beyond what is stated.

**Setup and notation.** For each integer $a$ the cup product with compact supports gives a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-bilinear map
$$\mu_a:\quad H^a_c\times H^{2d-a}\longrightarrow H^{2d}_c,\qquad (v,w)\longmapsto v\cup w,$$\nwhich is well defined because compactly supported cohomology is a module over ordinary cohomology (cap/cup product of a compact support class with an arbitrary class has compact support). The hypothesis of the lemma is that the induced linear map
$$\theta_a:\; H^a_c\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-a},\,H^{2d}_c\bigr),\qquad \theta_a(v)(w)=v\cup w,$$\nis an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, for **every** integer $a$.

**Step 1: fix a degree below the middle.** Let $m$ be an arbitrary integer with $m<d$. Since $m$ and $d$ are integers, $m\le d-1$. Consider the integer
$$n:=2d-m.$$
Then
$$n=2d-m\;\ge\;2d-(d-1)=d+1\;>\;d.$$
This inequality is valid for every $m<d$, including negative $m$: if $m<0$ then $n=2d-m>2d\ge d+1$ (as $d\ge1$), so the same conclusion $n>d$ holds. Thus the single estimate $n>d$ covers all cases uniformly; no case distinction on the sign of $m$ is required.

**Step 2: the dual ordinary group vanishes.** By the second hypothesis of the lemma, $H^t=0$ for every integer $t>d$. Applying this to $t=n=2d-m$, which we have just shown satisfies $n>d$, we obtain
$$H^{2d-m}=H^n=0,$$\nthe zero $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space.

**Step 3: the Hom-space out of the zero space is zero.** Let $W$ be any $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space (in our application $W=H^{2d}_c$, whose dimension, finite or not, is irrelevant). A $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map $0\to W$ is a function from the singleton set $\{0\}$ to $W$ preserving the vector-space structure; there is exactly one such function, namely the map sending $0$ to $0$. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,W)$ consists of a single element, the zero map, and is therefore the trivial $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space:
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,W)=0.$$
In particular $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-m},H^{2d}_c\bigr)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,H^{2d}_c)=0$.

**Step 4: conclude for $H^m_c$.** Apply the assumed isomorphism $\theta_a$ at $a=m$:
$$\theta_m:\; H^m_c\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(H^{2d-m},\,H^{2d}_c\bigr).$$
By Step 3 the target is the zero vector space. Since $\theta_m$ is in particular a bijection of underlying sets, $H^m_c$ is in bijection with a singleton; hence $H^m_c$ has exactly one element, namely $0$, i.e.
$$H^m_c=0.$$
(Concretely: for any $v\in H^m_c$, the linear functional $w\mapsto v\cup w$ on $H^{2d-m}=0$ is the zero functional, so $\theta_m(v)=0=\theta_m(0)$, and injectivity of $\theta_m$ forces $v=0$.)

**Step 5: remove the choice of $m$.** The integer $m<d$ was arbitrary, and Steps 1--4 apply verbatim to every such $m$ (positive, zero, or negative). Therefore
$$H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for every integer }m<d,$$\nwhich is exactly the desired conclusion.

**Remarks on the hypotheses used.** The argument used only (i) the stated isomorphism $\theta_a$ for the specific degree $a=m$, (ii) the vanishing $H^t=0$ for $t>d$, and (iii) the elementary inequality $m<d\Rightarrow 2d-m>d$. The assumptions that $k$ is algebraically closed of characteristic $p>0$, that $\ell\ne p$, that $U$ is separated of finite type, and that $U$ is of pure dimension $d\ge1$, are the natural geometric context in which the duality hypothesis $\theta_a$ is expected to hold (Poincar\'e duality for smooth $U$, where $H^{2d}_c\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$), but they play no further role in this formal implication; in particular no finite-dimensionality of any $H^a$ or $H^a_c$ is needed, since $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(0,W)=0$ holds for every $W$. This completes the proof.

lemma_339.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) be smooth projective varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). For \(Z\in\{X_1,X_2,X_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}X_2\}\) write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), for the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). If \(F_{X_1}\) and \(F_{X_2}\) are each diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_i)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\), then \(F_{X_1\times X_2}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((X_1\times_{\mathbb F_q}X_2)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
lemma_339.proof:
Write, for a scheme Z of finite type over F_q, H^i(Z) := H^i_et(Z_k, Q_ell) with k = overline(F_q), and write F_Z := (id_{Z_k} x Spec sigma)^* with sigma(c) = c^q. Put X := X_1 x_{F_q} X_2. We must show: for every n >= 0, the Q_ell-linear automorphism F_X of H^n(X) becomes diagonalizable after extending scalars to Qbar_ell.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of the Frobenius operators). Let Z range over {X_1, X_2, X}. Each of X_1, X_2 is smooth projective over F_q, and a product of smooth projective F_q-schemes is again smooth and projective over F_q (smoothness and projectivity are preserved under base change and composition, and X is a fibre product of projective F_q-schemes, hence projective; the fibre product of smooth F_q-schemes is smooth). Thus all three Z are smooth projective over F_q. By lemma_3 there is a canonical isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces with arithmetic Frobenius action, Ext^i_{D^b_c(Z_bar,Q_ell)}(IC_Z, IC_Z) ~-> H^i_et(Z_bar, Q_ell) = H^i(Z); by lemma_17 the group Ext^i_{D^b_c(Z_bar,Q_ell)}(IC_Z,IC_Z) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell. Hence each H^i(Z) is a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space. By lemma_6a, for every Z and every i the pullback F_Z = (id x sigma)^* is a Q_ell-linear automorphism of H^i(Z) (with inverse the geometric Frobenius (id x sigma^{-1})^*). In particular all operators appearing below are invertible Q_ell-linear operators on finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces, so the lemmas of linear algebra we invoke apply.

Step 2 (translation of the hypothesis). By lemma_5, for a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space V and a linear operator T on V, T is semisimple on V if and only if T tensor Qbar_ell is diagonalizable on V tensor_Qell Qbar_ell. The hypothesis of the present lemma therefore says precisely:
   (H1) F_{X_1} is semisimple on H^i(X_1) for every i >= 0;
   (H2) F_{X_2} is semisimple on H^j(X_2) for every j >= 0.
We shall prove that for each n >= 0 the operator F_X on H^n(X) is semisimple, and then conclude by the other direction of lemma_5.

Step 3 (semisimplicity on each tensor-product summand). Fix n >= 0. The index set I_n := {(i,j) in Z_{>=0}^2 : i + j = n} is finite (it has exactly n+1 elements). For each (i,j) in I_n set V_{i,j} := H^i(X_1) tensor_{Q_ell} H^j(X_2), which is finite-dimensional over Q_ell (its dimension is dim H^i(X_1) * dim H^j(X_2)), and set T_{i,j} := F_{X_1}|_{H^i(X_1)} tensor F_{X_2}|_{H^j(X_2)} in End_{Q_ell}(V_{i,j}). By Step 1 both restrictions are invertible, hence so is their tensor product (the tensor product of invertible maps is invertible, with inverse the tensor product of the inverses). By (H1), (H2) and Step 2, F_{X_1}|_{H^i(X_1)} and F_{X_2}|_{H^j(X_2)} are semisimple. Lemma_35(i) applied to these two invertible semisimple operators gives that T_{i,j} is semisimple on V_{i,j}. (Concretely, and as is checked inside lemma_35: choosing Q_ell-bases of eigenvectors e_1,...,e_a of F_{X_1}|_{H^i(X_1)} and f_1,...,f_b of F_{X_2}|_{H^j(X_2)} — possible by semisimplicity, equivalently by diagonalizability over Qbar_ell together with lemma_5 — the a*b elements e_p tensor f_q satisfy T_{i,j}(e_p tensor f_q) = alpha_p beta_q (e_p tensor f_q), and they form a basis of V_{i,j}, so T_{i,j} is semisimple.)

Step 4 (semisimplicity on the direct sum). Consider W_n := direct sum_{(i,j) in I_n} V_{i,j} and the operator A_n := direct sum_{(i,j) in I_n} T_{i,j}. Each T_{i,j} is invertible (Step 3), so A_n is an invertible Q_ell-linear automorphism of the finite-dimensional space W_n. By Step 3 every T_{i,j} is semisimple, and lemma_9 (a direct-sum operator is semisimple if and only if each block is) applied to the finite family {T_{i,j}}_{(i,j) in I_n} yields: A_n is semisimple on W_n.

Step 5 (transport across the Kunneth isomorphism). By lemma_146, applied with X := X_1 and Y := X_2, the Kunneth homomorphism
   kappa_n : W_n = direct sum_{i+j=n} H^i(X_1) tensor_{Q_ell} H^j(X_2) -> H^n(X_1 x_{F_q} X_2) = H^n(X),
   (x_{i,j})_{i+j=n} |-> sum_{i+j=n} pr_1^*(x_{i,j}) cup pr_2^*(x_{i,j}),
is an isomorphism of Q_ell-vector spaces, and under this isomorphism F_X corresponds to the operator which on the (i,j)-summand acts as F_{X_1} tensor F_{X_2}; that is, exactly A_n. In formulae, kappa_n circ A_n = F_X circ kappa_n. Both A_n (Step 3/4) and F_X (Step 1) are invertible, and W_n and H^n(X) are finite-dimensional, so lemma_8 applies to alpha := kappa_n, T_V := A_n, T_W := F_X and gives: since A_n is semisimple on W_n (Step 4), F_X is semisimple on H^n(X).

Step 6 (conclusion). Applying the forward implication of lemma_5 to the semisimple operator F_X on the finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space H^n(X), we obtain that the base change of F_X to Qbar_ell, i.e. its action on H^n(X) tensor_{Q_ell} Qbar_ell, is diagonalizable. Since n >= 0 was arbitrary, this holds for every n >= 0, which is precisely the required conclusion: F_{X_1 x_{F_q} X_2} is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et((X_1 x_{F_q} X_2)_k, Q_ell) for every n >= 0.

(Remarks on edge cases. For n = 0 the index set I_0 = {(0,0)} and the argument reduces to lemma_35(i) for i = j = 0; H^0 of a smooth projective variety is a finite direct sum of copies of Q_ell and F acts through the permutation of connected components, but no such description is needed — the general argument above covers it. There is nothing to prove for n < 0 since the statement quantifies only over n >= 0. No connectedness or equidimensionality hypothesis on X_1, X_2 was used anywhere: lemma_146, lemma_35, lemma_9, lemma_8, lemma_5, lemma_6a, lemma_3 and lemma_17 are all stated for arbitrary smooth projective (respectively proper) varieties over F_q.)

lemma_below_middle_induction.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) prime, and assume that for every integer \(m\ge1\), every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(X'\) of pure dimension \(e'\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), every effective ample divisor \(Y'\subset X'\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(e'-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and \(U'=X'\setminus Y'\), one has \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(j<e'\). Fix integers \(s\ge1\) and \(e\ge2\), and suppose that for every \(t\ge1\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(V\) of pure dimension \(e-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^t}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(0\le n\le e-1\). Then for every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(Z\) of pure dimension \(e\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^s}\) and every integer \(n<e\), the \(q^s\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_below_middle_induction.proof:
Throughout, write $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$ and $\sigma:k\to k$, $\sigma(c)=c^{q}$; for $r\ge 1$ write $\sigma_r=\sigma^{r}$, so $\sigma_r(c)=c^{q^{r}}$. For a variety $W$ over some $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ we write $W_k:=W\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $H^n(W):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(W_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$; by associativity of fibre products, if $r\mid r'$ then $W_{\mathbb F_{q^{r'}}}\times_{\mathbb F_{q^{r'}}}\operatorname{Spec}k=W\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k$, so the groups $H^n(W)$ and $H^n(W_{\mathbb F_{q^{r'}}})$ are literally the same $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space.

We prove: for every $s\ge1$, every smooth projective geometrically connected $Z$ of pure dimension $e$ over $\mathbb F_{q^s}$, and every integer $n<e$, the $q^s$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $H^n(Z)$ is semisimple.

Step 0 (negative degrees). If $n<0$, then $H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ by definition of étale cohomology (cohomology of a topos vanishes in negative degrees), and the operator on the zero space is diagonalizable over $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$. Henceforth assume $0\le n\le e-1$.

Step 1 (an ample line bundle over the ground field). Since $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^s}$ is projective, there is a closed immersion $Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^s}}$ over $\mathbb F_{q^s}$; the pullback $\mathcal L$ of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^N}(1)$ is an ample line bundle on $Z$, and it is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^s}$ because the immersion and $\mathcal O(1)$ are.

Step 2 (a smooth ample hyperplane section after a finite extension). Apply lemma_306 (Spark) with $q$ replaced by $q^s$, $X=Z$, $d=e$ (valid since $e\ge2$) and $\mathcal L$ as above. It yields integers $m\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and a section $s_0\in H^0(Z_{\mathbb F_{q^{sm}}},\mathcal L^{\otimes r})$ whose zero scheme $Y:=V(s_0)$ is an effective ample Cartier divisor on $Z_{\mathbb F_{q^{sm}}}$, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension $e-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^{sm}}$. Put $t:=sm$; then $t\ge1$ and $Y\subset Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$ is an effective ample Cartier divisor, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension $e-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$, defined over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$ by construction.

Being an effective Cartier divisor, $Y$ is a closed subscheme of $Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$, so its structural morphism $i:Y\hookrightarrow Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$ is a closed immersion. Being a closed subscheme of the projective $\mathbb F_{q^t}$-scheme $Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$, $Y$ is projective over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$. Thus $Y$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension $e-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$.

We also record that $X:=Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension $e$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$: smoothness and projectivity are preserved by the base change $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^t}\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^s}$; for geometric connectedness, the geometric fibre of $X$ is $X\times_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}\operatorname{Spec}k=Z\times_{\mathbb F_{q^s}}\operatorname{Spec}k=Z_k$, which is connected because $Z$ is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^s}$; pure dimension is $e$ because $\mathbb F_{q^t}/\mathbb F_{q^s}$ is a finite (hence flat) extension, so all irreducible components of $X$ have dimension $e$.

Step 3 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of Frobenius). The constant complex $\mathbb Q_\ell$ on $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$), viewed as an object of $D^b_c$, carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism $\psi:F^*\mathbb Q_\xrightarrow{\sim}\to\mathbb Q_\ell$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are proper over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$ (projective), lemma_45_finite_frob (eoinm), applied with $q$ replaced by $q^t$ and $K=\mathbb Q_\ell$, gives that $H^n(X)$ and $H^n(Y)$ are finite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$ for every $n$, and that the induced $q^t$-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms $F_X,F_Y$ are the usual pullbacks $(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_t)^*$. By lemma_6a (eoinm) these pullbacks are $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear automorphisms (with inverse the geometric Frobenius). By lemma_5 (eoinm), "semisimple" for these operators is equivalent to diagonalizability of the base change to $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; we use the two words interchangeably, and this is the same notion that appears in the conclusion of the present lemma.

Step 4 (compact-support vanishing for the complement). Let $U:=X\setminus Y=Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}\setminus Y$, an open subscheme, with open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow X$. Apply the hypothesis (A) of the lemma with $m:=t$, $X':=X=Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$ (smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $e'=e\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$), $Y':=Y$ (an effective ample divisor defined over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension $e-1=e'-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$), and $U':=U$. All hypotheses are satisfied by Steps 1--2, and $t\ge1$. The conclusion is
$$H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for every integer } j<e,$$
hence in particular for every $j\le e-1$.

Step 5 (injectivity of the restriction to $Y$). Apply lemma_287 (Spark) with $q$ replaced by $q^t$, $X=Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$, $d=e$, $Y$, $U$, $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^t}=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$. Its hypotheses are exactly what Steps 1--4 provide: $X$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d=e\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$; $Y\subset X$ is an effective ample divisor defined over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$, smooth of pure dimension $d-1=e-1$; and $H^n_c(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0$ for all $n\le d-1$. (For completeness: the long exact sequence of the pair whose existence is used inside lemma_287 is the one of lemma_283, whose terms are finite-dimensional by lemma_45_finite_frob; the vanishing of $H^n_c(U_k)$ and of $H^{n-1}_c(U_k)$ for $n\le e-1$ makes $H^n_c(U_k)\to H^n(X_k)$ zero and its cokernel inject into $H^n(Y_k)$, giving injectivity of $i^*$.) We conclude
$$i^*:H^n(Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}})\longrightarrow H^n(Y)\quad\text{is injective for every } n\le e-1.$$
In particular it is injective for our fixed $n$ (which satisfies $0\le n\le e-1$). Note also that if $H^n(Y)=0$ then injectivity forces $H^n(X)=0$, and the conclusion is then trivial; the argument below covers this case automatically.

Step 6 (semisimplicity on $Y$ by the induction hypothesis). Apply the second hypothesis (B) of the lemma with $t$ as above and $V:=Y$: $Y$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $e-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$, so the $q^t$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F_Y=(\mathrm{id}_{Y_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_t)^*$ is semisimple on $H^n(Y)$ for every $0\le n\le e-1$, in particular on $H^n(Y)$ for our $n$. (When $e=2$ this is precisely the statement for smooth projective geometrically connected curves, where $0\le n\le1$; the case $e-1=0$ does not arise because $e\ge2$.)

Step 7 (lifting semisimplicity to $X$). Apply lemma_292 (Spark) with $q$ replaced by $q^t$, $X=Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}}$, $V=Y$, and the closed immersion $i:V\hookrightarrow X$ of Step 2 (both $V$ and $X$ are smooth projective geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^t}$), and with the integer $n$ of the lemma. Its hypotheses are: $i^*:H^n(X)\to H^n(V)$ injective (Step 5) and $F_V=F_Y$ semisimple on $H^n(V)=H^n(Y)$ (Step 6). Its conclusion is that $F_X=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_t)^*$ is semisimple on $H^n(X)=H^n(Z_{\mathbb F_{q^t}})=H^n(Z_k)$ (the equality of vector spaces being the associativity-of-base-change identification of the preamble). In other words, the $q^t$-power arithmetic Frobenius of $H^n(Z_k)$ is semisimple.

Step 8 (descent from $q^t$-power to $q^s$-power Frobenius). Apply lemma_320 (Spark) to the proper $\mathbb F_{q^s}$-scheme $Z$ (proper because projective), to the degree $n$, and to the integer $m\ge1$ of Step 2. It considers $F_1=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*$, the $q^s$-power arithmetic Frobenius, and $F_m=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{m})^*$. Since $\sigma^m(c)=c^{q^{sm}}=c^{q^t}=\sigma_t(c)$ as automorphisms of $k$, the morphism $\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^m$ is exactly $\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_t$, so $F_m$ is precisely the $q^t$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F_X$ of Step 7. (Equivalently: $\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_t=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^m$, and pullback turns composition into composition, so $F_m=F_1^{m}$.) lemma_320 asserts that $F_1$ is semisimple on $H^n(Z_k)$ if and only if $F_m$ is. By Step 7, $F_m$ is semisimple; hence $F_1$ is semisimple on $H^n(Z_k)$.

This is exactly the desired conclusion for $Z$ and $n$. Since $Z$ and $n<e$ were arbitrary, the lemma is proved. $\blacksquare$

Remark on the edge cases. (i) For $n=0$ the argument above is complete as written: $i^*$ is injective by Step 5 and $F_Y$ is semisimple on $H^0(Y)=\mathbb Q_\ell$ by Step 6. (ii) If $H^n(Y)=0$, Step 5 gives $H^n(Z)=0$ and semisimplicity is trivial, so no case distinction is needed. (iii) The hypothesis $e\ge2$ is used exactly twice: to apply lemma_306 (which needs $d\ge2$) and to ensure $Y$ has pure dimension $e-1\ge1$; the case $e=1$ is not part of the statement.

lemma_frob_hc_affine_top.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(m\ge 1\). Let \(F\) denote the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^m_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) induced by \(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb A^m_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\). Then \(F\) is multiplication by \(q^m\).
lemma_frob_hc_affine_top.proof:
Fix the integer m \ge 1 and write d := m for the dimension parameter used in Spark's lemma_compact_top_trace.

Step 1. The compactification and its boundary. Let
  X := \mathbb P^m_{\mathbb F_q} = \operatorname{Proj} \mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_m]
with homogeneous coordinates T_0,\dots,T_m, let Y := V_+(T_0) \subset X be the hyperplane T_0=0, and let j: U := X\setminus Y \hookrightarrow X be the open immersion.

Step 2. Identification of U with affine space, defined over \mathbb F_q. One has U = D_+(T_0) = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb F_q[T_1/T_0,\dots,T_m/T_0]; sending the i-th coordinate function x_i on \mathbb A^m_{\mathbb F_q} to T_i/T_0 defines an isomorphism of \mathbb F_q-schemes \iota: U \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb A^m_{\mathbb F_q}. Because \iota is defined over \mathbb F_q, base change to k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q commutes with id \times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma: for every \mathbb F_q-scheme W the square with vertical arrows given by id_W \times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma and horizontal arrows the base-changed morphism commutes (functoriality of base change, using \sigma\circ c = c\circ \sigma on \mathbb F_q-valued scalars). Hence \iota_k^*: H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^m_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) intertwines the operator of the statement with F := (\mathrm{id}_{U_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^q. It therefore suffices to prove F = q^m\cdot\mathrm{id} on H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 3. Verification of the hypotheses of lemma_compact_top_trace with d = m.

(3.1) X is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension m \ge 1 over \mathbb F_q. The standard opens D_+(T_i), i=0,\dots,m, are each isomorphic to \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q[x_1,\dots,x_m] = \mathbb A^m_{\mathbb F_q}; the polynomial algebra over a field is standard smooth (finitely presented, \Omega is free with basis dx_1,\dots,dx_m, and all fibres are geometrically regular), so X is smooth of pure relative dimension m. Projectivity holds because \mathcal O_X(1) is ample. For geometric connectedness, X_k = \mathbb P^m_k is covered by the opens D_+(T_i), each the spectrum of the domain k[x_1,\dots,x_m], hence irreducible, and all of them contain the k-point [1:\dots:1]; a union of irreducible subschemes with a common point is irreducible, hence connected.

(3.2) Y is an effective ample divisor defined over \mathbb F_q. Y is the zero scheme of the global section T_0 \in H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(1)). It is an effective Cartier divisor: for i \ge 1 the ideal of Y on D_+(T_i) is generated by T_0/T_i, which is a non-zero-divisor in the domain \mathbb F_q[T_1/T_i,\dots,T_m/T_i], while on D_+(T_0) the section restricts to the unit T_0/T_0 = 1 (so Y does not meet D_+(T_0)). The associated invertible sheaf is \mathcal O_X(Y) \simeq \mathcal O_X(1), which is very ample, hence ample; so Y is ample. Since T_0 has coefficients in \mathbb F_q, Y is a closed subscheme of X over \mathbb F_q, i.e. it is defined over \mathbb F_q.

(3.3) Y is smooth of pure dimension m-1 over \mathbb F_q. Eliminating T_0 gives Y = \operatorname{Proj}\mathbb F_q[T_1,\dots,T_m] \simeq \mathbb P^{m-1}_{\mathbb F_q}, and the argument of (3.1) with m replaced by m-1 shows smoothness and pure dimension m-1 (when m=1 this is \mathbb P^0_{\mathbb F_q}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q, which is smooth of pure dimension 0).

(3.4) The extra vanishing hypothesis: H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every n > 2(m-1). The scheme Y_k = \mathbb P^{m-1}_k is projective over k, hence separated of finite type, of Krull dimension m-1. Its m standard opens W_i := D_+(T_i|_Y), i=1,\dots,m, are affine (each isomorphic to \mathbb A^{m-1}_k) and they cover Y_k, because every point of \mathbb P^{m-1}_k has at least one non-zero homogeneous coordinate T_i with 1 \le i \le m. Applying lemma_ordinary_vanishing_affine_cover to Y_k with e := m-1 and with the t := m (\ge 1) affine opens W_1,\dots,W_m gives H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for all n > e + t - 1 = (m-1)+m-1 = 2m-2 = 2(m-1), which is exactly the required vanishing. In the boundary case m=1 this is the same argument with e=0 and t=1, giving H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for n>0.

(3.5) Normalisation of the Tate twist. The statement of lemma_compact_top_trace uses that the q-power arithmetic Frobenius acts on \mathbb Q_\ell(-m) as multiplication by q^m. This is precisely the convention established in eoinm's lemma_77(a): applied to the smooth projective geometrically connected \mathbb F_{q^1}-variety \mathbb P^m (so that the extension degree there is 1), the trace tr_X is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant once F is made to act on \mathbb Q_\ell(-m) as the positive rational number q^{1\cdot m}=q^m. Thus the normalisation clause of lemma_compact_top_trace holds for our X and d=m.

All hypotheses of lemma_compact_top_trace are therefore satisfied for X = \mathbb P^m_{\mathbb F_q}, Y = V_+(T_0), U = \mathbb A^m_{\mathbb F_q} and d = m.

Step 4. Application of lemma_compact_top_trace. The lemma yields that
  \Phi := \operatorname{tr}_X \circ j_! : H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-m)
(where j_! is the extension-by-zero map of the localisation long exact sequence of the pair (X,Y) and \operatorname{tr}_X is the Poincar\'e duality trace normalised by \operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(x))=[\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism, and that
  \Phi(Fx) = q^m\,\Phi(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
where F=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* is the q-power arithmetic Frobenius.

Step 5. Conjugating the scalar back. Since \Phi is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear, q^m\Phi(x)=\Phi(q^m x), so the relation of Step 4 reads \Phi(Fx - q^m x)=0 for every x. As \Phi is injective (being an isomorphism), Fx - q^m x = 0 for every x; hence F = q^m\,\mathrm{id} on H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Conjugating by the isomorphism \iota_k^* of Step 2, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^{2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^m_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is also multiplication by q^m. (In particular it is invertible, as q^m \neq 0 in \mathbb Q_\ell.)

This proves the claim. Note that no generator of H^{2m}_c(\mathbb A^m_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) was chosen and its dimension was never used: the scalar is forced by the Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism \operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_!, so the argument does not depend on any identification of a "fundamental class".

lemma_337.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p>0\) and let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime. Let \(X\) be an integral projective scheme of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(k\), let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\), let \(n\ge1\), and let \(s\in H^0(X,\mathcal L^{\otimes n})\) be a section whose vanishing locus \(V(s)\) is a nonempty proper closed subscheme. Then \(U=X\setminus V(s)\) is an affine \(k\)-scheme of Krull dimension \(d\) and \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(m>d\).
lemma_337.proof:
Proof.

Step 1. Affineness and finite type.
For a section s of a line bundle L^{tensor n}, the usual vanishing locus is the support of the cokernel of the map O_X -> L^{tensor n}. Hence the V(s) in the statement is the V(s) of lemma_318. By lemma_318, U = X - V(s) = X_s is an affine k-scheme.

Since X is projective over k, X is of finite type and noetherian. The open subscheme U of the noetherian scheme X is quasi-compact and locally of finite type over k; therefore U is of finite type over k. Because V(s) is proper, U is nonempty; because X is integral, U is integral.

Step 2. Algebraic dimension facts.
Claim 1. If B is a finitely generated domain over k and r = trdeg_k Frac(B), then dim Spec B = r.
Proof of Claim 1. By Noether normalization (k is algebraically closed, hence infinite), there are algebraically independent elements y_1,...,y_r in B such that B is finite over P = k[y_1,...,y_r]. Since B is finite over P, Frac(B) is algebraic over Frac(P), and the algebraic independence of the y_i gives trdeg_k Frac(B) = r.

For an integral extension B over P, the dimension of Spec B equals the dimension of Spec P. Indeed, if q_0 strictly ... strictly q_m is a chain of primes of B, then its contractions p_i = q_i cap P form a strictly increasing chain in Spec P: if p_i = p_{i+1}, then q_i and q_{i+1} are comparable primes of B lying over the same prime of P, contradicting incomparability for integral extensions. Hence dim Spec B <= dim Spec P. Conversely, given a chain p_0 strictly ... strictly p_m in Spec P, lying over gives q_0 over p_0, and going-up gives inductively q_i over p_i with q_{i-1} subset q_i. The contractions are distinct, so the q_i are distinct; hence dim Spec B >= dim Spec P.

It remains to compute dim Spec P. The chain (0) strictly (y_1) strictly ... strictly (y_1,...,y_r) has length r, so dim Spec P >= r. For the reverse inequality, the generalized principal ideal theorem (Krull height theorem) says that every prime of the r-generated k-algebra P has height at most r; hence no chain of primes in Spec P has length greater than r. Thus dim Spec P = r, and Claim 1 is proved.

Claim 2. If Y is an integral scheme of finite type over k, then dim Y = trdeg_k k(Y).
Proof of Claim 2. Put r = trdeg_k k(Y).

Lower bound. Choose a nonempty affine open W = Spec B of Y. Then B is a finitely generated k-domain. Since W is a nonempty open subset of the irreducible space Y, it contains the generic point eta_Y of Y; hence Frac(B) = O_{Y,eta_Y} = k(Y). By Claim 1, dim W = r. Any chain of irreducible closed subsets of W gives a chain of irreducible closed subsets of Y of the same length: if C is closed in W and D is its closure in Y, then C = D cap W because C is closed in W, and strict inclusions are preserved by taking closures. Hence dim W <= dim Y, so dim Y >= r.

Upper bound. We first prove the drop lemma.

Drop lemma. If Z is a proper integral closed subscheme of an integral finite type k-scheme Y, then trdeg_k k(Z) <= trdeg_k k(Y) - 1.
Proof of drop lemma. Let s = trdeg_k k(Y). Let eta_Z be the generic point of Z. Choose an affine open W' = Spec B' of Y containing eta_Z. Since Y is integral and W' is nonempty, W' also contains eta_Y. Thus B' is a finitely generated k-domain and Frac(B') = k(Y); by Claim 1, dim Spec B' = s.

The closed subset Z cap W' is proper in W'. If it were all of W', then W' would be contained in Z; but W' is a nonempty open subset of the irreducible space Y, hence dense, and a closed subset containing a dense subset is all of Y, contradicting that Z is proper. Since Z is irreducible, Z cap W' = V(p) for a nonzero prime p of B'. The subset Z cap W' is dense in Z, so k(Z) = Frac(B'/p). By Claim 1, trdeg_k k(Z) = dim Spec(B'/p).

By Noether normalization, B' is finite over P' = k[t_1,...,t_s]. Let q = p cap P'. If q = 0, then the primes (0) and p of B' are comparable and have the same contraction (0) in P', contradicting incomparability for integral extensions (p is nonzero). Thus q is a nonzero prime of P'.

The quotient B'/p is finite over P'/q. By the integral-extension dimension equality proved in Claim 1, dim Spec(B'/p) = dim Spec(P'/q). If there is a chain of primes in P'/q of length e, it corresponds to a chain q strictly ... in Spec P' of length e. Prefixing this chain by (0) strictly q gives a chain of length e+1 in Spec P'. Since dim Spec P' = s by Claim 1, we have e+1 <= s, so e <= s-1. Therefore dim Spec(P'/q) <= s-1, and consequently trdeg_k k(Z) <= s-1. This proves the drop lemma.

Now take any chain of irreducible closed subsets Y_0 strictly ... strictly Y_m in Y. Give each Y_i its reduced induced structure; it is an integral finite type k-scheme. Applying the drop lemma to each inclusion Y_{i-1} subset Y_i gives trdeg_k k(Y_{i-1}) <= trdeg_k k(Y_i) - 1. Inducting, trdeg_k k(Y_0) <= trdeg_k k(Y_m) - m <= r - m. Since trdeg_k k(Y_0) >= 0, we get m <= r. Thus every chain of irreducible closed subsets of Y has length at most r, so dim Y <= r. Together with the lower bound, dim Y = r. This proves Claim 2.

Step 3. Dimension of U.
By Claim 2 applied to X, dim X = trdeg_k k(X). Since X is integral and pure of dimension d, its unique irreducible component is X itself, so dim X = d. Hence trdeg_k k(X) = d.

The scheme U is a nonempty open subscheme of the integral scheme X, so U is integral and of finite type over k, and its function field is the same as that of X: k(U) = k(X). Applying Claim 2 to U gives dim U = trdeg_k k(U) = trdeg_k k(X) = d.

Step 4. Etale cohomology vanishing.
Since U is affine and of finite type over k with Krull dimension d, apply lemma_288 to U and to K = Q_ell[0], the constant Q_ell-sheaf concentrated in degree 0. The constant Q_ell-sheaf is constructible, so K lies in D^b_c(U_et,Q_ell), and its cohomology sheaves satisfy H^q(K) = 0 for q > 0. Lemma_288 gives H^q(RGamma(U_et,K)) = 0 for every integer q > d. By definition of etale cohomology, H^m_et(U,Q_ell) = H^m(RGamma(U_et,Q_ell)) = H^m(RGamma(U_et,K)). Therefore H^m_et(U,Q_ell) = 0 for every integer m > d.

This completes the proof.

lemma_343.statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let X be a smooth projective variety over F_q, let k=overline{F}_q, and let ell != p be prime. Suppose the q-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism induced by (id x Spec sigma), sigma(c)=c^q, permutes the connected components of X_k transitively. Let X_0 be one component, and let m>=1 be minimal such that the m-th iterate of this automorphism sends X_0 to itself. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_0,Q_ell) for every n>=0, then the q-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n>=0.
lemma_343.proof:
Fix an integer n >= 0 throughout; we prove the semisimplicity of the q-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) and then let n vary.

NOTATION. Write Phi := id_X x Spec sigma : X_k -> X_k for the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism (a sigma-semilinear automorphism of schemes, with inverse id_X x Spec sigma^{-1}), and write Phi^* for the induced Q_ell-linear automorphism of the etale cohomology of any Phi-stable subscheme. For i in Z put X_i := Phi^i(X_0) (image as a subset of X_k), and set H^n(Z) := H^n_et(Z, Q_ell) for a k-scheme Z.

STEP 1 (the components of X_k and the action of Phi on them). X_k is of finite type over the field k, hence noetherian; a noetherian topological space has only finitely many connected components, each of which is open (the complement of a component is a finite union of components, hence closed). Thus X_k = X_0 disjunion ... disjunion X_{r-1} as a disjoint union of open-and-closed subschemes. Since Phi is a homeomorphism of the underlying topological space of X_k, it permutes the components, and by hypothesis this permutation is transitive. We claim r = m and {X_0,...,X_{m-1}} = pi_0(X_k). Indeed: (a) distinctness -- if Phi^i(X_0) = Phi^j(X_0) with 0 <= i < j <= m-1, applying Phi^{-i} gives Phi^{j-i}(X_0) = X_0 with 0 < j-i < m, contradicting the minimality of m; (b) exhaustion -- transitivity says every component equals Phi^i(X_0) for some i in Z, and Phi^i(X_0) = Phi^{i mod m}(X_0) because Phi^m(X_0) = X_0. Hence X_k = coproduct_{i=0}^{m-1} X_i (indices taken mod m, so X_m = X_0). Each X_i is an open-and-closed subscheme of the smooth projective k-scheme X_k, hence itself smooth and projective over k, and connected; since k is algebraically closed, connected implies geometrically connected. Moreover Phi restricts to an isomorphism of schemes Phi_i := Phi|_{X_i} : X_i -> X_{i+1} (an isomorphism because Phi is an automorphism of X_k with inverse id_X x Spec sigma^{-1}, and the inverse carries X_{i+1} onto X_i).

STEP 2 (identification of the operator in the hypothesis). As a morphism of schemes over Spec F_q one has Phi^m = (id_X x Spec sigma)^m = id_X x Spec sigma^m, and sigma^m(c) = c^{q^m}. By definition of m, Phi^m(X_0) = X_0, so Phi^m restricts to a sigma^m-semilinear automorphism Phi^{(m)}_0 := Phi^m|_{X_0} : X_0 -> X_0. This is exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius of X_0 whose semisimplicity is assumed. For completeness we record why: the action of Gal(k/F_q) = <sigma> on pi_0(X_k) factors through the finite cyclic permutation group generated by Phi, and the stabiliser of X_0 is <sigma^m> = Gal(k/F_{q^m}) (minimality of m); hence X_0 is a Gal(k/F_{q^m})-stable open-and-closed subscheme of X_k and therefore descends, by Galois descent for schemes along the Galois extension k/F_{q^m}, to a unique open-and-closed subscheme Y of X_{F_{q^m}} with Y_k = X_0, the descent datum being precisely Phi^{(m)}_0, i.e. Phi^{(m)}_0 = id_Y x Spec sigma^m under Y_k = X_0. Thus the hypothesis is: the operator phi := (Phi^{(m)}_0)^* in GL(H^n(X_0)) is semisimple. (Only this concrete operator is used below.)
