STEP 3 (finite-dimensionality). X is projective over F_q, hence proper. Applying eoinm lemma_45_finite_frob to the proper F_q-variety X with K = Q_ell the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism gives dim_{Q_ell} H^n(X_k) < infinity.

STEP 4 (decomposition of H^n(X_k) over the components). Each X_i is open-and-closed in X_k. Applying Spark lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum repeatedly (first to X_k with the open-and-closed subscheme X_0 and its complement X_1 disjunion ... disjunion X_{m-1}, then to that complement, and so on; the hypotheses are satisfied since k is algebraically closed and ell != char k) we obtain that restriction to the components is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism
   res : H^n(X_k) --~-->  (+)_{i=0}^{m-1} H^n(X_i),   alpha |--> (alpha|_{X_i})_{i=0}^{m-1}.
Consequently each H^n(X_i) is a Q_ell-direct summand of the finite-dimensional space H^n(X_k), hence finite-dimensional.

STEP 5 (the matrix of Phi^* in a convenient basis). For 0 <= i <= m-1 put psi_i := Phi_i^* : H^n(X_{i+1}) -> H^n(X_i) (with X_m = X_0); each psi_i is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism, with inverse (Phi_i^{-1})^*, because Phi_i is an isomorphism of schemes. Set V := H^n(X_0), a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space, and define Q_ell-linear isomorphisms theta_i : V -> H^n(X_i) by
   theta_0 := id_V,   theta_i := (psi_0 o psi_1 o ... o psi_{i-1})^{-1}  for 1 <= i <= m-1.
For 0 <= i <= m-2 one has the key relation
   psi_i o theta_{i+1} = psi_i o (psi_0 o ... o psi_i)^{-1} = (psi_0 o ... o psi_{i-1})^{-1} = theta_i        (*)
(the middle equality is just the cancellation psi_i o (psi_0...psi_i)^{-1} = (psi_0...psi_{i-1})^{-1}, both sides being the inverse of psi_0...psi_{i-1}).
Define Theta : V^{m} -> H^n(X_k) by letting Theta(v_0,...,v_{m-1}) be the unique class alpha with alpha|_{X_i} = theta_i(v_i) for all i; by STEP 4, Theta is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism.

CLAIM. Theta^{-1} o Phi^* o Theta = T, where T : V^m -> V^m is
   T(v_0,...,v_{m-1}) = (v_1, v_2, ..., v_{m-1}, phi(v_0)).
Proof of the claim. Let alpha = Theta(v_0,...,v_{m-1}). For 0 <= i <= m-2, using functoriality of pullback along Phi o incl_{X_i} = incl_{X_{i+1}} o Phi_i,
   (Phi^* alpha)|_{X_i} = (Phi|_{X_i})^*( alpha|_{Phi(X_i)} ) = psi_i( alpha|_{X_{i+1}} ) = psi_i( theta_{i+1}(v_{i+1}) ) = theta_i(v_{i+1})
by (*). Hence the i-th coordinate of Theta^{-1} Phi^* Theta(v) is v_{i+1}, for 0 <= i <= m-2. For i = m-1 the same functoriality gives
   (Phi^* alpha)|_{X_{m-1}} = psi_{m-1}( alpha|_{X_0} ) = psi_{m-1}(v_0),
and the m-1-th coordinate of Theta^{-1}Phi^*Theta(v) is theta_{m-1}^{-1} psi_{m-1}(v_0) = (psi_0 o ... o psi_{m-2}) psi_{m-1}(v_0) = (psi_0 o psi_1 o ... o psi_{m-1})(v_0). Finally, since Phi_t : X_t -> X_{t+1} and Phi^m|_{X_0} = Phi_{m-1} o ... o Phi_1 o Phi_0 as morphisms X_0 -> X_0, contravariance ((g o f)^* = f^* o g^*) yields
   phi = (Phi^m|_{X_0})^* = Phi_0^* o Phi_1^* o ... o Phi_{m-1}^* = psi_0 o psi_1 o ... o psi_{m-1},
so that coordinate equals phi(v_0). This proves the claim. 
Note also that Phi^* is invertible (inverse (Phi^{-1})^*), and correspondingly T is invertible with T^{-1}(w_0,...,w_{m-1}) = (phi^{-1} w_{m-1}, w_0, ..., w_{m-2}); in particular T in GL(V^m) and phi in GL(V) (the latter also follows directly, since Phi^{(m)}_0 is an automorphism).

STEP 6 (computation of T^m). We claim that for 0 <= r <= m,
   (T^r v)_i = v_{i+r}                 if i + r <= m-1,
   (T^r v)_i = phi(v_{i+r-m})          if i + r >= m.
Proof by induction on r. For r = 0 this is the identity; for r = 1 it is the definition of T. For the induction step, take r < m and i. If i <= m-2 then (T^{r+1}v)_i = (T^r v)_{i+1}, and since (i+1)+r >= i+r, the induction hypothesis applied to the index i+1 gives v_{i+1+r} in the first case and phi(v_{i+1+r-m}) in the second, exactly as required. If i = m-1 then (T^{r+1}v)_{m-1} = phi((T^r v)_0) = phi(v_r) because r <= m-1 gives (T^r v)_0 = v_r; and the stated formula gives phi(v_{m-1+1+r-m}) = phi(v_r). This completes the induction. Taking r = m (where i + m >= m always) we obtain
   T^m(v_0,...,v_{m-1}) = (phi(v_0), phi(v_1), ..., phi(v_{m-1})),
that is, T^m = phi (+) phi (+) ... (+) phi on V^m = V (+) ... (+) V (m copies).

STEP 7 (the chain of equivalences). All vector spaces involved are finite-dimensional over Q_ell and all operators are invertible. We prove: Phi^* is semisimple on H^n(X_k) if and only if phi is semisimple on V.
 (a) Theta o T = Phi^* o Theta by the claim of STEP 5, and Theta is an isomorphism; eoinm lemma_8 (conjugate invertible operators on finite-dimensional Q_ell-spaces are simultaneously semisimple or not) gives
        T semisimple on V^m  <=>  Phi^* semisimple on H^n(X_k).
 (b) eoinm lemma_5 applied to T on V^m gives
        T semisimple on V^m  <=>  T_{bar} := T tensor id is diagonalizable on V^m tensor_{Q_ell} bar{Q}_ell.
 (c) Spark lemma_319 applied to T in GL(V^m) and the integer m >= 1 (note m >= 1 always, and (T^m)_{bar} = (T_{bar})^m) gives
        T_{bar} diagonalizable  <=>  (T^m)_{bar} diagonalizable.
 (d) eoinm lemma_5 applied to T^m on V^m gives
        (T^m)_{bar} diagonalizable  <=>  T^m semisimple on V^m.
 (e) By STEP 6, T^m = (+)_{i=0}^{m-1} phi with each block equal to phi; eoinm lemma_9 gives
        T^m semisimple on V^m  <=>  phi semisimple on V.
Concatenating (a)-(e): Phi^* is semisimple on H^n(X_k) if and only if phi = (Phi^m|_{X_0})^* is semisimple on H^n(X_0).

STEP 8 (conclusion). By hypothesis, for every n >= 0 the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius of X_0, which is phi by STEP 2, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_0, Q_ell). By the equivalence of STEP 7 applied for this n, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius Phi^* = (id x Spec sigma)^* is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell). Since n >= 0 was arbitrary, the conclusion holds for every n >= 0. This completes the proof.

(Remarks on the edge cases: m = 1 means X_k is connected and X_0 = X_k; then Theta = id, T = phi and every step above is literally the m = 1 case of the same formulas, including lemma_319 with exponent 1. If H^n(X_k) = 0 the assertions are vacuous and the argument still applies verbatim.)

lemma_345.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphism of \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then for every integer \(n\) with \(0\le n\le d\), \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) if and only if \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), that is, diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).
lemma_345.proof:
Fix data as in the statement: q = p^a a prime power, X a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over F_q, k = \overline{F}_q, \ell \neq p prime, and
F = (\mathrm{id}_{X_k} \times \operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \quad \sigma(c) = c^q,
the q-power arithmetic Frobenius acting on each H^n_{\acute et}(X_k, \mathbb Q_\ell). We must show, for each integer n with 0 \le n \le d, that F is semisimple on H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) if and only if it is semisimple on H^{2d-n}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), where semisimplicity means diagonalizability after extending scalars to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.

Step 0 (the case d = 0). If d = 0 then X is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of dimension 0 over F_q, hence X = \operatorname{Spec} k' with k'/F_q finite; geometric connectedness forces k' = F_q, so X = \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q and X_k = \operatorname{Spec} k. Then H^0_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = \mathbb Q_\ell and H^i = 0 for i > 0; the only n with 0 \le n \le d is n = 0 = 2d - n, and the two sides of the claimed equivalence are literally the same assertion. Henceforth assume d \ge 1 (in fact the argument below works verbatim for d = 0 as well).

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality and invertibility of F). X is proper over \mathbb F_q. Apply eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob to X, to m = 1, and to K = \mathbb Q_\ell, the constant sheaf on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism \psi: F_X^*\mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell (F_X being the q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphism of X_k). It yields that for every integer n the hypercohomology H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = \mathbb H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell, and that the Frobenius structure induces a canonical \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism; for the constant sheaf with its natural structure this automorphism is exactly the pullback F = (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*. Independently, eoinm/lemma_6a (applied with the q-power automorphism \sigma of k) gives that F_{\mathrm{ar}} := (\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma)^* is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) with inverse F_{\mathrm{geo}} = (\mathrm{id}_X\times\sigma^{-1})^*. Thus, writing
  V := H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \qquad W := H^{2d-n}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
both V and W are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces and the restrictions T_V := F|_V \in \mathrm{GL}(V), T_W := F|_W \in \mathrm{GL}(W) are well-defined invertible \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operators. (Since 0 \le n \le d we have d \le 2d-n \le 2d, so both degrees lie in the range [0,2d] where Poincar\'e duality applies; for degrees outside [0,2d] the groups vanish by finiteness of \acute etale cohomological dimension of the d-dimensional variety X_k, and in particular no out-of-range group is involved here.)

Step 2 (the Frobenius-equivariant perfect pairing). Apply eoinm/lemma_77 with m = 1, Y = X and \ell as above; its hypotheses (smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_{q^1} = \mathbb F_q) are exactly ours, and its F is our F.

Part (a) provides the Poincar\'e duality trace, an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces
  \operatorname{tr}: H^{2d}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbb Q_\ell(-d),
normalised on cycle classes of closed points, which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant once \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is given the action by which F acts as multiplication by the positive rational number q^{1\cdot d} = q^d.

Part (b) asserts that for every integer r with 0 \le r \le 2d the pairing
  \langle\ ,\ \rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} : H^r_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \times H^{2d-r}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-d),
  \qquad \langle x, y\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} := \operatorname{tr}(x \cup y),
is a perfect pairing of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces, and that
  \langle Fx, Fy\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} = q^{d}\,\langle x, y\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} \quad\text{for all } x, y.
Taking r = n (which satisfies 0 \le n \le 2d) we obtain a perfect \mathbb Q_\ell-bilinear pairing V \times W \to \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) with the stated q^d-twisted equivariance. Bilinearity is immediate from the \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of the cup product and of \operatorname{tr}.

Step 3 (reducing the pairing to a \mathbb Q_\ell-valued one). The Tate twist \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space. Choose once and for all a nonzero element \xi \in \mathbb Q_\ell(-d); then \lambda \mapsto \lambda\xi is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism \mathbb Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell(-d). Define
  (v,w) := \lambda \in \mathbb Q_\ell \quad\text{where}\quad \langle v,w\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} = \lambda\,\xi,
for v \in V, w \in W. This is a \mathbb Q_\ell-valued bilinear form. It is perfect: if v \in V satisfies (v,w) = 0 for all w \in W, then \langle v,w\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} = 0 for all w, so v = 0 by perfectness of \langle\ ,\ \rangle_{\mathrm{PD}}; symmetrically, (v,w) = 0 for all v \in V forces w = 0.

We compute the Frobenius behaviour. For v \in V, w \in W,
  (T_V v, T_W w)\,\xi \;=\; \langle Fv, Fw\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} \;=\; q^{d}\,\langle v,w\rangle_{\mathrm{PD}} \;=\; q^{d}\,(v,w)\,\xi,
by the equivariance from Step 2. Since \xi \neq 0 and \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is a free \mathbb Q_\ell-module of rank 1, we may cancel \xi and obtain
  (T_V v,\, T_W w) \;=\; c\,(v,w) \qquad \text{with } c := q^{d} \in \mathbb Q_\ell^{\times},
for all v \in V, w \in W. (Note c = q^d \neq 0 in \mathbb Q_\ell.)

Step 4 (applying the pairing criterion). We are now exactly in the situation of Spark/lemma_324: V and W are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces, (\ ,\ ): V \times W \to \mathbb Q_\ell is a perfect bilinear pairing, T_V \in \mathrm{GL}(V) and T_W \in \mathrm{GL}(W) satisfy (T_V v, T_W w) = c (v,w) with c = q^d \in \mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}. That lemma concludes that the base change of T_V to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalizable if and only if the base change of T_W to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell is diagonalizable. Concretely:
  F \text{ is diagonalizable on } V \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell \iff F \text{ is diagonalizable on } W \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell.
(If V = 0, perfectness forces W = 0; both operators act on the zero space, which is diagonalizable, so the equivalence holds trivially and is also covered by lemma_324.)

Step 5 (semisimplicity versus diagonalizability over \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell). By eoinm/lemma_5, for a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space U and a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear operator T, T is semisimple on U if and only if T is semisimple (equivalently diagonalizable) on U \otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell. Applying this to U = V, T = T_V and to U = W, T = T_W, the equivalence of Step 4 becomes
  F \text{ is semisimple on } H^n_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \iff F \text{ is semisimple on } H^{2d-n}_{\acute et}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Step 6 (conclusion). This is precisely the desired assertion for the given n with 0 \le n \le d. Since n was arbitrary in that range, the lemma is proved. \hfill \blacksquare

Remark on the logical flow, to make clear that nothing circular is used: the only geometric input is the Frobenius-equivariant Poincar\'e duality statement eoinm/lemma_77(a),(b) (its part (c) and the semisimplicity criterion eoinm/lemma_71 are not used); the linear-algebra input is Spark/lemma_324 together with eoinm/lemma_5; finite-dimensionality and invertibility of F come from eoinm/lemma_45_finite_frob and eoinm/lemma_6a. In particular no semisimplicity statement is assumed anywhere.

lemma_top_trace_affine_space.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, and let \(d\ge1\). Let \(\operatorname{tr}_c:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the Poincaré duality trace isomorphism of the smooth \(d\)-dimensional \(\mathbb F_q\)-scheme \(\mathbb A^d_{\mathbb F_q}\), and let \(F=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^q\), be the \(q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of \(H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), acting on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) as multiplication by \(q^d\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}_c(Fx)=q^d\operatorname{tr}_c(x)\) for every \(x\in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_top_trace_affine_space.proof:
We fix throughout the prime power q = p^a, the algebraic closure k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, the prime \ell \neq p, the integer d \ge 1, and we write
  V \;:=\; H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
for the group occurring in the statement, and F_{\mathbb A^d} for the operator (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* on V with \sigma(c)=c^q. The only property of the map tr_c that will be used is that it is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism V \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell(-d), as stipulated in the hypothesis; the scalar action of arithmetic Frobenius on \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is multiplication by q^d, also stipulated.

STEP 1. The compactification X = \mathbb P^d_{\mathbb F_q}.
Let X := \mathbb P^d_{\mathbb F_q} = \mathbf{Proj}\,\mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d]. We verify the hypotheses that Spark's lemma_compact_top_trace will require of X.
(i) X is projective over \mathbb F_q: X is \mathbf{Proj} of the graded \mathbb F_q-algebra \mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d] generated in degree 1 over the degree-0 part \mathbb F_q, and \mathcal O_X(1) is ample; by definition this makes X projective over \mathbb F_q.
(ii) X is smooth of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_q: X is covered by the standard affine opens D_+(T_i) = \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q[T_0/T_i,\dots,\widehat{T_i/T_i},\dots,T_d/T_i] \cong \mathbb A^d_{\mathbb F_q}. Smoothness over \mathbb F_q can be checked on an open cover of the source, and for each i the coordinate ring is a polynomial algebra \mathbb F_q[u_1,\dots,u_d], which is smooth over \mathbb F_q: its module of K\u00e4hler differentials \Omega^1 is the free module of rank d with basis du_1,\dots,du_d, and every geometric fibre is \overline{\mathbb F}_q[u_1,\dots,u_d], a regular ring; this is exactly the jacobian/regular-fibre criterion for smoothness of a finitely presented algebra. Since (0) is a prime ideal of the domain \mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d], X is irreducible with a single irreducible component, whose dimension is trdeg_{\mathbb F_q}\mathbb F_q(T_1/T_0,\dots,T_d/T_0) = d; hence X is of pure dimension d.
(iii) X is geometrically connected: for any field extension \mathbb F_q \subset K, \mathbb P^d_K = \mathbf{Proj} K[T_0,\dots,T_d] is irreducible (K[T_0,\dots,T_d] is a domain, so (0) is homogeneous prime and is the unique generic point, whence any two non-empty opens meet), hence connected. In particular X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q} is connected.
(iv) d \ge 1 is part of the hypothesis of the present lemma.

STEP 2. The divisor Y.
Let \mathcal L := \mathcal O_X(1) and let s := T_0 \in H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(1)) be the homogeneous coordinate; this section is defined over \mathbb F_q because T_0 \in \mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d]. Let Y := V_+(T_0) \subset X be its vanishing scheme. Then:
(a) Y is an effective ample divisor defined over \mathbb F_q: it is an effective Cartier divisor (T_0 is a non-zero-divisor, indeed a homogeneous prime element of the domain \mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d], so the ideal (T_0) is locally generated by a non-zero-divisor), its associated line bundle is \mathcal O_X(Y) \cong \mathcal O_X(1) = \mathcal L, which is ample; and the homogeneous ideal (T_0) is generated by an element with coefficients in \mathbb F_q, so Y is the base change of the \mathbb F_q-subscheme \mathbf{Proj}\,\mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d]/(T_0).
(b) Y is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over \mathbb F_q: there is a homogeneous \mathbb F_q-algebra isomorphism \mathbb F_q[T_1,\dots,T_d] \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d]/(T_0) sending T_i \ (1\le i\le d) to the class of T_i, hence a canonical \mathbb F_q-isomorphism Y = \mathbf{Proj}\,\mathbb F_q[T_0,\dots,T_d]/(T_0) \cong \mathbf{Proj}\,\mathbb F_q[T_1,\dots,T_d] = \mathbb P^{d-1}_{\mathbb F_q}. Since d \ge 1 we have d-1 \ge 0, and Step 1 applied with d replaced by d-1 (the case d-1 = 0 being the one-point scheme \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q, which is smooth of pure dimension 0 over \mathbb F_q) shows \mathbb P^{d-1}_{\mathbb F_q} is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over \mathbb F_q. Smoothness and pure dimension descend through the isomorphism Y \cong \mathbb P^{d-1}.

STEP 3. The complement is affine space, compatibly with Frobenius.
Let U := X \setminus Y, an open subscheme of X defined over \mathbb F_q (as Y is), and let j: U_k \hookrightarrow X_k be the base-changed open immersion; since base change to \operatorname{Spec} k is flat (k is a free, hence flat, \mathbb F_q-algebra), the open subscheme U_k = U \times_{\mathbb F_q} k identifies with X_k \setminus Y_k. By construction U = D_+(T_0) = \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q[T_1/T_0,\dots,T_d/T_0], and the \mathbb F_q-algebra isomorphism
  \varphi_0^\#: \mathbb F_q[x_1,\dots,x_d] \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb F_q[T_1/T_0,\dots,T_d/T_0], \qquad x_i \longmapsto T_i/T_0,
defined over \mathbb F_q, gives an \mathbb F_q-isomorphism \varphi_0: U \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb A^d_{\mathbb F_q}. Let \varphi: U_k \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb A^d_k be its base change to k.
We check that \varphi identifies the two q-power arithmetic Frobenius morphisms. For affine schemes W = \operatorname{Spec} A and W' = \operatorname{Spec} B over \mathbb F_q and an \mathbb F_q-morphism \psi_0: W \to W' induced by \mathbb F_q-algebra maps \beta: B \to A, the q-power arithmetic Frobenius pullback on W_k = \operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_{\mathbb F_q} k) is \mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma: a\otimes c \mapsto a\otimes c^q, and
  (\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)\bigl(\beta^\#(b\otimes c)\bigr) = (\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)(\beta(b)\otimes c) = \beta(b)\otimes c^q = (\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)\bigl(\beta^\#(b\otimes c)\bigr),
while \psi_k^\#\bigl((\mathrm{id}\otimes\sigma)(b\otimes c)\bigr) = \psi_k^\#(b\otimes c^q) = \beta(b)\otimes c^q. The two composites agree on the generators b\otimes c, so (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)\circ\psi_k = \psi_k\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma). Applying this to \psi_0 = \varphi_0 gives
  (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)_{\mathbb A^d_k}\circ\varphi \;=\; \varphi\circ(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)_{U_k}.
Pulling back \u00e9tale cohomology with compact supports (which is functorial for \u00e9tale maps, and in particular for isomorphisms, and for which (\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^* is the pullback along the displayed morphism) we obtain, writing F_U and F_{\mathbb A^d} for the two Frobenius operators,
  \varphi^* \circ F_{\mathbb A^d} \;=\; F_U \circ \varphi^* \qquad\text{on } V = H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). \tag{1}

STEP 4. The extra vanishing hypothesis on Y_k.
We must show H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 0 for every m > 2(d-1). Two cases.
Case d \ge 2. Then n := d-1 \ge 1 and Y_k \cong \mathbb P^{d-1}_k. eoinm's lemma_201 (applied with n = d-1) says that \mathbb Q_\ell[t]/(t^{d}) \to \bigoplus_{m\ge0} H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\mathbb P^{d-1}_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), t^i \mapsto h^i (h = c_1(\mathcal O(1)) of cohomological degree 2), is an isomorphism of graded \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces. The source is nonzero only for 0 \le i \le d-1, i.e. only in cohomological degrees 0,2,\dots,2(d-1). Hence H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 0 for all m > 2(d-1).
Case d = 1. Then Y \cong \mathbb P^0_{\mathbb F_q} = \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q, so Y_k = \operatorname{Spec} k with k separably closed. Every object of the \u00e9tale site (\operatorname{Spec} k)_{\mathrm{\acute et}} is a finite disjoint union of copies of \operatorname{Spec} k (a finite \u00e9tale k-algebra is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of k, hence a product of copies of k), so \operatorname{Spec} k is a final object of the site. Therefore the global-sections functor is evaluation at a final object, hence exact, and the higher \u00e9tale cohomology of any sheaf of abelian groups on \operatorname{Spec} k vanishes: H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec} k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 0 for all m \ge 1. Since 2(d-1) = 0 in this case, the required vanishing holds for all m > 0.
Thus in all cases H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 0 for m > 2(d-1).

STEP 5. Application of Spark's lemma_compact_top_trace.
The quadruple (X, Y, j, k, \ell) now satisfies every hypothesis of Spark's lemma_compact_top_trace: X = \mathbb P^d_{\mathbb F_q} is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d \ge 1 (Step 1); Y \subset X is an effective ample divisor defined over \mathbb F_q and smooth of pure dimension d-1 (Step 2); j: U_k \hookrightarrow X_k is the open immersion of the complement (Step 3); and the vanishing of Step 4 holds. The lemma yields that
  \theta \;:=\; \operatorname{tr}_X\circ j_! \;:\; H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbb Q_\ell(-d)
(a composition of the extension-by-zero map of the localisation sequence of the pair (X_k, Y_k) with the \mathbb F_q-normalised Poincar\u00e9 duality trace of X) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism and satisfies
  \theta(F_U x) \;=\; q^d\,\theta(x) \qquad\text{for all } x \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), \tag{2}
where on the right q^d \in \mathbb Q_\ell^\times acts by the scalar action of arithmetic Frobenius on \mathbb Q_\ell(-d).
Define
  \widetilde\theta \;:=\; \theta\circ\varphi^* \;:\; V \longrightarrow \mathbb Q_\ell(-d).
Since \varphi is an isomorphism, \varphi^* is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism V \xrightarrow{\sim} H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell); composing with the isomorphism \theta, \widetilde\theta is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism. Moreover, by (1) and (2), for every x \in V,
  \widetilde\theta(F_{\mathbb A^d} x) = \theta\bigl(\varphi^* F_{\mathbb A^d} x\bigr) = \theta\bigl(F_U \varphi^* x\bigr) = q^d\,\theta(\varphi^* x) = q^d\,\widetilde\theta(x). \tag{3}

STEP 6. Comparison of the two traces: they differ by a scalar.
By eoinm's lemma_hc_affine_space applied with m = d, H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 0 for n \neq 2d and \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = 1; in particular V is a one-dimensional nonzero \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space, so the hypothesis that tr_c: V \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is an isomorphism is consistent and both tr_c and \widetilde\theta are non-zero \mathbb Q_\ell-linear functionals on V.
Consider the \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism
  \lambda \;:=\; \operatorname{tr}_c\circ\widetilde\theta^{-1} \;\in\; \operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\bigl(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\bigr).
The Tate twist \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is a one-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space (it is the \mathbb Q_\ell-linear dual of \mathbb Q_\ell(d), which is the d-th tensor power of the one-dimensional space \mathbb Q_\ell(1)), so \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)) = \mathbb Q_\ell, the scalar multiplications; hence \lambda is multiplication by a unique element of \mathbb Q_\ell^\times, which we also denote by \lambda. Thus
  \operatorname{tr}_c(v) \;=\; \lambda\,\widetilde\theta(v) \qquad\text{for every } v \in V. \tag{4}
(No claim is made that \lambda = 1; the precise value of \lambda is irrelevant, as the next step shows.)

STEP 7. Conclusion.
Let x \in V be arbitrary. Using (4), then (3), then the commutativity of the field \mathbb Q_\ell (so that \lambda q^d = q^d \lambda in \operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(\mathbb Q_\ell(-d))), and finally (4) again,
  \operatorname{tr}_c(F_{\mathbb A^d} x) \;=\; \lambda\,\widetilde\theta(F_{\mathbb A^d} x) \;=\; \lambda\, q^d\, \widetilde\theta(x) \;=\; q^d\,\lambda\,\widetilde\theta(x) \;=\; q^d\,\operatorname{tr}_c(x).
This is exactly the required identity \operatorname{tr}_c(Fx) = q^d\operatorname{tr}_c(x) for every x \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(\mathbb A^d_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), where F on \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) is multiplication by q^d. This completes the proof.

(Remarks on edge conditions: d \ge 1 is used exactly where Spark's lemma_compact_top_trace requires it, and the case d = 1 was handled separately in Step 4 because eoinm's lemma_201 is stated only for n \ge 1; \ell \neq p and k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q are as in the hypotheses of all cited lemmas.)

lemma_stable_range_frobenius_semisimplic.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(d\ge2\) and \(m\ge1\) be integers, and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Suppose that for every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(Z\) of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), the operator \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\neq d-1\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) admitting an effective ample divisor \(Y\), defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), such that \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}((X\setminus Y)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every \(j<d\). Then \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every integer \(n<d-1\) and every integer \(n>d+1\).
lemma_stable_range_frobenius_semisimplic.proof:
Write Q := q^{m} = p^{am}, K := F_{Q} = F_{q^{m}}, and let \(\sigma:k\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{Q}\), be the \(Q\)-power automorphism of \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}\). For a \(K\)-variety \(T\) put \(H^{n}(T):=H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(T_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\) and \(H^{n}_{c}(T):=H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(T_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\), and write \(F_{T}:=(\mathrm{id}_{T_{k}}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}\) for the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. By lemma_6a (applied over the base field \(K\), whose \(Q\)-power automorphism is \(\sigma\)) each \(F_{T}\) is a \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear automorphism of \(H^{n}(T)\); its inverse is the geometric Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma^{-1})^{*}\). We must prove that \(F_{X}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) on \(H^{n}(X)\) for every \(n<d-1\) and every \(n>d+1\).

STEP 0 (finite-dimensionality). Apply lemma_283 with the prime power \(q\) of its statement replaced by \(Q\) (the lemma holds for every prime power; here the base field is \(K=\mathbb F_{Q}\)): for \(U=X\setminus Y\) with open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) and closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) there is a long exact sequence
\[ \cdots\to H^{n}_{c}(U)\to H^{n}(X)\xrightarrow{i^{*}}H^{n}(Y)\to H^{n+1}_{c}(U)\to\cdots \]
of FINITE-DIMENSIONAL \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-vector spaces, in which every map commutes with the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. In particular \(H^{n}(X)\) and \(H^{n}(Y)\) are finite-dimensional for all \(n\), so the notions of semisimplicity and of diagonalisability after \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\)-base change of lemma_5 and lemma_8 apply to them.

STEP 1 (the isomorphism below the middle degree). The hypotheses of lemma_299, again read with its prime power \(q\) replaced by \(Q\) (so that its base field is \(K=\mathbb F_{q^{m}}\)), are all satisfied: \(X\) is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge 2\) over \(K\); \(Y\subset X\) is an effective ample divisor defined over \(K\), smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) (a fortiori the lemma's requirement that \(Y\) be smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) holds; we only use more than is required); and \(H^{m}_{c}(U)=0\) for every \(m<d\) is assumed in the statement of the present lemma. Hence
\[ i^{*}:H^{n}(X)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{n}(Y)\qquad\text{is an isomorphism for every } n<d-1. \tag{1}\]

STEP 2 (degrees \(n<d-1\)). Fix an integer \(n<d-1\).

If \(n<0\): the étale cohomology groups of a sheaf vanish in negative degrees, so \(H^{n}(X)=0\), and the (unique) endomorphism of the zero \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-vector space is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\). Henceforth assume \(n\ge 0\).

(2a) The map \(i^{*}\) of (1) is the pullback along the closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) occurring as the middle arrow of the localisation long exact sequence of the pair \((X,Y)\); by STEP 0 (lemma_283) that arrow commutes with the \(Q\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on the two terms. Thus
\[ i^{*}\circ F_{X}=F_{Y}\circ i^{*} \quad\text{on } H^{n}(X), \tag{2}\]
and by (1) \(i^{*}\) is a \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear isomorphism. So \(F_{X}\) and \(F_{Y}\) are conjugate operators.

(2b) We now know semisimplicity of \(F_{Y}\) on \(H^{n}(Y)\). Indeed, apply the induction hypothesis of the present lemma to \(Z:=Y\). This is legitimate: \(Y\) is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m}}=K\), so it is one of the varieties \(Z\) quantified over; and the degree \(n\) satisfies \(n<d-1\), hence \(n\neq d-1\), which is precisely the exclusion required by the hypothesis. The hypothesis therefore says exactly that \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^{m}}=c^{Q}\), i.e. \(F_{Y}\), is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) on \(H^{n}(Y)\).

(2c) By lemma_5 (a \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear operator on a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-space is semisimple if and only if its base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) is diagonalizable), \(F_{Y}\) is semisimple on \(H^{n}(Y)\).

(2d) Apply lemma_8 with \(V=H^{n}(X)\), \(W=H^{n}(Y)\), \(T_{V}=F_{X}\), \(T_{W}=F_{Y}\) and \(\alpha=i^{*}\); these are finite-dimensional spaces and invertible operators (STEP 0, and \(F_{T}\in\mathrm{GL}\) by lemma_6a), and \(\alpha\circ T_{V}=T_{W}\circ\alpha\) by (2). Lemma_8 gives that \(F_{X}\) is semisimple on \(H^{n}(X)\).

(2e) Applying lemma_5 once more, \(F_{X}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) on \(H^{n}(X)\). This completes the proof for all \(n<d-1\).

STEP 3 (vanishing above the top degree). We show \(H^{n}(X)=0\) for \(n>2d\). Since \(X\) is projective over \(K\), \(X_{k}\) is a projective variety over the algebraically closed field \(k\) of dimension \(d\); choose a closed immersion \(X_{k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{N}_{k}\) and let \(A=k[T_{0},\dots,T_{N}]/I\) be the homogeneous coordinate ring of \(X_{k}\), a graded \(k\)-domain generated by \(A_{1}\) with \(\dim A=d+1\). Because \(k\) is algebraically closed, hence infinite, the graded Noether normalisation lemma with linear forms applies: after a \(k\)-linear change of coordinates there are algebraically independent linear forms \(y_{0},\dots,y_{d}\in A_{1}\) such that \(A\) is a finite graded module over \(B:=k[y_{0},\dots,y_{d}]\). Finiteness of a graded algebra extension implies that \(f:=\operatorname{Proj}(A)\to\operatorname{Proj}(B)=\mathbb P^{d}_{k}\) is a finite morphism; it is surjective because \(B\subset A\) is integral, so the lying-over property gives, for every homogeneous prime \(\mathfrak p\subset B\) with \(B_{+}\not\subset\mathfrak p\), a homogeneous prime \(\mathfrak P\subset A\) with \(\mathfrak P\cap B=\mathfrak p\).

Let \(D_{i}\subset\mathbb P^{d}_{k}\) be the standard affine open \(y_{i}\neq 0\) (\(0\le i\le d\)). Since finite morphisms are affine, each \(V_{i}:=f^{-1}(D_{i})\) is an affine scheme; since the \(D_{i}\) cover \(\mathbb P^{d}_{k}\) and \(f\) is surjective, the \(V_{i}\) cover \(X_{k}\). Thus \(X_{k}\) is a separated scheme of finite type over the algebraically closed field \(k\) of Krull dimension \(d\), covered by \(m=d+1\) affine open subschemes. Lemma_ordinary_vanishing_affine_cover with \(e=d\) and this cover yields \(H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})=0\) for every \(n>d+(d+1)-1=2d\). Hence for \(n>2d\) the operator \(F_{X}\) acts on the zero space and is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\).

STEP 4 (degrees \(n>d+1\) with \(n\le 2d\)). Let \(n\) be an integer with \(d+2\le n\le 2d\) (this is exactly \(n>d+1\) together with \(n\le 2d\)), and put \(r:=2d-n\). Then \(0\le r\le d-2<d-1\), so by STEP 2 the operator \(F_{X}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) on \(H^{r}(X)\).

(4a) Apply lemma_77 to \(Y:=X\), with the same \(m\) and \(d\) (its hypotheses are satisfied: \(X\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m}}\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q}\), \(\ell\ne p\), and its \(F\) is our \(F_{X}\), the \(q^{m}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius). Part (a) supplies a \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear isomorphism \(\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-d)\) which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, \(F_{X}\) acting on \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-d)\) as multiplication by \(q^{md}\). Part (b) says that for every \(0\le n\le 2d\) the pairing
\[ H^{n}(X)\times H^{2d-n}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-d),\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}:=\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y), \]
is perfect and satisfies \(\langle F_{X}x,F_{X}y\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}=q^{md}\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}\) for all \(x,y\). We use this for our chosen \(n\) and \(r=2d-n\), both of which lie in \([0,2d]\).

(4b) Reduce the target to \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\). The Tate twist \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-d)\) is a one-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-vector space, so it contains a nonzero element \(\xi\). The map \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}(-d)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_{\ell}\) sending \(t\,\xi\mapsto t\) is a \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)-linear isomorphism; composing the perfect pairing of (4a) with it gives a bilinear pairing
\[ \langle-,-\rangle:H^{n}(X)\times H^{r}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_{\ell},\qquad \operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)=\langle x,y\rangle\,\xi, \]
which is still perfect (composing a perfect pairing with an isomorphism of the target vector space preserves non-degeneracy in each variable, and all spaces are finite-dimensional). Moreover, using the equivariance of \(\operatorname{tr}\) and \(\xi\ne0\),
\[ \langle F_{X}x,F_{X}y\rangle\,\xi=\operatorname{tr}(F_{X}x\cup F_{X}y)=q^{md}\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)=q^{md}\langle x,y\rangle\,\xi, \]
hence \(\langle F_{X}x,F_{X}y\rangle=q^{md}\langle x,y\rangle\) for all \(x\in H^{n}(X)\), \(y\in H^{r}(X)\).

(4c) Apply lemma_324 with \(V=H^{n}(X)\), \(W=H^{r}(X)\), \(T_{V}=T_{W}=F_{X}\) (invertible by lemma_6a) and \(c=q^{md}\in\mathbb Q_{\ell}^{\times}\) (a positive rational number, hence nonzero in \(\mathbb Q_{\ell}\)). Its hypotheses — finite-dimensionality (STEP 0), perfectness of \(\langle-,-\rangle\) (4b), and the compatibility \(\langle T_{V}v,T_{W}w\rangle=c\langle v,w\rangle\) (4b) — are all satisfied, and it concludes that the base change of \(T_{V}=F_{X}\) to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) is diagonalizable if and only if the base change of \(T_{W}=F_{X}\) on \(H^{r}(X)\) is. The latter holds by STEP 2, so \(F_{X}\) is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) on \(H^{n}(X)\).

STEP 5 (conclusion). Let \(n\) be any integer with \(n<d-1\) or \(n>d+1\). If \(n<0\) or \(n>2d\), then \(H^{n}(X)=0\) (STEP 2 for \(n<0\), STEP 3 for \(n>2d\)) and the operator is diagonalizable. If \(0\le n<d-1\), this is STEP 2. If \(d+2\le n\le 2d\), this is STEP 4. These four cases are exhaustive: an integer \(n\) with \(n<d-1\) falls in the first or second case, and an integer with \(n>d+1\) satisfies \(n\ge d+2\) and so falls in the third or fourth case. In every case \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^{*}\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^{m}}\), is diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_{\ell}\) on \(H^{n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{k},\mathbb Q_{\ell})\), which is what was to be shown. \(\blacksquare\)

lemma_353.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(f:Y\to X\) be a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree prime to \(\ell\) between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(H\) be an ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), \(\eta\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle classes of \(H\) and of \(f^{-1}H\) via a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\). If cup product with \(\eta\) induces isomorphisms \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(0\le n\le D\), then cup product with \(\xi\) induces isomorphisms \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2D-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(0\le n\le D\).
lemma_353.proof:
Proof. Write V_Z^m = H^m_et(Z_k, Q_ell) for Z = X, Y. The statement about cup product with eta (resp. xi) from V_Z^n to V_Z^(2D-n) is understood as the degree-compatible Lefschetz map L_Z^(n): V_Z^n -> V_Z^(2D-n), a -> zeta_Z^(D-n) cup a, where zeta_X = xi and zeta_Y = eta. If D = 0 then n = 0 and both maps are the identity, so assume D >= 1.

1. Finite-dimensionality and Poincare duality. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant sheaf Q_ell on X_k and on Y_k (with their natural arithmetic Frobenius structures), each V_Z^m is finite-dimensional over Q_ell. By lemma_77 (with m = 1 and dimension D) there are trace isomorphisms tr_Z: V_Z^(2D) -> Q_ell(-D) such that for every 0 <= n <= 2D the pairing < , >_Z: V_Z^n x V_Z^(2D-n) -> Q_ell(-D), (a,b) -> tr_Z(a cup b), is perfect. In particular V_Z^n is isomorphic to Hom_Q_ell(V_Z^(2D-n), Q_ell(-D)); since Q_ell(-D) is one-dimensional, dim V_Z^n = dim V_Z^(2D-n).

2. Compatibility of divisor classes. Fix the nonzero element tau in Q_ell(1) used in the statement. For a Cartier divisor E on a smooth variety Z over F_q, its cycle class in V_Z^2 is characterized by cl_Z(E) tensor tau = c_1(O_Z(E)) in H^2_et(Z_k, Q_ell(1)). Since X is smooth, H is Cartier and xi tensor tau = c_1(O_X(H)). The pullback divisor f^{-1}H is the Cartier divisor associated with the line bundle f^*O_X(H); hence eta tensor tau = c_1(O_Y(f^{-1}H)) = c_1(f^*O_X(H)). By functoriality of first Chern classes under pullback, c_1(f^*L) = f^*c_1(L) for any line bundle L on X_k. (Equivalently, c_1 is the boundary map from the Kummer sequence, and pullback commutes with this boundary map.) Therefore eta tensor tau = f^*(xi tensor tau) = f^*xi tensor tau. Tensoring with the fixed nonzero tau is an isomorphism V_Y^2 tensor Q_ell(1) -> H^2_et(Y_k, Q_ell(1)), so eta = f^*xi.

3. The trace pushforward. For each n with 0 <= n <= D, define f_*: V_Y^n -> V_X^n as follows. Given a in V_Y^n, the map b -> tr_Y(a cup f^*b) is a Q_ell-linear functional on V_X^(2D-n). By perfectness of the pairing on X, there exists a unique element f_*a in V_X^n satisfying tr_X(f_*a cup b) = tr_Y(a cup f^*b) for all b in V_X^(2D-n). This defines a Q_ell-linear map f_* (linearity follows from Q_ell-linearity of cup product, pullback, and trace).

4. The relation f_* f^* = d id. Let d = deg(f). By hypothesis d is prime to ell, hence d is invertible in Q_ell. For x in V_X^n and b in V_X^(2D-n), tr_X(f_* f^*x cup b) = tr_Y(f^*x cup f^*b) = tr_Y(f^*(x cup b)). By lemma_top_trace_generically_finite applied to f: Y -> X, tr_Y circ f^* circ tr_X^{-1} is multiplication by d on Q_ell(-D); equivalently tr_Y(f^*z) = d tr_X(z) for every z in V_X^(2D). Taking z = x cup b gives tr_X(f_* f^*x cup b) = d tr_X(x cup b) = tr_X((d x) cup b). Since the pairing on X is perfect, f_* f^*x = d x. Thus f_* f^* = d id on V_X^n. Because d is invertible in Q_ell, f^*: V_X^n -> V_Y^n is injective: if f^*x = 0 then d x = f_*0 = 0, hence x = 0.

5. Equivariance of Lefschetz maps. Pullback on etale cohomology is a graded Q_ell-algebra homomorphism. Using eta = f^*xi, for a in V_X^n, f^*(L_X^(n)a) = f^*(xi^(D-n) cup a) = f^*(xi^(D-n)) cup f^*a = (f^*xi)^(D-n) cup f^*a = eta^(D-n) cup f^*a = L_Y^(n)(f^*a). Hence f^* circ L_X^(n) = L_Y^(n) circ f^*.

6. Injectivity and conclusion. Suppose a in V_X^n and L_X^(n)a = 0. Applying f^* and using the previous identity gives 0 = L_Y^(n)(f^*a). By hypothesis L_Y^(n) is an isomorphism, so f^*a = 0. Since f^* is injective, a = 0. Thus L_X^(n) is injective. From step 1, V_X^n and V_X^(2D-n) are finite-dimensional of the same dimension. An injective linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces of equal dimension is an isomorphism. Therefore L_X^(n) is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= D. This is exactly the desired hard Lefschetz statement for cup product by the appropriate power of xi. QED.

lemma_dual_long_exact_sequences.statement:
Let \(K\) be a field. Suppose that for each integer \(n\) one is given finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector spaces \(A_n,B_n,C_n,A'_n,B'_n,C'_n\), exact sequences
\[\cdots\to A_n\xrightarrow{f_n}B_n\xrightarrow{g_n}C_n\xrightarrow{\delta_n}A_{n+1}\to\cdots\]
and
\[\cdots\to C'_n\xrightarrow{\iota_n}B'_n\xrightarrow{\rho_n}A'_n\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_n}C'_{n-1}\to\cdots,\]
and bilinear pairings \(\langle-,-\rangle^{A}_n:A_n\times A'_n\to K\), \(\langle-,-\rangle^{B}_n:B_n\times B'_n\to K\), \(\langle-,-\rangle^{C}_n:C_n\times C'_n\to K\) such that the \(B\)- and \(C\)-pairings are perfect and, for all \(n\), one has \(\langle f_n a,b'\rangle^{B}=\langle a,\rho_n b'\rangle^{A}\) for all \(a\in A_n,\,b'\in B'_n\), \(\langle g_n b,c'\rangle^{C}=\langle b,\iota_n c'\rangle^{B}\) for all \(b\in B_n,\,c'\in C'_n\), and \(\langle\delta_n c,a'\rangle^{A}=\langle c,\varepsilon_{n+1}a'\rangle^{C}\) for all \(c\in C_n,\,a'\in A'_{n+1}\). Then \(\langle-,-\rangle^{A}_n\) is perfect for every \(n\).
lemma_dual_long_exact_sequences.proof:
We prove the statement as a theorem of pure linear algebra over the field $K$; no geometry is involved. All vector spaces that appear are finite-dimensional over $K$.

=== 0. Notation and elementary facts ===

For each $n\in\mathbb Z$ define the three $K$-linear "left-regular" maps
$$\alpha_n:A_n\to (A_n')^{*},\quad \alpha_n(a)(a')=\langle a,a'\rangle^{A},$$
$$\beta_n:B_n\to (B_n')^{*},\quad \beta_n(b)(b')=\langle b,b'\rangle^{B},$$
$$\gamma_n:C_n\to (C_n')^{*},\quad \gamma_n(c)(c')=\langle c,c'\rangle^{C}.$$
By hypothesis the $B$- and $C$-pairings are perfect, so $\beta_n$ and $\gamma_n$ are isomorphisms for every $n$. The theorem asserts that $\alpha_n$ is an isomorphism for every $n$; by the definition of perfectness for a bilinear pairing of finite-dimensional spaces, that is exactly the claim that $\langle-,-\rangle^{A}_n$ is perfect (non-degeneracy on both sides follows from $\alpha_n$ being an isomorphism: injectivity is left non-degeneracy, surjectivity gives that every functional on $A_n'$ is represented, which is right non-degeneracy, and $\dim A_n=\dim A_n'$ then forces $\dim A_n'=\dim A_n$).

We record two elementary facts that will be used repeatedly.

(F1) For a $K$-linear map $u:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional spaces, the transpose $u^{t}:W^{*}\to V^{*}$, $u^{t}(\Lambda)=\Lambda\circ u$, satisfies $\operatorname{im} u^{t}=\{\text{functionals on }V\text{ vanishing on }\ker u\}\cong (\operatorname{im}u)^{*}$; hence $\dim\operatorname{im} u^{t}=\dim\operatorname{im}u$. (Proof: $\ker u^{t}=\{\Lambda:\Lambda|_{\operatorname{im}u}=0\}$ has dimension $\dim W-\dim\operatorname{im}u$, so $\dim\operatorname{im}u^{t}=\dim W^{*}-(\dim W-\dim\operatorname{im}u)=\dim\operatorname{im}u$.)

(F2) If $p:V\twoheadrightarrow \overline V$ is a surjection and $T:\overline V\to X$ is linear, then $\ker(T\circ p)/\ker p\cong\ker T$ via $\bar v\mapsto T\bar v$; in particular $\dim\ker T=\dim\ker(T\circ p)-\dim\ker p$.

Exactness of the two long sequences gives, for every $n$, the following identities of subspaces, which we use without further comment:
\begin{align*}
&\ker f_n=\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1},\quad \ker g_n=\operatorname{im} f_n,\quad \ker\delta_n=\operatorname{im} g_n &&\text{(first sequence at }A_n,B_n,C_n),\\
&\ker\iota_n=\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_{n+1},\quad \ker\rho_n=\operatorname{im}\iota_n,\quad \ker\varepsilon_n=\operatorname{im}\rho_n &&\text{(second sequence at }C_n',B_n',A_n').
\end{align*}
In particular $\rho_n\iota_n=0$ and $\varepsilon_n\iota_{n-1}=0$.

Note on degrees (this is the point at which an earlier argument failed, so we state it explicitly): the third adjointness identity as hypothesised reads, at index $n-1$,
$$\langle \delta_{n-1}c,a'\rangle^{A}=\langle c,\varepsilon_{n}a'\rangle^{C}\qquad(c\in C_{n-1},\ a'\in A_n'),\tag{$*$}_{n}$$
which is the identity we shall actually apply: $\delta_{n-1}:C_{n-1}\to A_n$ is paired with $\varepsilon_n:A_n'\to C_{n-1}'$, and both are maps occurring in the given sequences at the correct degrees. The $A$-pairings used in all three adjointness identities are the ones supplied in the hypotheses; no additional pairing data is introduced anywhere in the proof.

=== 1. Surjectivity of $\alpha_n$ for every $n$ ===

Fix $n$ and let $\varphi\in (A_n')^{*}$ be arbitrary.

Step 1.1 (pull $\varphi$ back to $B_n'$). Define $\lambda:B_n'\to K$ by $\lambda(b')=\varphi(\rho_n b')$. This is $K$-linear as a composite of linear maps. Since $\beta_n$ is surjective there is a **unique** $b_0\in B_n$ with $\beta_n(b_0)=\lambda$, i.e.
$$\langle b_0,b'\rangle^{B}=\varphi(\rho_n b')\qquad\text{for all }b'\in B_n'.\tag{1}$$

Step 1.2 ($b_0$ dies in $C_n$). For any $c'\in C_n'$, using the second adjointness identity at $n$, then (1), then exactness at $B_n'$:
$$\langle g_nb_0,c'\rangle^{C}=\langle b_0,\iota_nc'\rangle^{B}=\varphi(\rho_n\iota_nc')=\varphi(0)=0.$$
Since $\gamma_n$ is injective (perfectness of the $C$-pairing), $g_nb_0=0$. By exactness at $B_n$, $\ker g_n=\operatorname{im} f_n$, so there exists $a\in A_n$ with $b_0=f_na$.

Step 1.3 ($a$ represents $\varphi$ on $\operatorname{im}\rho_n$). For all $b'\in B_n'$, using the first adjointness identity at $n$ and (1):
$$\langle a,\rho_nb'\rangle^{A}=\langle f_na,b'\rangle^{B}=\langle b_0,b'\rangle^{B}=\varphi(\rho_nb').$$
Thus the functional $\varphi-\alpha_n(a)$ vanishes on $\operatorname{im}\rho_n=\ker\varepsilon_n$.

Step 1.4 (descend to $\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n\subseteq C_{n-1}'$ and lift to $C_{n-1}$). Define $\psi:\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n\to K$ by $\psi(\varepsilon_na')=(\varphi-\alpha_n(a))(a')$. This is well defined: if $\varepsilon_na_1'=\varepsilon_na_2'$ then $a_1'-a_2'\in\ker\varepsilon_n=\operatorname{im}\rho_n$, say $a_1'-a_2'=\rho_nb_0'$, and then
$$(\varphi-\alpha_n(a))(a_1'-a_2')=\varphi(\rho_nb_0')-\langle a,\rho_nb_0'\rangle^{A}=0$$
by Step 1.3. Choose a $K$-subspace $T\subseteq C_{n-1}'$ complementary to $\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n$ (possible since $C_{n-1}'$ is finite-dimensional) and extend $\psi$ by $0$ on $T$, obtaining $\Psi\in (C_{n-1}')^{*}$ with $\Psi|_{\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n}=\psi$.
Since $\gamma_{n-1}$ is surjective, pick $c_0\in C_{n-1}$ with $\gamma_{n-1}(c_0)=\Psi$, i.e. $\langle c_0,c'\rangle^{C}=\Psi(c')$ for all $c'\in C_{n-1}'$.

Step 1.5 (conclude). For every $a'\in A_n'$, using $(*)_{n}$:
$$(\varphi-\alpha_n(a))(a')=\psi(\varepsilon_na')=\Psi(\varepsilon_na')=\langle c_0,\varepsilon_na'\rangle^{C}=\langle\delta_{n-1}c_0,a'\rangle^{A}=\alpha_n(\delta_{n-1}c_0)(a').$$
Hence $\varphi=\alpha_n(a+\delta_{n-1}c_0)$. As $\varphi$ was arbitrary, $\alpha_n$ is surjective. Since this holds for the arbitrary integer $n$, $\alpha_n$ is surjective for all $n$. $\square_{(1)}$

=== 2. Injectivity of $\alpha_n$ (dimension count) ===

Put $d_n:=\dim\operatorname{im}\delta_n$ and $e_n:=\dim\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z$; these are well-defined non-negative integers.

Step 2.1 ($\ker\alpha_n\subseteq\ker f_n$). Let $a\in\ker\alpha_n$. For every $b'\in B_n'$, the first adjointness identity gives $\langle f_na,b'\rangle^{B}=\langle a,\rho_nb'\rangle^{A}=0$. Since $\beta_n$ is surjective, every functional on $B_n'$ is of the form $b'\mapsto\langle x,b'\rangle^{B}$, so $f_na=0$. Thus
$$\ker\alpha_n\subseteq\ker f_n=\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}.\tag{2}$$
Consequently $\ker\alpha_n=\ker\bigl(\alpha_n|_{\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}}\bigr)$.

Step 2.2 (the composite $\alpha_n\delta_{n-1}$). Consider $\alpha_n\circ\delta_{n-1}:C_{n-1}\to (A_n')^{*}$. For $c\in C_{n-1}$, $a'\in A_n'$, using $(*)_{n}$,
$$(\alpha_n\delta_{n-1}c)(a')=\langle\delta_{n-1}c,a'\rangle^{A}=\langle c,\varepsilon_na'\rangle^{C}=(\varepsilon_n^{\,t}\gamma_{n-1}(c))(a'),$$
where $\varepsilon_n^{\,t}:(C_{n-1}')^{*}\to (A_n')^{*}$ is precomposition with $\varepsilon_n$. Hence
$$\alpha_n\circ\delta_{n-1}=\varepsilon_n^{\,t}\circ\gamma_{n-1}.\tag{3}$$
Since $\gamma_{n-1}$ is an isomorphism and, by (F1), $\dim\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n^{\,t}=\dim\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n=e_n$, we get
$$\dim\operatorname{im}(\alpha_n\delta_{n-1})=e_n.\tag{4}$$

Step 2.3 (dimension of $\ker\alpha_n$). View $\delta_{n-1}$ as a surjection $C_{n-1}\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}$; by (2) and (F2) applied to $p=\delta_{n-1}$ and $T=\alpha_n|_{\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}}$,
$$\dim\ker\alpha_n=\dim\ker(\alpha_n\delta_{n-1})-\dim\ker\delta_{n-1}=(\dim C_{n-1}-e_n)-(\dim C_{n-1}-d_{n-1}),$$
using (4) and $\dim\ker\delta_{n-1}=\dim C_{n-1}-\dim\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}=\dim C_{n-1}-d_{n-1}$. Therefore
$$\dim\ker\alpha_n=d_{n-1}-e_n.\tag{5}$$

Step 2.4 (first expression for $\dim B_n$). By exactness of the first sequence at $A_n,B_n,C_n$ and the rank--nullity theorem,
$$\dim B_n=\dim\ker g_n+\dim\operatorname{im} g_n=\dim\operatorname{im} f_n+\dim\ker\delta_n=(\dim A_n-\dim\ker f_n)+(\dim C_n-\dim\operatorname{im}\delta_n),$$
so with $\ker f_n=\operatorname{im}\delta_{n-1}$:
$$\dim B_n=(\dim A_n-d_{n-1})+(\dim C_n-d_n).\tag{6}$$

Step 2.5 (second expression for $\dim B_n'$). By exactness of the second sequence at $C_n',B_n',A_n'$,
$$\dim B_n'=\dim\ker\rho_n+\dim\operatorname{im}\rho_n=\dim\operatorname{im}\iota_n+\dim\ker\varepsilon_n.$$
Now $\dim\ker\varepsilon_n=\dim A_n'-\dim\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_n=\dim A_n'-e_n$, and $\dim\operatorname{im}\iota_n=\dim C_n'-\dim\ker\iota_n=\dim C_n'-\dim\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_{n+1}=\dim C_n'-e_{n+1}$, using exactness at $C_n'$ ($\ker\iota_n=\operatorname{im}\varepsilon_{n+1}$, where $\varepsilon_{n+1}:A_{n+1}'\to C_n'$). Hence
$$\dim B_n'=(\dim C_n'-e_{n+1})+(\dim A_n'-e_n).\tag{7}$$

Step 2.6 (compare). Because $\beta_n$ is an isomorphism, $\dim B_n=\dim B_n'$; because $\gamma_n$ is an isomorphism, $\dim C_n=\dim C_n'$. Because $\alpha_n$ is surjective (Step 1.5) and $\dim (A_n')^{*}=\dim A_n'$,
$$\dim A_n-\dim A_n'=\dim\ker\alpha_n=d_{n-1}-e_n\qquad\text{by }(5).\tag{8}$$
Equating (6) and (7) and cancelling the common $\dim C_n=\dim C_n'$ terms gives
$$(\dim A_n-\dim A_n')-d_{n-1}-d_n+e_{n+1}+e_n=0.$$
Substituting (8):
$$(d_{n-1}-e_n)-d_{n-1}-d_n+e_{n+1}+e_n=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_n=e_{n+1}.\tag{9}$$
This holds for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

Step 2.7 (conclude injectivity). Applying (9) at index $n-1$ gives $d_{n-1}=e_{n}$; inserting into (5) yields
$$\dim\ker\alpha_n=d_{n-1}-e_n=0.$$
So $\alpha_n$ is injective. $\square_{(2)}$

=== 3. Conclusion ===

By Steps 1 and 2, $\alpha_n:A_n\to (A_n')^{*}$ is a $K$-linear isomorphism for every $n\in\mathbb Z$. Unwinding the definition of $\alpha_n$, this says precisely: (i) if $a\in A_n$ satisfies $\langle a,a'\rangle^{A}=0$ for all $a'\in A_n'$ then $a=0$; and (ii) for every linear functional $\varphi$ on $A_n'$ there is $a\in A_n$ with $\varphi(a')=\langle a,a'\rangle^{A}$ for all $a'$, which in particular implies that $\langle a,a'\rangle^{A}=0$ for all $a\in A_n$ forces $a'=0$ (take $\varphi$ to be evaluation at $a'$). Hence $\langle-,-\rangle^{A}_n:A_n\times A_n'\to K$ is a perfect pairing for every $n$.

(We remark that no five-lemma type argument is used: injectivity is obtained from the dimension count of Steps 2.4--2.6, which is where the hypothesis that all spaces are finite-dimensional is needed; a five-lemma shortcut would be circular, since it would require $\alpha_{n\pm1}$ to be known isomorphisms beforehand. Surjectivity in Step 1, by contrast, uses only the surjectivity of $\beta_n$ and $\gamma_{n-1}$, not their injectivity. No symmetry or alternating property of the pairings is used anywhere.)

lemma_354.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective ample divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_q\) and smooth of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) be the closed immersion, let \(U=X\setminus Y\) and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). If \(i^*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every integer \(n<d-1\) and is injective for \(n=d-1\), then \(H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for every integer \(j<d\).
lemma_354.proof:
Apply lemma_283 to the data (q, X, Y, U, k, \ell). It gives a long exact sequence of finite-dimensional \mathbb{Q}_\ell-vector spaces

  \cdots \to H^{n-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^{n+1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to \cdots

We use the standard fact that etale cohomology and cohomology with compact supports vanish in negative degrees; equivalently the long exact sequence begins with
  0 \to H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \to H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell).

Let j be an integer with j<d. If j<0, then H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0 by negative-degree vanishing. Hence assume j\ge 0. Since d\ge 2, the hypothesis applies to n=0,1,\dots,d-1: i^* is an isomorphism for 0\le n<d-1 and injective for n=d-1.

Case j=0. The beginning of the long exact sequence identifies H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) with the kernel of i^*:H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\to H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell). By hypothesis this map is an isomorphism (because 0<d-1), hence its kernel is zero. Thus H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0.

Case 1\le j\le d-1. Consider the exact fragment
  H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{\delta} H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{\alpha} H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell).
Since j-1<d-1, the hypothesis says i^*:H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\to H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) is surjective. Exactness at H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) in the preceding fragment
  H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{i^*} H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) \xrightarrow{\delta} H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)
gives \ker(\delta)=\operatorname{im}(i^*)=H^{j-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell), so \delta=0.
Since j<d and j\ge 1, we have j\le d-1; if j<d-1 the hypothesis says i^*:H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)\to H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) is an isomorphism, and if j=d-1 it says this map is injective. In either case i^* is injective. Exactness at H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) gives \operatorname{im}(\alpha)=\ker(i^*)=0, hence \alpha=0.
Now exactness at H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell) gives \ker(\alpha)=\operatorname{im}(\delta). Since \alpha=0, \ker(\alpha)=H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell); since \delta=0, \operatorname{im}(\delta)=0. Hence H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0.

Combining the cases, H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb{Q}_\ell)=0 for every integer j<d.

lemma_primitive_middle_pairing_perfect.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the \(\ell\)-adic cycle class of \(H\), and let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\). Suppose \(L^{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\). Let \(\operatorname{tr}:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\) be the isomorphism with \(\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]\) for closed points \(z\in X\), and put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\). Then the bilinear form \(P^d\times P^d\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\), \((x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(x\cup y)\), is a perfect pairing.
lemma_primitive_middle_pairing_perfect.proof:
Proof. Write H^n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) and define B(u,v)=tr(u cup v), where tr:H^{2d}->Q_l(-d) is the trace in the statement. All cohomology groups are Q_l-vector spaces.

Step 1: finite-dimensionality. Since X is smooth projective over F_q, it is proper. By lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant Q_l-sheaf on X_k, each H^n is finite-dimensional over Q_l.

Step 2: the ambient perfect pairing. By lemma_77 with m=1, there is a canonical trace tr_0:H^{2d}->Q_l(-d), normalised by tr_0(cl(z))=[kappa(z):F_q] for every closed point z of X, and the pairing (u,v)->tr_0(u cup v) on H^d x H^d is perfect. The trace tr in the statement has the same normalisation. This normalisation determines tr uniquely: lemma_77(a) makes H^{2d} one-dimensional, and for any closed point z, tr_0(cl(z)) is a positive integer, hence nonzero in Q_l, so cl(z) spans H^{2d}. Therefore tr=tr_0, and B is perfect on H^d x H^d.

Step 3: Lefschetz decomposition. Set V_n=H^n. For a smooth projective variety of pure dimension d, one has V_n=0 for n<0 and for n>2d (the usual cohomological dimension bound for smooth projective varieties). The endomorphism L=cup xi raises degree by 2, since xi lies in H^2. The hypothesis says that L^{d-m}:V_m->V_{2d-m} is an isomorphism for every 0<=m<=d. Apply lemma_316 with K=Q_l. For n=d it gives an isomorphism from the direct sum of the spaces P^{d-2r} (r>=0, with P^m=0 for m<0) to V_d, where P^m=ker(L^{d-m+1}:V_m->V_{2d-m+2}). Thus H^d is the direct sum of the subspaces W_r=L^r P^{d-2r}, r=0,...,floor(d/2). For m=d this kernel is ker(L:H^d->H^{d+2}), exactly the primitive piece P^d in the statement.

Step 4: orthogonality of the Lefschetz summands. The class xi has degree 2, hence is even. For homogeneous a,b and t>=0 such that deg(a)+deg(b)+2t=2d, associativity of the cup product, graded commutativity (with no sign because deg(xi)=2), and Q_l-linearity of tr give
B(L^t a,b)=tr(xi^t cup a cup b)=tr(a cup xi^t cup b)=B(a,L^t b).

Take r>s>=0, x0 in P^{d-2r}, and y0 in P^{d-2s}. By definition of P^{d-2s}, we have L^{2s+1}y0=0. Since r>s, we have r+s>=2s+1, hence L^{r+s}y0=0. Using the identity above with t=r, a=x0, and b=L^s y0, we get
B(L^r x0,L^s y0)=B(x0,L^{r+s}y0)=0.
Using the same identity with t=r, a=L^s y0, and b=x0, we get
B(L^s y0,L^r x0)=B(L^{r+s}y0,x0)=0.
If s>r, interchange the roles of r and s. Hence B(W_r,W_s)=0 for all r!=s.

Step 5: restriction to P^d is perfect. Let V=H^d. The perfect pairing B on V is orthogonal for the direct-sum decomposition V=direct sum W_r. Fix i and let v in W_i satisfy B(v,w)=0 for every w in W_i. For any u in V, write u=sum_j w_j with w_j in W_j. Then
B(v,u)=sum_j B(v,w_j)=0,
because terms with j!=i vanish by orthogonality and the term with j=i vanishes by assumption. Perfectness of B on V implies v=0. Thus the left radical of B restricted to W_i is zero. Since W_i is finite-dimensional, the map W_i -> Hom_{Q_l}(W_i,Q_l(-d)) is injective between vector spaces of the same finite dimension, hence an isomorphism. Therefore B restricted to W_i x W_i is perfect. Taking i=0 gives W_0=P^d, so the pairing P^d x P^d -> Q_l(-d), (x,y)->tr(x cup y), is perfect. QED.

lemma_hard_lefschetz_curve.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(H\) be a very ample divisor on \(C\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(H\) obtained from a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\). Then cup product with \(\xi\), \(L:H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.
lemma_hard_lefschetz_curve.proof:
Throughout, write H^n := H^n_et(C_k, Q_\ell) and put d := dim C = 1. Since C is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over F_q, the base change C_k is smooth (hence regular, hence locally integral), projective and connected over the algebraically closed field k; being locally noetherian, connected and having all local rings domains, C_k is integral (Stacks-Project-type characterisation: a connected locally noetherian scheme all of whose local rings are domains is integral). In particular C_k is non-empty and reduced, and every non-zero rational function/section argument below takes place on an integral curve.

STEP 1: H^0 = Q_\ell \cdot 1. For each n >= 1 the constant sheaf Z/\ell^n has global sections the locally constant functions on C_k with values in the discrete set Z/\ell^n; since C_k is connected these are exactly the constant functions, so H^0(C_k, Z/\ell^n) = \Gamma(C_k, \underline{Z/\ell^n}) \cong Z/\ell^n, and the transition map for n' > n is the natural reduction Z/\ell^{n'} \twoheadrightarrow Z/\ell^n. Global sections commute with inverse limits of sheaves, hence \varprojlim_n H^0(C_k, Z/\ell^n) \cong Z_\ell, and by the definition of degree-0 \ell-adic cohomology, H^0 = (\varprojlim_n H^0(C_k, Z/\ell^n)) \otimes_{Z_\ell} Q_\ell \cong Q_\ell. The generator 1 \in H^0 is the constant function 1, which is the multiplicative unit of the graded-commutative cohomology ring, so 1 \cup y = y for every y \in H^2.

STEP 2: H^2 is one-dimensional and the trace is an isomorphism. Apply eoinm/lemma_77 with m = 1, Y = C and d = 1. Part (a) gives a Q_\ell-linear isomorphism (the Poincar\'e duality trace)
   tr : H^2 \xrightarrow{\sim} Q_\ell(-1)
which is normalised on closed points by tr(cl_ref(x)) = [\kappa(x) : \mathbb F_q], where cl_ref denotes the class in H^2 of a closed point x \in C obtained from the \ell-adic cycle class in H^2(C_k, Q_\ell(1)) by tensoring with the chosen trivialising element of Q_\ell(1) used in that lemma. (This is the same convention as in Spark/lemma_314, which for a closed integral subscheme Z_0 \subseteq C of pure codimension 1 defines cl(Z) \in H^2 as the unique vector whose tensor with the fixed non-zero element of Q_\ell(1) is the \ell-adic cycle class of Z in H^2(C_k, Q_\ell(1)).) Since Q_\ell(-1) is a one-dimensional Q_\ell-vector space, tr being an isomorphism shows
   dim_{Q_\ell} H^2 = 1.                                    (2.1)
(Part (b) of lemma_77, the perfectness of (x,y) \mapsto tr(x \cup y) on H^0 \times H^2, is the equivalent formulation; we only need the isomorphism (a).)

STEP 3: the class \xi is non-zero. Let us first record that deg H > 0. By hypothesis \mathcal L := \mathcal O_C(H) is very ample; in particular \mathcal L is ample and globally generated, and it defines a closed immersion C \hookrightarrow \mathbb P^r (with r = h^0(\mathcal L)-1 >= 1, since a closed immersion preserves dimension and dim C = 1). Choose a non-zero section s \in H^0(C, \mathcal L); it exists because \mathcal L is globally generated and C \neq \emptyset. As C is integral, the vanishing locus V(s) is an effective Cartier divisor D = \sum_{i=1}^{t} n_i z_i (n_i >= 1, the z_i distinct closed points of C), and the section s identifies \mathcal O_C(D) with \mathcal L = \mathcal O_C(H); thus D and H are linearly equivalent. For a closed point z of the regular curve C one has \mathcal O_C(z)/\mathcal O_C \cong \kappa(z), an \mathbb F_q-vector space of dimension [\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q], so additivity of the Euler characteristic gives deg \mathcal O_C(D) = \sum_i n_i [\kappa(z_i):\mathbb F_q] =: deg D >= 0. Hence deg \mathcal L = deg \mathcal O_C(D) >= 0. If deg \mathcal L = 0 then D = 0, i.e. s is nowhere vanishing, which makes \mathcal L trivial; but \mathcal O_C would then be ample, and for a proper scheme over a field O_X is ample if and only if X is finite over the base, which would force dim C = 0, a contradiction (dim C = 1). Therefore
   deg H = deg \mathcal L = deg D = \sum_{i=1}^{t} n_i [\kappa(z_i):\mathbb F_q] \in \mathbb Z_{>0}.        (3.1)

The cycle-class map on codimension-1 cycles is, by construction, the additive extension of the Gysin classes of closed integral subschemes: cl_ref(\sum_i n_i z_i) = \sum_i n_i cl_ref(z_i); and it factors through rational equivalence, so linearly equivalent divisors have the same class. Consequently
   cl_ref(H) = cl_ref(D) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} n_i\, cl_ref(z_i).
By the normalisation of the trace from Step 2 and the Q_\ell-linearity of tr,
   tr(cl_ref(H)) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} n_i\, [\kappa(z_i):\mathbb F_q] = deg H,
viewed inside Q_\ell(-1) as the integer deg H times the fixed non-zero element of Q_\ell(-1) determined by the chosen trivialisation of Q_\ell(1).

The class \xi in the statement is obtained from the same \mathbb Q_\ell(1)-valued cycle class of H by tensoring with the fixed non-zero element \eta of Q_\ell(1) specified in the statement. The only possible discrepancy with the convention of lemma_77 is the choice of trivialising element of Q_\ell(1); the two choices differ by a fixed scalar \lambda \in Q_\ell^{\times} (the ratio of the two chosen elements), independently of the cycle. Hence \xi = \lambda \cdot cl_ref(H), and
   tr(\xi) = \lambda \cdot (deg H) \cdot e,
where e \in Q_\ell(-1) is the non-zero element determined by the chosen trivialisation. Since \mathbb Q_\ell has characteristic 0, the non-zero integer deg H of (3.1) maps to a non-zero element of Q_\ell; as \lambda \neq 0 and e \neq 0 we obtain tr(\xi) \neq 0, and therefore
   \xi \neq 0 \in H^2.                                          (3.2)

STEP 4: L is an isomorphism. The map L : H^0 \to H^2 is Q_\ell-linear (cup product is Q_\ell-bilinear) and, by the unit property of 1 \in H^0,
   L(1) = 1 \cup \xi = \xi.
Injectivity: ker L is a Q_\ell-subspace of the one-dimensional space H^0 = Q_\ell \cdot 1; since 1 \notin ker L (L(1) = \xi \neq 0 by (3.2)), the only subspace of H^0 not containing 1 is 0, so ker L = 0.
Surjectivity: im L = Q_\ell \cdot \xi is a non-zero subspace of the one-dimensional space H^2 by (2.1), hence im L = H^2.
Thus L is a Q_\ell-linear bijection, i.e. an isomorphism of Q_\ell-vector spaces.

(For completeness: the same argument shows more generally that for any divisor H of non-zero degree on a smooth projective geometrically connected curve, cup product with its cycle class identifies H^0 with H^2; the hypothesis that H is very ample is used only to guarantee deg H > 0 and effectivity up to linear equivalence.)

lemma_351.statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(H\) be an effective ample divisor on \(C\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the vector whose tensor with a fixed nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) is the \(\ell\)-adic cycle class of \(H\). Then cup product with \(\xi\) is a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
lemma_351.proof:
Notation. Write $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$, and write $H^i:=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ and $H^i(s):=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(s))$. Let $\eta\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ be the fixed nonzero element occurring in the statement; by definition of $\xi$ (the same convention as in Spark/lemma_314 with $j=1$, namely that $\mathrm{cl}(Z)$ denotes the unique vector whose tensor with the fixed nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is the $\ell$-adic cycle class of $Z$) one has
\[\xi\otimes\eta=\mathrm{cl}(H)\in H^2(1).\]
Since $C$ is geometrically connected of pure dimension $1$, $C_k$ is smooth, projective, connected and of pure dimension $1$ over $k$; in particular $C_k\neq\varnothing$ (every irreducible component has dimension $1$).

STEP 1 (the type-correct trace on the TWISTED group, and its value on point classes). We use Spark/lemma_gysin_trace_compatibility with the algebraically closed field $k$, with $d=1$, with $X=C_k$, and with $Y=\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $i_y:\operatorname{Spec}k\hookrightarrow C_k$ the closed immersion attached to a $k$-rational point $y$ of $C_k$. We check the hypotheses:
(i) $X=C_k$ is smooth, projective and geometrically connected of pure dimension $1=d$ over $k$ (base change of the corresponding properties of $C$).
(ii) $Y=\operatorname{Spec}k$ is integral, separated and of finite type over $k$, smooth (the identity morphism), projective ($\operatorname{Spec}k=\mathbb P^0_k$), geometrically connected (one point), of pure dimension $0=d-1$.
(iii) $i_y$ is a regular closed immersion of pure codimension $1$: $\mathcal O_{C_k,y}$ is the local ring of a smooth $1$-dimensional $k$-scheme at a closed point, hence a regular local ring of dimension $1$, i.e. a DVR; its maximal ideal is generated by a uniformiser, which is a non-zero-divisor, so the ideal sheaf of $\{y\}$ is locally generated by a single non-zero-divisor.
Existence of such a $y$: $C_k$ is nonempty, hence has a closed point (finite type over a field); for a finite type scheme over the algebraically closed field $k$, the residue field at a closed point is a finite algebraic extension of $k$ (Zariski's lemma), hence equals $k$, so every closed point of $C_k$ is $k$-rational.

The lemma then supplies the Poincar\'e duality trace isomorphisms
\[\operatorname{tr}_X:H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell(1))\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}_Y:H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell(0))\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell,\]
both $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, such that $\operatorname{tr}_X(i_{y,*}\alpha)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(\alpha)$ for every $\alpha\in H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\mathbb Q_\ell$. Note that all terms are type-correct: $\operatorname{tr}_X$ is the trace on the TWISTED group $H^{2\dim X}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(\dim X))$, and no identification of $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)$ with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ or $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is made anywhere.

Computation of $\operatorname{tr}_Y$: $\operatorname{Spec}k$ has exactly one closed point $z$, with $\kappa(z)=k$. The normalisation clause of Spark/lemma_gysin_trace_compatibility gives $\operatorname{tr}_Y(\mathrm{cl}_Y(z))=[\kappa(z):k]=[k:k]=1$. Here $\mathrm{cl}_Y(z)\in H^0(\operatorname{Spec}k,\mathbb Q_\ell(0))=\mathbb Q_\ell$ is the class of the fundamental $0$-cycle $[Y]=1\cdot[z]$, which is the unit $1$ of the cohomology ring (the cycle class of the fundamental class of a smooth variety is the unit in degree $0$). Since $\operatorname{tr}_Y$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear and $\operatorname{tr}_Y(1)=1$, $\operatorname{tr}_Y=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}$.

Value of $i_{y,*}$ on $1$: for a regular closed immersion $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ of pure codimension $c$, the Gysin map is the composition $H^a(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(b))\to H^{a+2c}_Z(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(b+c))\to H^{a+2c}(X,\mathbb Q_\ell(b+c))$ (localisation sequence with support), and the cycle class $\mathrm{cl}_X(Z)$ is BY DEFINITION the image of $1\in H^0(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell(0))$ under this composition (equivalently $c_1(\mathcal O_X(Z))\cup 1$). Hence $i_{y,*}(1)=\mathrm{cl}(y)$, the cycle class of the closed point $y$ in $H^2(1)$.

Taking $\alpha=1$ we obtain the normalisation
\[(\mathrm N)\qquad \operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(y))=\operatorname{tr}_Y(1)=1\]
for the point $y$ used. The map $\operatorname{tr}_X$ is the canonical Poincar\'e duality trace of $X=C_k$ appearing in the statement of Spark/lemma_gysin_trace_compatibility; it depends only on $X$, not on the chosen immersion. Repeating the argument with any other $k$-rational closed point in place of $y$ therefore gives the same $\operatorname{tr}_X$, so $(\mathrm N)$ holds for EVERY $k$-rational closed point of $C_k$, i.e. for every closed point of $C_k$.

STEP 2 (the degree functional on the untwisted group). The twist $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is a free $\mathbb Q_\ell$-module of rank $1$, and $\eta\neq0$, so $\{\eta\}$ is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-basis of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$. Hence
\[\theta:H^2\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ H^2\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ H^2(1),\qquad v\longmapsto v\otimes\eta,\]
is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism (the second map is the standard identification of cohomology with the constant rank-one coefficient system $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ with the twist of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-cohomology). Define
\[\tau:H^2\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad \tau(v):=\operatorname{tr}_X(v\otimes\eta)=\operatorname{tr}_X(\theta(v)).\]
This is a well-defined $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map, being the composition of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear maps. In particular, for every $0$-cycle class $w\in H^2(1)$ there is a unique vector $c\in H^2$ with $c\otimes\eta=w$, and $\tau(c)=\operatorname{tr}_X(w)$.

STEP 3 (decomposition of $H$ into closed points of $C$). Since $H$ is an effective Cartier divisor on the smooth curve $C$, it has an associated $0$-cycle $\sum_z n_z\,z$, where $z$ runs over the closed points of $C$, $n_z=\operatorname{ord}_z(H)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and $n_z=0$ for all but finitely many $z$. Base change to $k$ gives the effective Cartier divisor $H_k$ on $C_k$ with associated cycle $\sum_z n_z\,[z_k]$, where $[z_k]$ is the fundamental cycle of the $0$-dimensional scheme $z_k:=z\times_{\mathbb F_q}k$. The cycle class map on codimension-$1$ cycles of the smooth scheme $C_k$ is a group homomorphism $Z^1(C_k)\to H^2(1)$ (it is defined on the free abelian group on integral codimension-$1$ subschemes), and the class of an effective Cartier divisor on a smooth variety equals the class of its associated cycle. By additivity,
\[\mathrm{cl}(H)=\mathrm{cl}(H_k)=\sum_{z} n_z\,\mathrm{cl}(z_k),\qquad \mathrm{cl}(z_k):=\mathrm{cl}([z_k]).\]

STEP 4 (a closed point of degree $n$ splits into $n$ distinct $k$-points). Fix a closed point $z$ of $C$ and put $n:=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$. Since $C$ is of finite type over $\mathbb F_q$, $\kappa(z)$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb F_q$, hence $\kappa(z)\simeq\mathbb F_{q^{n}}$; it is separable over $\mathbb F_q$ because finite fields are perfect. Choose an $\mathbb F_q$-isomorphism $\kappa(z)\simeq\mathbb F_{q^n}$; then $\mathbb F_{q^n}=\mathbb F_q(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha$ whose minimal polynomial $f\in\mathbb F_q[T]$ is separable of degree $n$ and splits in $k$ as $f=\prod_{j=1}^{n}(T-\alpha_j)$ with the $\alpha_j\in k$ pairwise distinct. The Chinese remainder theorem gives
\[k\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}\kappa(z)\ \simeq\ k[T]/(f)\ \simeq\ \prod_{j=1}^{n} k[T]/(T-\alpha_j)\ \simeq\ k^{n},\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto\bigl(a\,\sigma_1(b),\dots,a\,\sigma_n(b)\bigr),\]
where $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n:\kappa(z)\hookrightarrow k$ are the $n$ distinct $\mathbb F_q$-embeddings. Hence
\[z_k=\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(k\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}\kappa(z)\bigr)\ \simeq\ \coprod_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Spec}k,\]
a disjoint union of $n$ distinct $k$-rational closed points $y_1,\dots,y_n$ of $C_k$. The ring $k^{n}$ is reduced and each factor is a field, so each local ring of $z_k$ is $k$ and the fundamental cycle of $z_k$ is $[z_k]=\sum_{j=1}^{n}1\cdot y_j$ (each multiplicity is exactly $1$). By additivity of the cycle class map and by $(\mathrm N)$,
\[\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(z_k))=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{tr}_X(\mathrm{cl}(y_j))=\sum_{j=1}^{n}1=n=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q].\]
Let $c_z\in H^2$ be the unique vector with $c_z\otimes\eta=\mathrm{cl}(z_k)$ (Step 2). Then $\tau(c_z)=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q]$.

STEP 5 (evaluation of $\tau$ on $\xi$). Define the degree of the effective divisor $H$ in the standard way,
